title: Unreleased cpaic has no QBA interface beyond box-bounded drift
text:
Statement
cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9); it is not on CRAN and a reader cannot install it. Its bridge_fragility() is stronger than the entry described: for each posterior draw it computes the absolute distance between the contrast and the decision threshold divided by the sum of the absolute component loadings, which is the smallest common absolute bound under which some component-specific drift vector could push a link-scale contrast to the decision boundary, so it is an adversarial worst case over an L-infinity box rather than a same-sign uniform scalar drift or a one-dimensional slice, and no correlated same-bound main-effect vector can reverse a draw it labels robust. What it does not cover is unequal component-specific bounds, a stochastic dependence model, component-by-modifier drift, omitted target variables, outcome measurement and censoring bias, joint bias interactions and marginal natural-scale standardization, and the package exports no qba() interface.

title: Unreleased cpaic has no QBA interface beyond box-bounded drift
text:
Why it is open
The fragility number is a single common bound on absolute component main-effect drift, so it says nothing about drift that is unequal across components, about component-by-modifier drift, or about omitted variables and measurement and censoring bias, any of which can reverse a decision the diagnostic reports as robust. It is computed on the link scale, so under non-collapsibility it does not translate into the marginal natural-scale effects that drive decisions. Extending it requires specifying a drift dependence structure and integrating over the target distribution, which multiplies both the elicitation burden and the computation. The result object it would need involves design decisions nobody has fixed, such as what counts as a feasible scenario, how to summarize a decision-reversal surface and what attribution rule assigns dominance to a bias layer, so QBA remains bespoke scripting whose assumptions are invisible to reviewers.

text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the fragility diagnostic from a single common bound to unequal component-specific bounds and an explicit dependence or covariance model, and add component-by-modifier drift, omitted target variables and measurement and censoring bias, reporting fragility on the marginal natural outcome scale as well as the link scale. Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “cpaic covers only uniform bridge drift and has no QBA interface” The title says the package covers only uniform bridge drift and implies an installable release, but its fragility measure is an adversarial worst case over a box of component-specific drift vectors.
The source said. “The cpaic package’s bridge_fragility() computes the smallest uniform per-component main-effect drift that would move a link-scale contrast across a decision threshold, and covers nothing else: no component-specific or correlated drift, no component-by-modifier drift, no omitted target variables, no outcome measurement or censoring bias, no nonlinearity of marginal natural-scale effects and no joint bias interactions. C9 is mathematically unsafe: a grid fraction is not a probability without a prespecified measure over the sensitivity region and changes with grid design. C10 is a roadmap characterization rather than a technical result. The broader QBA interface remains open, but the current fragility method is materially stronger than the report’s one-dimensional characterization.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text: QBA-19 Unverifiable Very high priority Emerging

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Statement
A Bayesian latent-U or fully joint QBA can conceal nonidentification: if the likelihood is flat in a sensitivity parameter and the prior factorizes, that parameter’s posterior equals its prior while the causal contrast derived from it stays prior-driven and looks fully probabilistic, and convergence diagnostics assess computation rather than identification. Soutar et al. 2025 (doi:10.1186/s12874-025-02551-z) avoid the fully joint construction for this reason, using a two-step data-augmentation design with user-specified sensitivity parameters and warning that fully Bayesian approaches, if not correctly performed, may result in estimation issues such as non-identifiability. Part of the diagnostic infrastructure the entry asks for already exists: cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) plots priors against posteriors and refits under tighter and looser priors to show which contrasts move, but these are generic cML-NMR diagnostics rather than a latent-U QBA module, and it offers no cut feedback or formal prior classes.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Why it is open
A nonidentified sensitivity parameter under a proper prior produces a finite, smooth, apparently well-behaved posterior that standard output cannot distinguish from an identified quantity, and no amount of sampler diagnostics changes that. Feedback from the outcome likelihood can update a clinically elicited sensitivity distribution that was never meant to be learned from the data, and where an external module is deliberately insulated or thought misspecified there is no modular fitting route in the ML-NMR software stack to prevent it. The diagnostics that do exist are generic parameter-level displays rather than a sensitivity module that labels parameters as identified, partially identified or nonidentified and shows how the causal conclusion depends on the prior class, and latent-U augmentation is computationally demanding on top of that.

Confirms the one-stage gap: QBA could be adapted for ML-UMR by incorporating bias parameters or simulated unmeasured covariates into the outcome regression and standardization steps, which means it has not yet been done.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build a prior-transparent sensitivity module on top of the prior-movement diagnostics that already exist, labeling parameters as identified, partially identified or nonidentified and reporting how far the causal contrast moves across a class of defensible priors rather than under one arbitrary choice. Offer modular or cut-feedback fitting as an option justified by an explicit modular argument rather than as a default, since a fully coherent joint fit is legitimate when the joint likelihood is what the analyst intends. Report deterministic parameter grids alongside the posterior mixture and cross-check the result against bias-function and partial-identification analyses of the same model.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “A one-stage Bayesian ML-UMR model can introduce a latent omitted variable with priors for its prevalence, source association, outcome association and treatment interaction, and a fully joint Bayesian QBA can specify observed-data, validation, target-distribution and sensitivity models together. In both cases the likelihood contains little or no information about the sensitivity parameters, so the posterior for the causal contrast can be prior-driven while appearing fully probabilistic.”
What was wrong with it. The auditors disagreed with evidence on both sides. GPT-5.6 Sol read cpaic at commit 9d150e9 and found prior-to-posterior plotting and prior-sensitivity refitting already implemented, so the claim that no PAIC software displays prior movement is false there; it also rejected modular or cut feedback as a requirement, since full feedback is coherent when the joint likelihood is scientifically intended and cut feedback breaks ordinary Bayesian coherence, and noted that a proper prior guarantees a proper posterior only when the marginal likelihood is finite and positive. The literature auditor kept the entry open and confirmed the one-stage gap from the ML-UMR paper (arXiv:2606.20341), whose authors say QBA could be adapted for ML-UMR, meaning it has not been.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): The central warning is correct under the intended nonidentified latent-U model. If the likelihood is flat in a sensitivity parameter and the prior factorizes, that parameter’s posterior equals its prior, while a derived causal contrast can remain prior-driven. C1, C2, C7, and the transparency objectives in C3 and C8 are therefore sound with model-specific qualifications. A proper prior does not literally always guarantee a proper posterior without a finite, positive marginal likelihood, although it does in the usual bounded-likelihood setup. Convergence diagnostics assess computation, not identification. C4 and C9 are false as requirements: full feedback is coherent when the stated joint likelihood is scientifically intended. Cut feedback is useful when an external module is deliberately insulated or thought misspecified, but it breaks ordinary joint Bayesian coherence and is redundant when the likelihood truly contains no information. C5 describes plausible flexibility rather than a guarantee. C6 should supplement, not replace, a justified primary prior; power scaling also does not address every structural sensitivity. C10 is too broad. At the requested cpaic snapshot, plot_prior_posterior() displays prior-to-posterior movement and prior_sensitivity() refits tighter and looser priors. These are not latent-U QBA diagnostics and do not provide cut feedback or formal prior classes, so the core module remains open but part of the requested diagnostic infrastructure already exists.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Retrieved Soutar et al. 2025 (PMC12066054). It is correctly described: Bayesian data augmentation treating the unmeasured confounder as missing data, imputed under user-specified exposure and outcome associations, with a dRMST estimand valid under proportional-hazards violation. Notably its authors deliberately avoid the fully joint construction the entry criticises, warning that fully Bayesian approaches ‘if not correctly performed may result in estimation issues such as non-identifiability’ and using a two-step design with only ‘user-specified sensitivity parameters’. That is a primary source corroborating claims 1, 2, 4 and 7. Claim 10 (‘No PAIC software currently labels nonidentified parameters, displays prior-to-posterior movement, or supports prior classes and cut-feedback’) is a no-feature-exists claim; multinma has no such interface as far as I could establish, but I did not read the source and treat it as unverified. Claim 3 and claims 5, 6, 8, 9 are normative design requirements. The ML-UMR paper (arXiv 2606.20341) confirms the gap on the one-stage side, stating QBA ‘could be adapted for ML-UMR by incorporating bias parameters or simulated unmeasured covariates’, i.e. it has not been.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text: QBA-17 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Statement
When no single probability distribution over the bias parameters is defensible, reporting the set of effects compatible with a justified assumption set plus the decisions that survive across it is an honest option, though not the uniquely honest one, since arbitrarily narrow bounds mislead as readily as an arbitrary prior. The identified set must be distinguished from a sampling or posterior interval, while a confidence region for an identified set may legitimately carry nominal coverage, and a set alone is not a robust decision region, which additionally requires a threshold or loss function. Set-based decision rules (minimax, minimax regret, dominance, robust Bayes) are already well developed in the statistical decision-theory literature, so the gap is PAIC-specific: no PAIC package the auditors could inspect returns identified sets or robust decision regions, and HTA appraisal practice, built around a point estimate and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, has no established procedure for acting on one.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Why it is open
The honesty of the approach is purchased by shifting the burden from an untestable point assumption to an untestable range, and clinicians have little experience specifying the magnitude of a bias parameter, so the bounds require clinically defensible constraints that nobody has codified for PAIC estimands. There is no accepted criterion for how wide a stress-test range should be, so width becomes another analyst degree of freedom, and a set wide enough to be honest can be vacuous. Appraisal processes are built around a point estimate and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio and provide no procedure for acting on an identified set, so honest wide ranges that span the decision threshold are experienced as uninformative and create direct pressure to narrow ranges without new evidence. Current PAIC software returns point estimates and intervals, so producing bounds requires bespoke code and the honest analysis is also the hardest one to produce.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
What has been tried
No prior work is identified for this problem in the reviewed sources.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Instantiate the decision rules that already exist, minimax, minimax regret, dominance and robust Bayes, on PAIC estimands rather than developing decision theory from scratch; the missing pieces are clinically defensible restrictions for these estimands and a set-valued output object in reference PAIC software. Standardize how a stress-test range is constructed so its width is justified by an evidence hierarchy rather than chosen, and report the identified set separately from any confidence region for it. Translate bounds into decision tipping surfaces so they remain usable for reimbursement, and calibrate sensitivity parameters against measured covariates where that is possible.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “For high-stakes unanchored comparisons, disconnected bridges and settings where evidence about bias parameters is weak, the defensible output is the set of effects compatible with bounded assumptions or prior neighborhoods plus a robust decision region, not a single selected estimate. Partial identification is currently dismissed for not returning one number, and no PAIC software has any representation for a set.”
What was wrong with it. The literature auditor found the claim that HTA decision rules provide no procedure for acting on an identified set too strong as a statement about decision theory, since minimax-regret and related rules for treatment choice under partial identification are well developed in econometrics; it is defensible only about appraisal practice. GPT-5.6 Sol added that partial identification is an honest option rather than the uniquely honest one, that its practical difficulties go well beyond producing a range (choosing defensible restrictions, vacuous sets, sampling uncertainty, computation, mapping effects to losses), and that a set and a robust decision region are different outputs.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The entry cites nothing, and that is its weakness rather than its substance. Claims 1, 2, 4, 8, 11 are definitional statements about partial identification and are correct. Claims 13 and 14 (no PAIC software returns identified sets; HTA decision rules provide no procedure for acting on one) are no-method-exists assertions I could not falsify: I checked multinma, maicplus, drMAIC, outstandR and gemtc documentation surfaces and found only point estimates with intervals. However, a large and directly applicable statistical-decision-theory literature on acting under partial identification exists and is not acknowledged: minimax-regret and mean-square-regret optimal treatment choice under an identified set, and optimal decision rules under partial identification, are well developed in econometrics. Claim 14 as written (‘provide no procedure for acting on an uninformative identified set’) is therefore too strong as a statement about decision theory; it is defensible only as a statement about HTA appraisal practice. The genuinely open work is instantiating those decision rules on PAIC estimands with clinically defensible bounds and set-valued software output.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, C2, C4, C8, and the narrow reading of C12 are correct. Partial identification returns values compatible with stated restrictions, and the identified set is not itself a probabilistic interval. C3 is generally true as a practical observation. C5 should call partial identification an honest option, not the uniquely honest option; arbitrary narrow bounds can be as misleading as an arbitrary prior. C6 understates the practical difficulties, which also include choosing defensible restrictions, vacuous sets, sampling uncertainty, computation, and mapping effects to losses. C7 and C9 are recommendations rather than technical necessities, and ranges should be justified rather than merely made deliberately wide. C10 should say can produce false precision: a diffuse or robust probabilistic model can instead be appropriately imprecise. C11 conflates outputs because partial identification yields a set, while a robust decision region additionally requires a decision threshold or loss function. C13 is a universal software claim not established here. C14 is false as a general technical claim: minimax, minimax-regret, dominance, and robust-Bayes rules can act on sets or prior classes. Whether particular HTA institutions operationalize those rules is a separate empirical question. The very-high severity applies when an unidentified point estimate is presented as identified, not simply because a method declines to return one number.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text: QBA-15 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Statement
Multiple omitted variables need a joint sensitivity specification whenever their dependence can affect the bias, and each may require its source and target distribution, its outcome association under each treatment, and its dependence with measured covariates and with the other omitted variables; the entry’s five-quantity list double-counts, since source and target joint distributions determine the association with study membership and treatment-specific coefficients already encode effect modification. The two usual escapes are unvalidated here: independent variation can understate joint extremes when bias contributions are positively dependent and directionally aligned, though it can overstate them under negative dependence, and a scalar composite U is exact only when it is a sufficient index for selection and for every treatment-specific outcome regression, which nobody has characterized for unanchored PAIC. Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) handle several omitted covariates and flag the problem their own elicitation route creates, noting that eliciting a distribution for each separately would ignore the correlation structure between them.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Why it is open
None of the parameters is identified by the data, so the specification burden grows with the number of omitted variables while no compensating information arrives, and a tensor grid over p axes at k levels needs k to the power p evaluations, which makes joint deterministic exploration expensive. Independence is assumed because independent priors and independent grid axes are convenient to specify and sample, but the decision-relevant region is often the tail where several parameters are jointly extreme and aligned, which is exactly what independence suppresses. Whether a scalar composite is conservative depends on whether it is a sufficient index for the selection and treatment-specific outcome models, and no accepted parameterization for dependence among several omitted variables exists in a population-adjustment setting.

Handles more than one omitted covariate and flags the dependence problem its own elicitation route creates: eliciting a distribution for each unmeasured quantity separately would ignore the correlation structure between them, pointing readers to multivariate elicitation methods.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop copula, latent-factor and robust moment-set specifications so dependence can be varied as part of the sensitivity region, and characterize the conditions under which a single composite index is sufficient rather than assuming the reduction is conservative. Require every QBA to state a non-redundant parameter set per omitted variable together with the assumed dependence, using treatment-specific outcome coefficients where interaction is in play and a common coefficient only under an explicit no-interaction assumption. Report how the tail of the joint distribution moves when independence is relaxed in both directions, since dependence can widen or narrow the decision-relevant region.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Each omitted variable requires at least five quantities (its source and target distribution, its association with study membership, its outcome association under each treatment, its treatment-effect modification, and its dependence with measured covariates and with other omitted variables), so a high-dimensional collection of omitted variables produces a sensitivity-parameter explosion. Varying each variable independently and collapsing everything into one composite U are the two usual escapes, and neither has been validated.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol found several claims too broad: the five quantities double-count, specifying a common outcome coefficient is sufficient under an explicit no-interaction assumption rather than being an error, independence understates tail scenarios only under positive and directionally aligned dependence, and the cost objection confuses parameter count, which grows roughly linearly (or quadratically for an unrestricted covariance), with grid size, which grows as k to the power p. The entry cited nothing; the literature auditor supplied Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13), which raises the same dependence problem in the PAIC setting.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. No prior_work and no citations, but the substantive claims survive scrutiny. Ren et al. 2025 explicitly handle multiple omitted covariates (their L can exceed 1) and explicitly flag the dependence problem their own elicitation route creates: ‘It may be easier to elicit a distribution for each U_i separately. However, this would ignore the correlation structure between the uncertain quantities U_i’, pointing readers to multivariate elicitation methods. That is direct support for claims 1 and 3 in the PAIC setting and should be cited. Claim 5 (treatment-specific outcome associations) is consistent with the unanchored identification problem. Claims 6 and 7 (the single-composite-U reduction has not been validated against copula or latent-factor alternatives for unanchored PAIC) are no-work-exists claims; I found no such validation and no PAIC copula or latent-factor sensitivity specification, but absence of a finding is not proof, so I do not treat them as verified. The general single-U-versus-multiple-confounder literature outside PAIC does exist and the entry would be stronger if it engaged with it.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The joint-dependence problem is technically real, but several claims are too broad. C1 is valid when independent variation substitutes for a joint analysis, although one-at-a-time variation remains useful diagnostically. C2 is correct for tensor grids, but the report confuses parameter count with grid size: p axes with k levels require k^p evaluations, while parameter count generally grows linearly, or quadratically for an unrestricted covariance. C3 is not universal. Independence understates joint extremes when bias contributions are positively dependent and directionally aligned, but may overstate them under negative dependence. Independence among sensitivity parameters is also distinct from independence among omitted variables. C4 double-counts quantities: source and target joint distributions can determine the study-membership association, while treatment-specific outcome coefficients already encode effect modification. C5 is false as a necessity because a common coefficient is sufficient under an explicit no-U-by-treatment-interaction assumption; a main effect plus interaction is equivalent to treatment-specific coefficients. C6-C7 are literature-validation claims that this technical audit cannot establish. A scalar composite can be exact when it is sufficient for both selection and every treatment-specific outcome regression. C8 identifies reasonable candidate approaches. The issue is decision-critical when several omitted variables plausibly contribute jointly, not automatically in every PAIC.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text: QBA-13 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Statement
Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) extend the NORTA-based marginal unanchored STC of Ren et al. 2024 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1718) by simulating an assumed synthetic joint distribution for covariates measured in the IPD but unreported in the comparator publication, averaging individual predictions on the natural outcome scale before transforming to the log odds scale, and presenting deterministic sensitivity curves with bootstrap confidence intervals; they do not present tipping-point plots, and the case study instead reads a significance-crossing value off the curve. This is the beginning of formal QBA for limited-aggregate-data PAIC rather than a completed solution: the workflow is implemented only for STC, and the authors restrict it there because a MAIC extension would suffer extreme effective-sample-size loss and might fail to produce feasible weights. Their statement that no additional assumptions are required cannot be read literally, since target marginals, dependence, source-to-target outcome associations, copula form and regression form are all assumed.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Why it is open
The workflow is embedded in an STC and g-computation route, so it does not transfer to weighting, one-stage or network estimators, and the authors themselves rule out the direct MAIC extension on effective-sample-size and feasibility grounds. Its inputs, the outcome association of the omitted variable and its dependence with measured covariates, are estimated in the source study and assumed to hold in the target, which cannot be checked against the published comparator data. It also inherits the requirements of the underlying estimator, a sufficiently correct outcome model and adequate overlap, neither of which a covariate-omission sensitivity analysis can repair.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Treat the simulated-covariate route as one family within a broader QBA framework, extend it to multiple correlated omitted variables and treatment-specific associations, and state its assumptions about target distributions, correlations, outcome associations, copula form and model form explicitly rather than describing it as assumption-free. Develop parallel routes for weighting and one-stage estimators so the same sensitivity question can be asked of any PAIC estimator, addressing the feasibility and effective-sample-size loss that led the authors to restrict the published version to STC. Report the sensitivity curve against a clinical or decision threshold rather than reading it off a significance boundary.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Ren et al. (2025) extend a NORTA-based marginal unanchored STC by simulating covariates measured in the IPD but unreported in the comparator publication, then marginalizing predictions and presenting tipping plots. The report judges this the beginning of formal QBA for limited-AgD PAIC rather than a completed solution.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors found the entry’s description of tipping plots inaccurate: Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) present deterministic sensitivity curves with bootstrap confidence intervals and read a significance-crossing point off them, and the phrase tipping point appears only in background prose about QBA modes. GPT-5.6 Sol also corrected the claim that the method simulates the comparator population’s full covariate distribution; it simulates an assumed synthetic joint distribution.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Read the Ren et al. 2025 full text. Claims 1 to 6 and 8 verified verbatim. NORTA/Gaussian copula: ‘Ren et al. (2024) developed a novel way to implement unanchored STC by incorporating marginalisation and the NORmal To Anything (NORTA) algorithm (also is known as a Gaussian copula method)’. STC-only: ‘MAIC approach would suffer an extreme reduction of the effect sample size and may even fail to produce feasible weights. Hence, we will only present the QBA for the STC approach.’ Marginal estimand preserved: prediction is done ‘based on the natural scale … and then transformed to the log odds scale for the indirect comparison step’. Overlap and model requirements are stated verbatim in the discussion. Claim 7’s target text is real: ‘No additional assumptions are required for our approach.’ Caveat on the entry’s statement (not a numbered claim): the paper presents no tipping plots. ‘Tipping point’ appears once, in background prose describing QBA modes generally; the case study presents deterministic sensitivity curves with bootstrap CIs, from which the authors read off a significance-crossing point (‘If the proportion is greater than 28%, then the treatment effect becomes statistically significant’), which is the p=0.05-anchored reading QBA-25 criticises.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. The locally available full text supports C1-C8. Ren et al. follow the 2024 NORTA or Gaussian-copula STC, average individual predictions on the natural outcome scale before transforming, restrict the implemented QBA to STC, require correct outcome-model specification and overlap, rely on important omitted covariates being measured in the IPD source, and warn of severe MAIC effective-sample-size loss. The report is also correct that the paper’s statement that no additional assumptions are required cannot be literal: target marginals, dependence, source-to-target outcome associations, copula form, and regression form are assumed. Two caveats remain. C2 should say the method simulates an assumed synthetic joint distribution, not the comparator population’s known full distribution. The entry’s statement that the paper presents tipping plots is inaccurate; it presents deterministic sensitivity curves and significance-crossing interpretations rather than formal tipping plots. The broader estimator-general QBA problem remains open.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text: QBA-11 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising Tractability 2/5

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Statement
A linear STC applied where thresholds, splines or interactions operate produces outcome-model misspecification bias, and QBA for an omitted covariate holds the outcome model fixed, so it does not repair it. Double robustness is a property of the measured-data layer only: Campbell and Remiro-Azocar (doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106) place externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored ITCs in one causal framework and augment entropy-balancing MAIC with a conditional outcome model, giving robustness to misspecification of one of the two measured-data nuisance models, while identification still rests on conditional data-source ignorability and positivity with no bias-parameter indexing. No published unanchored-PAIC estimator is simultaneously doubly robust and indexed by explicit residual-bias parameters; drMAIC on CRAN offers doubly robust MAIC with E-values, weight trimming and variable-exclusion analyses, which is a generic screen rather than such an estimator.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Why it is open
Sensitivity analysis for an omitted variable holds the outcome model fixed, so misspecification of the retained model propagates untouched into every scenario on the grid, and model-form error is not a scalar that can be indexed by a prevalence or an association. Double robustness is silent about omitted variables, selection on unmeasured prognosis, outcome misclassification, target-distribution error and bridge drift, but the guarantee sounds strong enough to be read as protection against residual bias in general and to remove the perceived need for sensitivity analysis. Constructing an estimator that is doubly robust and indexed by explicit bias parameters requires the influence-function theory to be redone under a perturbed identification condition, which has not been done for population-adjusted transport, and flexible learners would need cross-fitting and extrapolation-aware prediction intervals that no current PAIC implementation supplies.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Campbell and Remiro-Azocar 2026, Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for the analysis of externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons, Research Synthesis Methods
Unifies externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored ITCs in one causal framework and augments entropy-balancing MAIC with a model for the conditional outcome expectation, giving double robustness against misspecification of the measured-data weighting or outcome model. Identification rests on conditional data-source ignorability and positivity; it contains no sensitivity analysis and no bias-parameter indexing.


Campbell and Remiro-Azocar, preprint of the same work (2025)
Preprint version of the doubly robust augmented weighting estimator for externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons.


drMAIC 0.1.0 (CRAN)
Provides doubly robust MAIC with E-values, weight trimming and variable-exclusion analyses. A generic robustness screen rather than an estimator indexed by explicit residual-bias parameters, so it does not close the gap.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Take the doubly robust augmented MAIC that already exists and index it by bias parameters with cross-fitting, so the estimate is computed at every point of the sensitivity region and the measured-confounding layer and the residual-bias layer are reported separately, or apply bias functions and bounds to the existing doubly robust functional where that suffices. Publish an explicit demonstration of which failures double robustness does and does not cover. Treat unsupported target profiles as a positivity problem calling for support restrictions, bounds or stated extrapolation assumptions, and use flexible learner multiverses, residual-bias functions, model averaging across plausible forms and calibration against held-out trials as optional tools for functional-form error rather than as remedies for nonidentification.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “A linear STC applied where thresholds, splines or interactions operate produces outcome-model misspecification bias with its own sensitivity parameters, and QBA for an omitted covariate does not repair it. Doubly robust estimators protect only against misspecification of one of two measured-data nuisance models under the identifying assumptions, so the correct research target is an AIPW or TMLE family indexed by bias parameters, not a claim that double robustness makes QBA unnecessary.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed what the entry demands: a functional-form class is a model set rather than a sensitivity parameter, unsupported target profiles are positivity and extrapolation failures that flexible learners and cross-fitting cannot repair, and a bias-indexed AIPW or TMLE is one coherent construction rather than the uniquely correct target, since bias functions or bounds can sometimes be applied to an existing doubly robust functional without redoing the influence-function theory.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Retrieved Campbell and Remiro-Azocar 2026 (Research Synthesis Methods, 10.1017/rsm.2026.10106; preprint arXiv 2505.00113), title ‘Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for the analysis of externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons’. Claims 8 and 9 verified: it presents a unified causal inference framework for both designs and ‘develop[s] an estimator that augments a popular weighting approach based on entropy balancing - matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) - by fitting a model for the conditional outcome expectation’, which is ‘doubly robust (DR), providing increased robustness against model misspecification’. Claim 10 is supported by the same retrieval: the paper’s identification rests on conditional data-source ignorability and positivity and contains no sensitivity analysis or bias-parameter indexing for unmeasured confounding. drMAIC 0.1.0 on CRAN provides doubly robust MAIC with ‘E-values, weight trimming, and variable exclusion analyses’, which is a generic screen rather than an estimator indexed by residual-bias parameters, so it does not falsify claim 10 either. Claims 5 to 7 are standard semiparametric facts and are correct.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C5-C9 are technically correct: double robustness concerns the measured-data outcome and selection or weighting models while identification, consistency, positivity, correct measurement, and the target law remain assumed. It does not protect against omitted confounding or the other listed violations. C2 nevertheless overstates what is required: a functional-form class is a model set, not a sensitivity parameter, and omitted interaction size covers only one misspecification. Unsupported target profiles are positivity or extrapolation failures, not merely outcome-model misspecification; flexible learners and cross-fitting cannot identify unsupported counterfactuals. C3-C4 list useful tools but not sufficient or mandatory remedies. Bias-indexed AIPW or TMLE is one coherent construction, not the uniquely correct one; bias functions or bounds can sometimes be applied to an existing doubly robust functional without rebuilding all influence-function theory. C10 and claims that research is still needed are literature-exhaustiveness claims outside this audit lens. At cpaic@9d150e9, no QBA, AIPW, TMLE, or cross-fitting API exists. The integrated residual-bias layer remains open, but its necessity and proposed implementation are inflated.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text: QBA-09 Overstated High priority Emerging

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Statement
Censoring-weighted estimation has already been combined with weighting to an aggregate-data target population: Yan et al.’s TADA (doi:10.1002/pst.70029) forms final weights as the product of time-varying inverse-probability-of-censoring weights and method-of-moments participation weights derived from target aggregate data, with a simulation study and an NSCLC case study. It adjusts under censoring at random given covariates, so what remains open is the sensitivity layer: no method indexes departures from that assumption inside a population-adjusted indirect comparison, by a selection, censoring-outcome association, pattern-mixture, copula or bounds formulation, and PAIC implementations propagate no uncertainty about the censoring assumption. Differential follow-up alone does not establish informative censoring, and the parameters the entry listed are alternative factorizations rather than a set that must all be specified.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Why it is open
The comparator’s censoring mechanism is unobservable from a published survival curve, so a departure from conditionally independent censoring is not identifiable from the observed follow-up and can only be indexed by assumption. Reweighting on baseline covariates addresses who enters the comparison, not the dependence between the censoring process and the unobserved event time, so the population-adjustment step leaves that dependence untouched even when a censoring model is fitted alongside it. Missingness also interacts with study selection and transport, so a censoring model fitted in the source carries its own transport assumption to the target. Ordinary inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting identifies the effect only under conditionally independent censoring unless it is augmented by an explicit departure parameter, and PAIC implementations typically assume administrative censoring and propagate no uncertainty about that assumption.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Yan et al. 2025, Target Aggregate Data Adjustment Method for Transportability Analysis Utilizing Summary-Level Data From the Target Population, Pharmaceutical Statistics 24:e70029
Two-stage weighting whose final weights are the product of time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights and method-of-moments participation weights derived from target aggregate data, with simulations and an NSCLC case study. Adjusts under censoring at random given covariates; supplies no sensitivity-parameter layer, no bounds and no propagation of censoring-model uncertainty.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend TADA-style joint censoring and transport adjustment with an explicit departure parameter rather than building a censoring-aware PAIC estimator from scratch: choose one justified formulation, whether a selection model, a pattern-mixture shift, a copula or bounds, and index departure from conditionally independent censoring by it. Combine it with the weighting or standardization step rather than applying it separately, and include censoring-model uncertainty among the propagated uncertainty layers. Trigger the analysis when censoring is plausibly outcome-dependent after conditioning on measured history, not merely because follow-up differs between the studies.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Censoring-weighted estimation has been combined with weighting to an aggregate-data target population, but no method indexes departures from non-informative censoring by explicit sensitivity parameters (selection odds, censoring-outcome association, pattern-mixture shift) inside a population-adjusted indirect comparison, and PAIC implementations propagate no uncertainty about the censoring assumption.
The source titled this. “Informative censoring and differential dropout as a bias model” The title presents censoring as an unbuilt bias model, but TADA already combines a censoring model with weighting to an aggregate-data target.
The source said. “Differential follow-up and treatment-related dropout between the IPD source and the external comparator require selection-odds, censoring-outcome association and pattern-mixture shift sensitivity parameters, addressed with IPCW sensitivity analyses, selection or pattern-mixture models and bounds. The report is explicit that these mechanisms are not forms of confounding and need their own bias models.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors judged the claim overstated on the same evidence: Yan et al. 2025 (doi:10.1002/pst.70029), which the entry did not cite, already combines a censoring model with weighting to an external aggregate-data target, contradicting the entry’s central claim that this has not been done. GPT-5.6 Sol added that differing censoring rates do not imply dependent censoring, and that selection odds, censoring-outcome association and pattern-mixture shift are alternative parameterizations rather than three jointly required parameters.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. Claim 5 (‘Sensitivity methods for dependent censoring have not been combined with weighting or standardization to an external target population’) is materially narrowed by Yan et al. 2025 (Pharm Stat 24:e70029, PMID 40765487), which the entry does not cite. TADA is a two-stage weighting framework whose final weights are the product of time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights and method-of-moments participation weights derived from target aggregate-level data. That is precisely the combination of a censoring model with weighting to an external aggregate-data target population that the entry says does not exist, with a simulation study and an NSCLC case study. The paper’s own framing also corroborates the entry’s premise: ‘AgD-based transportability methods in the presence of informative-censoring remain underexplored.’ What genuinely remains open is the sensitivity layer: TADA adjusts under a censoring-at-random-given-covariates assumption; it does not index departures from non-informative censoring by selection-odds or pattern-mixture shift parameters, does not return bounds, and does not propagate censoring-model uncertainty as a QBA layer. The entry also has zero prior_work, which understates a mature general literature on IPCW sensitivity analysis under non-ignorable dropout. Cites 10.1002/pst.70029: Combines time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights with method-of-moments participation weighting to an aggregate-data target population, directly contradicting the claim that censoring models have not been combined with weighting to an external target. Does not provide the sensitivity-parameter layer..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. Differential follow-up alone does not imply informative censoring: censoring rates may differ while remaining independent of event times conditional on measured history. C1 also incorrectly presents selection odds, censoring-outcome association, and pattern-mixture shifts as jointly required; these are alternative factorizations or sensitivity parameterizations. C2 names appropriate families, but ordinary IPCW identifies effects only under conditional independent censoring unless augmented by an explicit departure parameter. C3 and C4 correctly separate post-entry selection from baseline confounding. C5 is false under its broad reading because target participation weighting has been combined with time-varying censoring weights. That work does not, however, solve sensitivity to residual dependent censoring. At cpaic@9d150e9 there is no IPCW or censoring-sensitivity API, so that package does not close the residual layer. Cites 10.1002/pst.70029: Combines time-varying inverse-probability-of-censoring weights with method-of-moments target participation weights. It addresses joint censoring and transport adjustment under conditional censoring assumptions, but not residual MNAR sensitivity..

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text: QBA-07 Unverifiable High priority Promising

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Statement
Protocol-driven trial assessment and routine-care capture detect the same events at different times and with different completeness, so using detection time as event time can make progression curves depend on the assessment grid, and baseline covariate balancing generally cannot remove a residual study-specific observation process. Ackerman et al. 2024 (doi:10.3389/fdsfr.2024.1423493) quantify this for external control arms, simulating bias from misclassified progression events and irregular assessment timing and showing that together they may generate bias greater than the sum of their parts, but they measure the problem rather than correct it. The sub-mechanisms need different parameters and not all are always required: sensitivity and specificity address event classification, lag and interval endpoints address timing, linkage completeness addresses missing capture, and visit-process association parameters are needed only when observation is informative. Where visit times are noninformative given modeled covariates and the event is known to lie between visits, an interval-censored likelihood already accommodates different grids without an extra bias parameter, and cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) implements exactly that.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Why it is open
The event time recorded in an external data source is a function of the observation process as well as the underlying event, and that process differs systematically between a protocol-driven trial and routine care. Ascertainment parameters cannot be estimated from the comparison data because the true event process is never observed in either source, and assessment schedules and linkage completeness are rarely reported in enough detail in an aggregate publication to be bounded from protocol information. Missed events, informative visit intensity, death-recording lag and incomplete linkage each require their own sensitivity parameters or an explicit observation-process model, which sits outside the covariate-balancing toolkit and which no PAIC implementation attempts.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gray et al. 2024, Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety
Illustrates QBA for external controls including an outcome-evaluation scenario, that is misclassification of survival, which matches the ascertainment element of this entry.


Ackerman et al. 2024, Measurement error and bias in real-world oncology endpoints when constructing external control arms, Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation
Simulates and quantifies bias from misclassified progression events and irregular assessment timing in external control arms, with disease-specific magnitudes, and shows the two mechanisms interact non-additively. A quantification and planning tool, not a correction framework, and not integrated with weighting or standardization.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
cmlnmr() implements exact likelihood contributions for observed events, right, left and interval censoring and delayed entry, which handles differing assessment grids when the observation process is conditionally noninformative. It does not model missed events, sensitivity, specificity, informative visit intensity, death-recording lag or incomplete linkage.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on the interval-censored likelihood that already exists for the noninformative case and add what it does not cover: event misclassification through sensitivity and specificity, informative visiting through a joint visit-outcome or inverse-intensity model, recording lag through a lag distribution, and incomplete linkage through a capture parameter, invoking the parameters the setting actually warrants rather than all of them by default. Integrate the correction with the weighting or standardization step rather than treating it as a separate appendix analysis, and report the sensitivity surface jointly with the confounding and censoring parameters. Require reporting of assessment schedules and linkage completeness in both studies so the parameters can be bounded.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Protocol-driven trial assessment (imaging schedules, active follow-up) and routine-care capture (EHR-recorded progression, registry death recording, incomplete linkage) detect the same events at different times and with different completeness, producing ascertainment bias that covariate balancing cannot touch. Sensitivity analysis requires sensitivity, specificity, lag-distribution, linkage-completeness and visit-process association parameters inside an outcome-process or joint observation model.”
What was wrong with it. The auditors disagreed and both brought evidence. GPT-5.6 Sol read cpaic at commit 9d150e9 and found exact likelihood contributions for right, left and interval censoring plus delayed entry, which covers the noninformative interval-censoring case the entry treated as unaddressed, and objected that the entry requires every listed parameter in every analysis. The literature auditor kept the problem open and supplied Ackerman et al. 2024 (doi:10.3389/fdsfr.2024.1423493), which the entry did not cite and which quantifies the bias without modeling the visit process, supplying lag or linkage models, or integrating with a weighting or standardization step.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Claims 1, 4, 5 and 7 are supported by a substantial paper the entry does not cite: Ackerman et al. 2024 in Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation, ‘Measurement error and bias in real-world oncology endpoints when constructing external control arms’, which simulates and quantifies bias from misclassified progression events and from irregular assessment timing in ECAs, with disease-specific magnitudes (for example roughly 13 months of bias at 50% sensitivity). Critically it also states that these mechanisms interact rather than add. It is a quantification and planning tool, not a correction framework: it does not model the visit process jointly with the outcome, nor supply lag-distribution or linkage-completeness bias models, and it does not integrate with a weighting or standardization step. So the problem stands as open and the entry’s characterisation is accurate, but its sole citation (Gray et al. 2024) understates the existing literature. Gray et al. 2024’s third scenario is ‘outcome evaluation’ / misclassification of survival, which does match claim 3’s ascertainment element. codex dissented (overstated): The core claim is correct: using detection time as event time can make progression curves depend on the assessment grid, and baseline covariate balancing generally cannot remove a residual study-specific observation process. C2 nevertheless conflates distinct submechanisms. Sensitivity and specificity address event classification; lag and interval endpoints address timing; linkage completeness addresses missing capture; visit-process association parameters are needed when observation is informative. Not every analysis requires all of them. C4 is also too absolute. If visit times are noninformative conditional on modeled covariates and the event is known to lie between visits, an interval-censored likelihood can account for different grids without an additional bias parameter. A joint visit-outcome model or inverse-intensity method becomes necessary when visiting is informative. At cpaic 9d150e9, cmlnmr() implements exact likelihood contributions for right, left, and interval censoring plus delayed entry, materially addressing the noninformative interval-censoring subproblem. It does not model missed events, sensitivity, specificity, informative visit intensity, death-recording lag, or incomplete linkage. The broader observation-process QBA therefore remains only partially solved and is critical mainly for endpoints and data sources where ascertainment differences are plausible.

text: QBA-05 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Statement
Trial eligibility, referral patterns, performance status, treatment candidacy and calendar time can leave source-to-target selection bias after conditioning on measured covariates, and a bias function that perturbs the assumed equality of source and target potential-outcome means expresses that departure directly. Dahabreh et al. (doi:10.1002/sim.9550, doi:10.1002/sim.70083) do this without positing a concrete latent variable, but Nguyen et al. 2017 (doi:10.1214/16-AOAS1001) is not a clean example of the contrast, because it represents unobserved moderation as a composite moderator U and only two of its five methods are bias-formula based. These templates were built for individual-level transportability and have not been adapted to the limited aggregate-data structure of PAIC, while a generic E-value, which inherits the population and estimand of the estimate it is applied to but carries no target, aggregate-data or bridge structure of its own, occupies the role by default.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Selection on unmeasured prognosis leaves no signature in the measured covariate distribution, so balance diagnostics are uninformative about it and only an explicit perturbation of exchangeability can express it. The bias-function parameterization avoids inventing a specific latent variable but is harder to elicit and defend unless it is indexed by treatment, covariates and target stratum, and no such indexing exists for the limited aggregate-data structure PAIC works with. An E-value is a scalar defined for one comparison on one association scale; it adds nothing about the target population, the marginal versus conditional choice, correlation with measured effect modifiers, non-collapsibility, outcome-definition differences or component-bridge assumptions, and it is cheap and familiar enough to displace analyses that would encode the operative mechanism.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Nguyen et al. 2017, Annals of Applied Statistics
Sensitivity analysis for generalizing trial results, offered by the entry as a closer conceptual template than E-values. Two of its five methods are bias-formula based; its unobserved-moderator analysis explicitly introduces a composite moderator U, so it is not a latent-variable-free bias-function method.


Nguyen et al., preprint of the same work
Preprint carrying the counter-evidence quote both auditors cited: the concern that the treatment effect may be moderated by factors not observed even in the RCT, which we represent as a composite moderator U.


Dahabreh et al. 2023, Statistics in Medicine
Bias-function sensitivity analysis for extending trial inferences, parameterizing violations of source-target exchangeability directly.


Dahabreh et al. 2026, Global Sensitivity Analysis for Studies Extending Inferences From a Randomized Trial to a Target Population, Statistics in Medicine 45:13-14
Global sensitivity framework for transportability, modeling violations of conditional exchangeability through potential-outcome distributions. Built for individual-level data.


Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA workshop recommendations whose first item restricts E-values to unknown-unknowns, corroborating the entry’s claim that an E-value is a screen rather than a primary sensitivity analysis.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adapt the direct potential-outcome bias functions to limited-aggregate-data PAIC by indexing the perturbation by treatment, covariates and target stratum, choosing one coherent parameterization rather than stacking a selection-odds parameter on top of a potential-outcome shift that already encodes the same departure. Calibrate them with negative controls and selection models rather than a generic latent confounder. Keep E-values as a rapid screen when only an effect estimate is available and treat them as supplementary rather than as the decision-grade sensitivity analysis for an unanchored comparison, which is the position the Leahy et al. 2023 workshop already takes.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Statement
Bias correction, deterministic grid QBA, probabilistic QBA, partial identification and tipping-point analysis answer different questions and emit differently interpretable objects, yet applied analyses blur them and confidence, systematic-error, total-error and identified-set ranges are all published as 95% intervals. The distinctions are long established rather than new: they organize the Lash, Fox and Fink bias-analysis textbook (doi:10.1007/978-3-030-82673-4) and Greenland’s multiple-bias literature, and Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) make the PAIC-specific point that a deterministic grid treats every sensitivity-parameter value as equally likely. What remains open is narrower than the source said, because some labeling already exists: cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) tags contrasts by whether they are identified by IPD, by aggregate data or by neither, returns nonidentified effects as NA and diagnoses prior-driven movement, but no PAIC package carries the QBA mode or the interval type as metadata, and no ITC or PAIC reporting guideline enforces the taxonomy, including the 2025 PAIC framework of Ishak et al. (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1), which covers risk of bias and reporting but not interval semantics.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Why it is open
All five modes emit an estimate and a range, and nothing in current PAIC software carries the mode or the interval type as metadata, so the distinction survives only in the analyst’s prose. Summarizing a grid as the fraction of scenarios favoring a decision imposes a uniform measure over an arbitrarily chosen and arbitrarily spaced set of points, producing a number that looks probabilistic with no elicited distribution behind it. Where bias parameters have no validation or auxiliary data behind them the observed-data likelihood does not update them, so a probabilistic output is the analyst’s input distribution passed through the estimator while presenting in the same visual form as a data-driven posterior. Because no ITC or PAIC reporting guideline enforces the taxonomy, economic models and appraisal committees downstream cannot tell a sensitivity envelope from a confidence interval.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Lash, Fox, Fink and colleagues, Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data (Springer)
Textbook whose organizing structure is the distinction between simple or deterministic, probabilistic and multiple-bias analysis, and between conventional confidence intervals, systematic-error intervals and total-error intervals. Supplied by the literature auditor as the source the entry presented uncited.


Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
States, in the exact PAIC setting, that a deterministic sensitivity analysis treats all possible sensitivity-parameter values as equally likely, which may not be realistic in practice.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Refutes the claim that no PAIC software labels identified versus analyst-specified quantities: estimable_effects_at() labels contrasts by identified_by (IPD, aggregate or none) and basis (exact, first-order screen or not identified), nonidentified effects are returned as NA, and prior_sensitivity() with plot_prior_posterior() diagnose prior-driven movement. It carries no QBA-mode or interval-type metadata.


Ishak, Chandler, Liu and Klijn 2025, A Framework for Reliable, Transparent, and Reproducible Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons, PharmacoEconomics 43:691-710
Published PAIC framework covering estimand definition, method and adjustment-variable selection, application, risk-of-bias assessment and comprehensive reporting. It occupies part of the reporting-guideline space but does not cover QBA mode or interval semantics.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the labeling that already exists rather than specify it from scratch: cpaic’s identification tags and prior-movement diagnostics show the pattern, and what is needed is QBA-mode and interval-type metadata on the result object so a systematic-error interval, a total-error interval and an identified set are never printed as one thing. Enforce a reporting vocabulary that names the mode and the interval type for every reported range and never labels a set with nominal coverage, while allowing a confidence region for an identified set to state its coverage explicitly. Attach a method-appropriate support or feasibility diagnostic to every grid point, using effective sample size where weights are involved and feasibility or overlap measures where they are not, so unsupported scenarios are not plotted with equal visual weight.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text: QBA-01 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Statement
Quantitative bias analysis for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparison is fragmented rather than absent: the published methods are each tied to one estimator, one outcome type or one bias mechanism, and they share no common notation, no benchmark and no rule for choosing among them. Generic summary-level bias formulas can already be applied to a MAIC or STC estimate, as Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) state directly, so what is missing is a unified estimand-explicit parameterization and selection guidance, not a usable formula. The mathematics is narrower than the source claimed: under an additive identity-link conditional-mean model with a constant arm-specific coefficient for the omitted factor, arm-mean bias equals that coefficient times the difference in the omitted-factor prevalence the standardization actually uses, and on nonlinear or non-collapsible scales the correction requires integrating the conditional mean over the target covariate law, which finite summation, analytic formulas or quadrature can do exactly.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Why it is open
In an unanchored comparison treatment and study are the same unit, so any cross-study difference can contaminate the contrast, yet no shared parameterization links weighting, outcome-regression and one-stage estimators to a common bias object. A bias specified on a conditional linear predictor does not transfer mechanically to a marginal effect on a non-collapsible scale, so each estimand needs its own analytic summation, quadrature or simulation over the target covariate law, and corrections computed by different families are not comparable. Because the families return different kinds of object (a corrected point estimate, a distribution, or a set), an analyst can choose the one that yields the most convenient answer, and no published benchmark compares them on shared PAIC scenarios with known truth.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ren et al. 2025, Quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparisons, Research Synthesis Methods
Extends unanchored STC by simulating important covariates unreported in the comparator study; also states that the general class of bias formulas for mean difference, risk ratio and odds ratio can be applied directly to a MAIC or STC estimate as a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.


Soutar et al. 2025, Flexible quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in subject-level indirect treatment comparisons with proportional hazards violation, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Bayesian data-augmentation QBA for subject-level indirect comparisons using the RMST difference under non-proportional hazards. Estimator-, outcome- and mechanism-specific.


Gray et al. 2024, Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety
Illustrates QBA for external controls across three separately run scenarios: missing confounder, misclassification of exposure, and outcome evaluation. The literature auditor corrected the entry’s description of the second scenario as index-date error.


Nourredine et al. 2025, Statistics in Medicine
Likelihood correction and validation-informed likelihood for misclassified binary outcomes in unanchored external-control comparisons, in an unweighted design with no population adjustment.


Shi et al. 2024, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Systematic review counting 57 summary-level QBA methods, 53 designed for observational studies and 4 for meta-analyses. It never mentions indirect comparison, MAIC, STC, transportability or PAIC, so it cannot support a claim about PAIC frameworks specifically.


Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA expert workshop recommending QBA to quantify magnitude, direction and uncertainty of residual bias, with ten recommendations on sourcing, transparency and use.


Chandler and Ishak 2026, Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR)
Supplies the ML-UMR estimator a general framework would have to cover, and asserts the gap: QBA could be adapted for ML-UMR by incorporating bias parameters or simulated unmeasured covariates into the outcome regression and standardization steps, meaning it has not been.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build one estimand-explicit notation covering MAIC, STC and ML-UMR with marginal and conditional estimands and named target populations, and state for each estimand whether the correction is available in closed form, by finite summation or quadrature, or only by simulation, rather than letting collapsibility decide. Cover the ML-UMR estimator of Chandler and Ishak (arXiv:2606.20341), whose authors say QBA has yet to be adapted to it. Benchmark the families against one another on shared PAIC scenarios with known truth and publish selection guidance keyed to bias mechanism, available information, estimand and decision context, treating the QBA output as a decision object propagated into the economic model rather than an appendix table.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Quantitative bias analysis for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparisons has no unified estimand-specific theory: the conventional primary analysis sets residual confounding, selection, measurement and design bias to exactly zero, and the few existing methods are each tied to one estimator, one outcome type or one bias mechanism. Six recognisable QBA families exist but share no notation, no common benchmark, and no rule for choosing among them.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol found the mathematical claims overstated against Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13): covariate dependence does not break the additive decomposition, arm-specific coefficients already accommodate treatment interaction, exact correction needs only the conditional mean integrated over the target covariate law rather than simulation of the full outcome distribution, and collapsibility is neither sufficient nor necessary for a closed form. The literature auditor verified the Shi et al. 2024 counts (57 summary-level QBA methods, 4 designed for meta-analysis, doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2024.111507) but found the review never mentions indirect comparison, MAIC, STC, transportability or PAIC, so it cannot testify that none of the 57 is a mature PAIC framework.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): The core need for estimand-specific sensitivity analysis remains real, but C15 and C17-C19 overstate the mathematics. The identity-link formula is exact only under an additive conditional-mean model with a constant arm-specific U coefficient and when p_S denotes the U prevalence actually induced by the standardization, not necessarily the raw source prevalence. Covariate dependence does not itself break that decomposition, and treatment interaction is already accommodated by using beta_U,a separately by arm, contrary to C18. For nonlinear or non-collapsible estimands, direct subtraction of a link-scale scalar is generally invalid, but one need only integrate the conditional mean over the target covariate law, not the full outcome distribution. Finite summation, analytic bias formulas, or quadrature may be exact; simulation is not required. Collapsibility is neither sufficient for a closed form nor necessary for exact calculation. title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text: OVL-05 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
Statement
Matching a finite list of moments, the basis of MAIC and entropy balancing, leaves the rest of the distribution unconstrained, so source and target can agree on every balanced moment while differing in the tails and in the joint dependence structure. Optimal transport aligns fully specified empirical measures under an explicit cost function and makes the amount and location of transport visible, and it has already reached causal inference: Dunipace derives optimal-transport weights that minimize the transport distance between treatment and control (arxiv:2109.01991), and Gunsilius and Xu match for causal effects via multimarginal unbalanced optimal transport (arxiv:2112.04398). Neither addresses the PAIC data structure in which the target is known only through published marginal moments, which is where an adaptation would be new. Two auditors searched and found no such adaptation, so the absence is a negative search result rather than a verified fact, and the transport cost is a weaker diagnostic than the source claimed, since it measures separation under a chosen and scaled cost function rather than positivity failure as such.

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Balancing a finite list of moments leaves tails and joint dependence unconstrained, exactly where nonlinear outcome models and survival estimands are most sensitive, so the failure mode the source identifies is real. Optimal transport addresses it in principle only when both measures are fully specified, and in PAIC the target usually is not: aligning entire distributions requires first imposing a synthetic joint distribution that published marginals do not identify, so the transport is computed against an assumption rather than against data. Robust optimal transport over a moment-constrained ambiguity set is a coherent response but naturally returns worst-case criteria or ranges rather than a unique target distribution or effect. Computation, per-covariate cost specification, and uncertainty quantification for transport-based weights in a network context are all unresolved, so there is no estimator to evaluate, and none of this would repair an identification failure in any case.

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC

What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Dunipace, Optimal transport weights for causal inference (2021)
derives weights by minimizing the optimal-transport distance between treatment and control groups, targeting distributional rather than moment balance; does not address the PAIC setting where the target is known only through published marginal moments


Gunsilius and Xu, Matching for causal effects via multimarginal unbalanced optimal transport
