title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text: OUT-03 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Statement
Binary outcomes can be misclassified differently in the source and comparator trials, and differential sensitivity and specificity can move an indirect contrast in either direction rather than only toward the null: if the true arm risk is p, the observed risk is Sep + (1-Sp)(1-p). The claim that population-adjusted analyses assume perfect and equal classification holds only where the intended estimand concerns a latent true outcome, since an ordinary model consistently estimates the effect on the recorded endpoint without that assumption. What requires measurement comparability or an explicit error model is the step of treating two trials as measuring the same true endpoint. Neither auditor found any quantitative bias analysis of outcome misclassification applied inside a population-adjusted synthesis.

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Why it is open
Population adjustment balances baseline covariates and leaves the outcome measurement process untouched, so differential misclassification passes through weighting or outcome regression into the transported effect. Sensitivity and specificity of endpoint ascertainment are almost never reported in trial publications, so without validation data, a gold standard or replicate measurements the bias parameters are not identified from the data at hand and have to be supplied from outside. Because the parameters are not estimable from what publications report, this is structurally a sensitivity-analysis problem, which means no single paper can close it. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, has no outcome-misclassification model at the audited commit.

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
What has been tried

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build sensitivity analyses for differential outcome misclassification into binary PAIC, parameterized by study- and arm-specific sensitivity and specificity, and report how much misclassification would be required to overturn the conclusion. State explicitly whether the estimand is the recorded endpoint or a latent true outcome, since the error model is needed only for the latter. Where validation data, a gold standard or replicate measurements exist for either trial, use them to anchor the bias parameters instead of eliciting them, and reserve the elicited version for endpoints where nothing better is available.

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Binary outcomes in the source and comparator trials may be misclassified, and the misclassification may differ between studies, arms, or assessment schemes, yet population-adjusted analyses implicitly assume perfect and equal classification.”
What was wrong with it. The source said population-adjusted analyses implicitly assume perfect and equal classification; the code auditor narrowed this to analyses whose estimand is a latent true outcome, and added that true risk, sensitivity and specificity are not jointly identified from one fallible binary measurement but are not unestimable under every data design, since validation data, a gold standard, replicate measurements or identifying restrictions can identify them. The literature auditor noted that the absence of PAIC-specific work rests on a failed search rather than on any source asserting the absence, so the correct framing is unaddressed rather than unsolved.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I searched PubMed and the web for quantitative bias analysis of outcome misclassification applied to indirect comparisons, MAIC, STC or ML-NMR and retrieved nothing PAIC-specific; the general QBA apparatus for sensitivity/specificity bias parameters is long established in epidemiology but I found no application inside a population-adjusted synthesis. That supports the entry’s direction but means the three claims rest on my failure to find contrary work, which is weak evidence. The third claim, that differential misclassification can bias in either direction, is standard measurement-error epidemiology and is the strongest of the three; the first claim (that PAIC ‘implicitly assumes’ perfect equal classification) is really a statement that no PAIC paper models it, which I could not confirm from any source that asserts the absence. Because the bias parameters are not estimable from trial publications, this problem is structurally a sensitivity-analysis problem, and per the audit calibration no sensitivity-analysis paper could ever close it; the correct framing is ‘unaddressed’, not ‘unsolved’.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C3 is correct. If true arm risk is p, observed risk is Sep + (1-Sp)(1-p); study- or arm-specific sensitivity and specificity can therefore move an indirect contrast in either direction. C1 is accurate only when the intended estimand concerns a latent true outcome. An ordinary model can consistently estimate an effect on the recorded endpoint without assuming perfect classification, but interpreting trials as measuring the same true endpoint requires measurement comparability or an explicit error model. Without validation data, a gold standard, replicated measurements, external information, or identifying restrictions, true risk, sensitivity, and specificity are not jointly identified from one fallible binary measurement. They are not unestimable under every possible data design. C2’s claim that such analysis is non-standard is a practice or coverage claim outside this lens, although the proposed sensitivity analysis is technically appropriate. cpaic at the audited commit has no outcome-misclassification model. The issue can be decision-critical when ascertainment plausibly differs, but High priority is not automatic for well-defined, blinded, consistently assessed endpoints.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text: OUT-01 Overstated Very high priority Established

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Statement
Outcome-regression population-adjusted comparisons that report covariate-conditional coefficients, namely plug-in-means STC and conditional ML-NMR effects, return odds ratios that are not the marginal contrast the aggregate-data trial published, because the odds ratio is non-collapsible. This is not a property of binary PAIC as a class: a MAIC that fits a weighted outcome model containing treatment only already returns a marginal effect in the target population. Estimators and software for target-standardized marginal risks, risk differences and risk ratios already exist, including parametric G-computation (pmid:35485582), multiple-imputation marginalization, outstandR, maicplus and multinma’s marginal_effects(). What remains is that these are not the reporting default in HTA submissions, and that marginal component effects are not generally additive, so the scale chosen for standardization has to be compatible with component synthesis.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Why it is open
The gap is between available methods and prevailing practice: conditional coefficients are still reported alongside marginal aggregate-data effects, and nothing in the output signals the mismatch because both are labeled odds ratios of plausible magnitude. Standardizing the conditional side requires both a fitted outcome model and an explicit target covariate distribution, which aggregate publications rarely supply, so the comparator side cannot be moved onto the conditional scale after the fact. Conditional and marginal odds ratios do coincide under the null, with no prognostic heterogeneity, or with a degenerate covariate distribution, so the mismatch is decision-critical when incompatible estimands are actually combined rather than automatically. Within cpaic, the unreleased development package, cML-NMR still has no marginal standardization path.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2022, Target estimands for population-adjusted indirect comparisons, Statistics in Medicine
establishes that HTA agencies make reimbursement decisions at the population level and therefore require marginal estimands, and diagnoses the conditional versus marginal conflation in PAIC


Parametric G-computation for compatible indirect treatment comparisons with limited individual patient data, 2022 (PMID 35485582)
outcome-regression estimator that targets a marginal treatment effect compatible with the aggregate-data trial’s published marginal effect, for binary outcomes


outstandR: Model-Based Standardisation for Indirect Treatment Comparison with Limited Subject-Level Data (CRAN)
CRAN implementation of model-based standardization for PAIC, producing marginal contrasts on user-chosen scales


maicplus 0.1.2 (CRAN)
the literature auditor quotes its release notes, ‘changed the link function to binomial for RD and RR in binary analysis’, so it produces risk differences and risk ratios rather than only odds ratios


multinma 0.7.0 (2024-05-07), marginal_effects()
produces population-average marginal treatment effects on difference, ratio and link scales, standardized to a target population supplied through newdata or baseline, from an ML-NMR fit


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, README.md and R/cmaic.R
documents the estimand distinction, that cstc() returns a conditional effect at the target covariate values while cmaic() returns a marginal weighted effect in the target population and that these differ on non-collapsible scales, and records that marginal component effects are not generally additive; cML-NMR has no marginal standardization path

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The estimators exist, so the work is adoption and extension rather than construction. Make a named target-population estimand and marginal standardization the declared default in submissions, using the existing implementations, and add a marginal standardization path to cML-NMR where one is still missing. Check in each analysis that the effect scale chosen for standardization is compatible with component synthesis, since marginal component effects add exactly when the standardized treatment effects remain affine in the component design.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Plug-in-means STC and conditional ML-NMR coefficients return covariate-conditional odds ratios that, because the odds ratio is non-collapsible, are not the marginal contrast published by the AgD trial; methods (parametric G-computation, multiple-imputation marginalisation, multinma marginal_effects) and software (outstandR, maicplus, multinma) that produce target-standardised marginal risks, risk differences and risk ratios already exist, but they are not yet the reporting default in HTA submissions.
The source titled this. “Odds-ratio default and conditional-marginal mismatch in binary PAIC” The title attributes the conditional-marginal mismatch to binary PAIC as a class, which both auditors rejected since weighted MAIC already returns a marginal target-population effect.
The source said. “Binary population-adjusted indirect comparisons report conditional odds ratios because logistic models are convenient, but the odds ratio is non-collapsible, so the covariate-adjusted coefficient estimated from individual patient data is neither the marginal contrast in any named population nor on the same scale as the marginal effect published by the aggregate-data trial it is combined with.”
What was wrong with it. The source attributed the conditional-marginal mismatch to binary PAIC as a class and to the convenience of logistic models, and both auditors rejected that scope. The literature auditor found the estimand problem already named in Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio (doi:10.1002/sim.9413), solved by parametric G-computation (pmid:35485582), and implemented in outstandR, maicplus and multinma; the code auditor confirmed at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, that cmaic() returns a marginal weighted effect while cstc() and cmlnmr() return conditional ones.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. Retrieved Remiro-Azocar/Heath/Baio, ‘Target estimands for population-adjusted indirect comparisons’ (Stat Med 2022, doi 10.1002/sim.9413) and ‘Parametric G-computation for compatible ITCs with limited IPD’ (RSM 2022, PMID 35485582), plus the CRAN package outstandR, maicplus 0.1.2 NEWS (‘changed the link function to binomial for RD and RR in binary analysis’), and multinma NEWS 0.7.0 (‘The new marginal_effects() function produces marginal treatment effects’), whose docs describe mtype=‘difference’/‘ratio’/‘link’ standardised to a target population via newdata/baseline. The estimand-compatibility problem is named, formalised and implemented in three packages, so the methodological gap is largely closed; what remains is HTA default practice. The statement also over-generalises: MAIC fits a weighted outcome model containing treatment only, so its binary output is already a marginal effect in the AgD population. The conditional-marginal mismatch is specific to plug-in-means STC and to reporting ML-NMR conditional coefficients, not to ‘binary PAIC’ as a class. No source supports the motive claim about logistic convenience. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.9413: Establishes that HTA decisions are made at population level and therefore require marginal estimands, and diagnoses the conditional/marginal conflation in PAIC.. Cites pmid:35485582: Provides an outcome-regression estimator that targets a marginal treatment effect compatible with the AgD trial’s published marginal effect, for binary outcomes.. Cites cran:outstandR: CRAN implementation of model-based standardisation for PAIC, producing marginal contrasts on user-chosen scales.. Cites repo:dmphillippo/multinma NEWS 0.7.0 (2024-05-07): Produces population-average marginal treatment effects (difference, ratio, link scales) standardised to a specified target population from an ML-NMR fit..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, cmaic() returns a marginal weighted effect, whereas cstc() and cmlnmr() report conditional profile-specific effects. Thus C2, C3, C5, and C6 are correct when read as general possibilities, not universal identities. Conditional and marginal odds ratios can coincide under the null, with no prognostic heterogeneity, or with a degenerate covariate distribution. C1’s motive claim and C7’s prevalence claim are not technically verifiable. C4 is too prescriptive: standardized risks, risk differences, and risk ratios are coherent named estimands, but require sufficient target-distribution and outcome information, and marginal component effects need not obey the component-additivity model. cpaic now documents the mismatch and already provides a marginal MAIC path, but cML-NMR still lacks marginal standardization. The issue is decision-critical when incompatible estimands are actually combined, not automatically for every binary PAIC. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca:README.md#L184-L187: The package no longer silently presents cSTC and cMAIC effects as the same estimand.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca:R/cmaic.R#L208-L221: cMAIC already supplies a marginal weighted path, while explicitly delimiting when marginal component synthesis is coherent..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Mixture-weight calibration is unvalidated for subnetwork bridges
text: MOD-12 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 2/5

title: Mixture-weight calibration is unvalidated for subnetwork bridges
text:
Statement
Both devices already exist and are standard. Commensurate priors that link sources while allowing drift are Hobbs et al. 2011 (doi:10.1111/j.1541-0420.2011.01564.x), extended to survival with non-exchangeable sources by Murray et al. 2014 (doi:10.1111/biom.12115), and the robust mixture prior with an informative component plus a deliberately vague one is the robust meta-analytic-predictive prior of Schmidli et al. 2014 (doi:10.1111/biom.12242). What is new is only the application to subnetwork bridges and, as the entry itself says, the calibration and validation of the mixture weight or commensurability parameter. The non-identification claim also needs a sharper condition than absence of cross-gap randomized evidence: the weight stays at its prior value when the bridge-valid and bridge-invalid components induce the same likelihood for every observed datum, whereas replicated bridges, shared parameters or external validation data can give the components different observable implications and permit updating.

title: Mixture-weight calibration is unvalidated for subnetwork bridges
text:
Why it is open
When the bridge-valid and bridge-invalid states are observationally equivalent on all available data, the mixture weight and the commensurability parameter are fixed by prior belief and can dominate the posterior for exactly the contrast the decision depends on, so a robust or commensurate prior represents an assumption about exchangeability rather than validating it. There is no empirical validation of exchangeability across subnetworks that would calibrate either parameter, and validation rather than construction is the binding constraint. Where the competing states do differ in observable implications the parameter can be updated, so the residual problem is specific to decision-driving gaps with no observable consequence.

title: Mixture-weight calibration is unvalidated for subnetwork bridges
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Schmidli, Gsteiger, Roychoudhury, O’Hagan, Spiegelhalter & Neuenschwander 2014, Robust meta-analytic-predictive priors in clinical trials with historical control information, Biometrics 70(4):1023-32 (PMID 25355546)
The robust mixture prior with an informative component and a deliberately vague one already exists and is standard in historical borrowing, giving heavy tails and reaction to prior-data conflict. Only its application to subnetwork bridges and the calibration of its weight are new.


Hobbs, Carlin, Mandrekar & Sargent 2011, Hierarchical commensurate and power prior models for adaptive incorporation of historical information in clinical trials, Biometrics 67(3):1047-56 (PMID 21361892)
Establishes commensurate priors that link sources while allowing drift, letting the commensurability of the information determine how much is borrowed. This is the device the entry proposes for linking subnetworks.


Murray, Hobbs, Lystig & Carlin 2014, Biometrics
Extends commensurate priors to survival outcomes with non-exchangeable historical sources.

title: Mixture-weight calibration is unvalidated for subnetwork bridges
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Apply the existing robust mixture and commensurate-prior machinery to subnetwork bridges with components corresponding to explicit scientific states, and report how much of the posterior for each cross-gap contrast is generated by the mixture weight rather than by data, using prior-to-posterior movement, prior classes or power-scaling and tipping-point analysis. Check first whether the competing bridge states have any differing observable implications, since that determines whether empirical calibration is possible at all. Calibrate commensurability from connected component networks where cross-gap evidence does exist, and validate by bridge deletion.

title: Mixture-weight calibration is unvalidated for subnetwork bridges
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Robust mixture priors for bridge-valid versus bridge-invalid states” The title names robust mixture priors as the object to build, but the audit found commensurate and robust mixture priors established methods 12 to 15 years old.
The source said. “The report proposes commensurate priors that link subnetworks while allowing drift, and robust mixture priors containing an explicit bridge-valid and bridge-invalid component, so uncertainty about whether a bridge holds enters the posterior instead of being assumed away.”
What was wrong with it. The source proposed building commensurate and robust mixture priors with an empty prior_work list; the literature auditor identified both as established methods 12 to 15 years old (doi:10.1111/j.1541-0420.2011.01564.x, doi:10.1111/biom.12242), so construction is solved and packaged and only calibration is open. GPT-5.6 Sol tightened the non-identification condition to observational equivalence rather than the absence of randomized cross-gap evidence.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. prior_work is empty, yet both named devices are 12-15-year-old established methods that I retrieved. Commensurate priors: Hobbs, Carlin, Mandrekar & Sargent, Biometrics 2011;67(3):1047-56 (PMID 21361892), which ‘present several models that allow for the commensurability of the information in the historical and current data to determine how much historical information is used’; extended to survival with non-exchangeable sources by Murray, Hobbs, Lystig & Carlin, Biometrics 2014 (doi 10.1111/biom.12115). Robust mixture priors with an explicit valid and invalid component: Schmidli, Gsteiger, Roychoudhury, O’Hagan, Spiegelhalter & Neuenschwander, Biometrics 2014;70(4):1023-32 (PMID 25355546), whose robust MAP prior is a two- or three-component mixture in which one component is deliberately vague so the model reacts to prior-data conflict. So construction is solved and packaged; what is genuinely open, and what the entry itself correctly identifies as the binding constraint, is empirical calibration of the mixture weight and commensurability parameter when no cross-gap randomized evidence exists, plus validation by bridge deletion. A novelty score of 5 is hard to defend against this prior art. The report-scoring claim is self-referential and unverifiable externally. Cites doi:10.1111/biom.12242 (PMID 25355546): The robust mixture prior with an informative (bridge-valid) and a vague (bridge-invalid) component already exists and is standard in historical borrowing; only its application to subnetwork bridges and the calibration of its weight are new.. Cites doi:10.1111/j.1541-0420.2011.01564.x (PMID 21361892): Establishes commensurate priors that link sources while allowing drift, the exact device the entry proposes for linking subnetworks..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C2 are valid candidate constructions, but the nonidentification claim needs a sharper condition. A bridge-valid/bridge-invalid mixture weight remains equal to its prior weight when the components induce the same likelihood for every observed datum. Absence of a direct randomized cross-gap comparison alone is not sufficient: replicated bridges, shared parameters, external validation data or other differing observable implications can sometimes update a commensurability parameter. Conversely, when the components differ only along a likelihood-null cross-gap direction, no robust or commensurate prior empirically validates exchangeability; it only represents assumptions about it. C3 is therefore too categorical. C4 accurately reports the agenda’s internal scoring but supplies no methodological evidence for those scores. Calibration and validation remain open, especially for a decision-driving gap with no observable implications.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Flexible interaction surfaces inside network evidence synthesis
text: MOD-10 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Promising

title: Flexible interaction surfaces inside network evidence synthesis
text:
Statement
Neither Bayesian additive regression trees nor Gaussian-process treatment-covariate interaction surfaces have been developed for network population adjustment; the literature auditor searched for either embedded in a hierarchical evidence-synthesis model with target standardization and found none. Both are legitimate candidates, and neither identifies target expectations outside the observed support, where numerical predictions are model or prior extrapolations that cross-fitting cannot repair. Reading a fitted surface as evidence of causal effect modification is invalid when it rests on feature importance alone, although conditional treatment-effect heterogeneity can carry a causal interpretation under a randomized or otherwise identified design. Gaussian-process scaling is implementation-dependent, since sparse and inducing-point approximations reduce the computational cost, but no approximation creates support.

title: Flexible interaction surfaces inside network evidence synthesis
text:
Why it is open
A flexible interaction surface is estimated where the source trials have data and is then integrated over a target distribution that may lie partly outside the observed support, so added flexibility can amplify extrapolation error instead of removing bias. Embedding either device inside a hierarchical multi-study likelihood with numerical integration over an aggregate-data target adds computational burden on top of an already heavy ML-NMR fit, which is a research-engineering barrier rather than a conceptual one. There is also a standing temptation to read the fitted surface as a claim about which covariates modify treatment effect, which the fit alone does not license.

title: Flexible interaction surfaces inside network evidence synthesis
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wager & Athey 2018, Estimation and Inference of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects using Random Forests, JASA
Asymptotic theory and confidence intervals for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation with causal forests on a single i.i.d. sample. It does not address multi-study evidence synthesis, population adjustment, study-aware splitting or target-aware aggregation, and covers neither BART nor Gaussian processes.

title: Flexible interaction surfaces inside network evidence synthesis
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Embed BART or Gaussian-process interaction surfaces as nuisance components of a hierarchical evidence-synthesis model with target standardization, coupled to support diagnostics that flag the parts of the target distribution where the surface is extrapolating. Separate discovery from inference with cross-fitting or an equivalent device, and use sparse or inducing-point approximations where Gaussian-process cost is the barrier, while treating support as the limit no approximation removes. Use flexible fits for standardization and stress testing, and make causal effect-modification claims from the design rather than from the fitted surface.

title: Flexible interaction surfaces inside network evidence synthesis
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Gaussian-process treatment-covariate interactions and Bayesian additive regression trees placed inside a hierarchical evidence-synthesis model are listed as replacements for the linear interaction terms used in STC and ML-NMR. Neither has been developed for network population adjustment.”
What was wrong with it. The entry’s only citation, Wager and Athey 2018, concerns causal forests on a single i.i.d. sample and mentions neither BART, Gaussian processes, evidence synthesis nor population adjustment; the clause ‘requiring study-aware splitting and target-aware aggregation for PAIC use’ is the source’s own inference presented as the paper’s content, which the literature auditor flagged. The citation is kept below with an honest description.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Searched for BART or Gaussian-process treatment-covariate interaction surfaces embedded in a hierarchical evidence-synthesis model with target standardization and found none, so the entry’s core claim stands. The citation, however, is decorative and slightly mis-described. Wager & Athey 2018 JASA (doi 10.1080/01621459.2017.1319839) is ‘Estimation and Inference of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects using Random Forests’: it concerns causal forests on a single i.i.d. sample, and says nothing about multi-study evidence synthesis, population adjustment, study-aware splitting or target-aware aggregation. The clause ‘requiring study-aware splitting and target-aware aggregation for PAIC use’ is the agenda’s own extrapolation presented as if it were the paper’s content. It is also the only citation attached to a statement whose named methods are BART and Gaussian processes, neither of which appears in Wager & Athey. Recommend either re-describing the citation honestly as a general causal-forest reference or replacing it with BART/GP sources.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 through C4 and C6 are technically sound. BART and Gaussian processes can model flexible response or treatment-interaction surfaces, but neither identifies target expectations outside observed support; numerical predictions there remain model or prior extrapolations. Cross-fitting can address overfitting and some inferential bias but cannot repair absent support. C5 needs qualification: feature importance alone is not evidence of causal effect modification, although conditional treatment-effect heterogeneity can receive a causal interpretation under an appropriate randomized or otherwise identified design. Gaussian-process scaling is also implementation-dependent because sparse and inducing-point approximations can reduce computational cost without resolving support. The methodological integration and inference problem remains open, but it is primarily a research-engineering roadmap item rather than a correction that every current decision-grade PAIC analysis requires. The claim that neither construction has appeared in prior work is outside this audit’s assigned lens.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Cross-fitting folds and rate conditions undefined for PAIC
text: MOD-08 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 2/5

title: Cross-fitting folds and rate conditions undefined for PAIC
text:
Statement
For a specified PAIC estimator, cross-fitting must split the independent units that appear in its likelihood or estimating equations: participant folds are invalid when held-out scores share study-level information, study-level folds are appropriate but may leave too few clusters in a network of a handful of trials, and no PAIC-specific fold construction or rate theory has been written down. The general answer to the fold question exists outside ITC and needs porting rather than inventing, since multiway cluster-robust double machine learning (Chiang et al., doi:10.1080/07350015.2021.1895815) supplies cross-fitting and cluster-robust standard errors for exactly this dependence structure. The target-distribution half is a different problem from the one the source framed: a target law estimated independently of the source outcomes can be reused across source-data folds without train-test leakage, and splitting synthetic target records creates no independent information, so what it needs is sampling-uncertainty propagation and partial-identification analysis rather than fold assignment. The joint target law is genuinely not identified by published means, standard deviations and proportions, which is why ML-NMR imposes correlation structure with copulas (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579) rather than estimating it.

title: Cross-fitting folds and rate conditions undefined for PAIC
text:
Why it is open
PAIC dependence is clustered by study, so ordinary random participant folds let nuisance information leak across fold boundaries and the bias correction cross-fitting is supposed to deliver is not obtained, while study-level folds remove the leakage and leave very few units. Aggregate arms contribute no participant records, so the fold object for the aggregate half of the evidence has to be defined by which independent contribution is held out with its study rather than by participants. Because implementations treat the reconstructed target as fixed known data, both its sampling uncertainty and its unidentified dependence structure are absent from intervals that look correct and are silently too narrow. Meanwhile component-by-modifier interaction terms grow multiplicatively while studies, arms and events do not, so the product-rate conditions invoked for debiased machine learning may be unattainable at realistic network sizes, and no rate theory covers a design where part of the evidence contributes only integrated aggregate summaries.

title: Cross-fitting folds and rate conditions undefined for PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chiang, Kato, Ma & Sasaki 2022, Multiway Cluster Robust Double/Debiased Machine Learning, Journal of Business and Economic Statistics (preprint arXiv:1909.03489)
Supplies a multiway cross-fitting algorithm and cluster-robust standard errors for clustered dependence, so folding by the dependence unit is established theory that needs porting to PAIC rather than new derivation.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A (PMID 32684669)
Accounts for covariate correlation structures using copulas, which is the standard response to the fact that the joint target covariate law is not identified by published marginal means, standard deviations and proportions.

title: Cross-fitting folds and rate conditions undefined for PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Port multiway cluster-robust cross-fitting to PAIC rather than deriving fold rules from scratch: fold by the independent likelihood or estimating-equation contribution, hold an aggregate arm out with its study, and use contrast or subnetwork folds only where those define nonoverlapping independent units. Handle the reconstructed target law as an estimated and partly unidentified nuisance in its own right, propagating sampling uncertainty and reporting structural uncertainty through maximum-entropy reconstruction, copula-based dependence sensitivity, distributionally robust standardization or bounds, rather than through fold assignment. Establish rate requirements for cross-fitted component transport estimators under sparsity or heredity constraints on the interaction set, accounting for aggregate-data contributions, and pair the theory with hierarchical shrinkage so effective dimension is controlled rather than assumed small.

title: Cross-fitting folds and rate conditions undefined for PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Cross-fitting is required when flexible learners estimate nuisance functions, but population adjustment leaves its basic ingredients undefined: whether folds should be formed by participant, study, treatment contrast, or subnetwork; how aggregate-data arms should be assigned to folds at all; how a target distribution reconstructed from published moments should be cross-fitted; and what nuisance convergence rates are required when component-by-covariate interactions are high dimensional.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented fold construction, aggregate-arm assignment and target-reconstruction cross-fitting as undefined ingredients with no prior work cited. The literature auditor supplied the general clustered-dependence solution (doi:10.1080/07350015.2021.1895815), and GPT-5.6 Sol found that the target-reconstruction claims conflate cross-fitting with uncertainty propagation and partial identification of an external target law.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Found no PAIC-specific treatment of fold construction, aggregate-arm fold assignment, cross-fitting a reconstructed target distribution, or rate conditions for high-dimensional component-by-covariate interactions, so the entry’s core open claims survive. Caveat on two points. First, the general fold-construction question is not unresolved outside ITC: Chiang, Kato, Ma & Sasaki, ‘Multiway Cluster Robust Double/Debiased Machine Learning’, J Bus Econ Stat 2022 (doi 10.1080/07350015.2021.1895815, arXiv:1909.03489) supplies a multiway cross-fitting algorithm and cluster-robust standard errors for exactly the clustered-dependence structure the entry describes, so ‘fold by the dependence unit’ is established theory that only needs porting; the entry cites nothing. Second, the claim that a joint target covariate distribution is not identified by published marginal means, SDs and proportions is correct and is precisely why Phillippo et al. 2020 JRSS-A impose correlation structure via copulas rather than estimating it: ‘Covariate correlation structures are accounted for by using copulas.’ The remaining claims (flexible learners invalidating standard asymptotics, what cross-fitting does) are textbook DML and uncontested.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, C2, C9, C10 and C13 are correct. C3 holds when studies are the independent sampling clusters and held-out scores retain within-study dependence, but PAIC does not automatically make participant-level folds invalid after conditioning on fixed study effects. C4, C7 and C8 conflate cross-fitting with uncertainty and partial identification of an external target law. A target-law estimate obtained independently of source outcomes may be reused across source-data folds without train-test leakage; its sampling uncertainty still requires propagation, while its unidentified dependence structure requires assumptions, sensitivity analysis or bounds. Splitting synthetic target records does not create independent information. C5 and C6 also overstate the ambiguity: folds should follow the independent likelihood or estimating-equation contributions, and an aggregate arm can be held out with its study. Contrast or subnetwork folds are valid only when they define nonoverlapping independent units. C11 is estimator-specific and C12 is qualitative rather than a general theorem. PAIC-specific rate theory for mixed IPD and AgD with high-dimensional component interactions remains open, but this is high severity only for analyses attempting flexible or debiased inference.

Decision path

title: No TMLE or RMST-targeted estimator for population-adjusted transport
text: MOD-06 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: No TMLE or RMST-targeted estimator for population-adjusted transport
text:
Statement
Doubly robust estimators for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparison with time-to-event outcomes and aggregate-data comparators have been proposed and applied in a case study (Park et al. 2024, doi:10.1016/j.jval.2023.11.011) and are implemented on CRAN in drMAIC 0.1.0, which states support for binary and time-to-event (hazard ratio) outcomes; Campbell and Remiro-Azocar (doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106) extend augmented MAIC to an aggregate-only external control. What does not exist is narrower: no targeted (TMLE) estimator using a transport clever covariate with cross-fitted nuisances for PAIC, none targeting RMST, survival probabilities or net benefit in a declared population, and no formal handling of incompletely reported aggregate covariate summaries. GPT-5.6 Sol added that these estimands are not one generic clever covariate away, because each needs its own efficient influence function and, for survival, treatment, event and censoring nuisances handled separately.

title: No TMLE or RMST-targeted estimator for population-adjusted transport
text:
Why it is open
The residual gap is the combination of incomplete target reporting with absolute-scale or decision-scale estimands. A membership or weighting model cannot be fitted from a table of published summaries when the required moments are not all published, and the transport density ratio would then have to be estimated from those same summaries. Survival adds a censoring nuisance and a time-varying estimand, and each decision-relevant target (risk at a horizon, survival probability, RMST, net benefit across several outcomes) needs its own influence function and fluctuation, none of which have been worked out here. Because no implementation exists for that combination, the head-to-head comparison against MAIC, STC and ML-NMR that would justify adoption cannot be run.

title: No TMLE or RMST-targeted estimator for population-adjusted transport
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Start from the doubly robust survival PAIC estimators that already exist rather than building from scratch, and extend them in the two directions that are actually missing: incompletely reported target covariate summaries, and absolute-scale or decision-scale estimands (survival probabilities, RMST, net benefit) with their own efficient influence functions and with treatment, event and censoring nuisances treated separately. Add cross-fitted nuisance estimation and a targeted variant using a transport clever covariate, with software and validation in ITC settings rather than generic transport settings. Evaluate against existing PAIC methods under adversarial simulation and keep the residual-bias layer explicit, because AIPW and TMLE do not address unmeasured modifiers, absent overlap or a false bridge.

title: No TMLE or RMST-targeted estimator for population-adjusted transport
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Doubly robust estimators for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparison with time-to-event outcomes and aggregate-data comparators have been proposed and applied in a case study (Park et al. 2024) and are now implemented on CRAN (drMAIC), but no targeted (TMLE) estimator using a transport clever covariate with cross-fitted nuisances exists for PAIC, none targets RMST or net benefit in a declared population, and none formally handles incompletely reported aggregate covariate summaries.
The source titled this. “No doubly robust estimator for aggregate-only targets and survival” The title says no doubly robust estimator exists for aggregate-only survival targets, which the audit found false: the estimator is published and ships on CRAN as drMAIC.
The source said. “The report ranks as one of its most consequential open questions whether doubly robust and targeted estimators can be made usable under the HTA data regime: limited target data, survival outcomes, and partial aggregate-data reporting. TMLE with a transport clever covariate could in principle target marginal risks, survival probabilities, RMST, or net benefit in a declared population, but the report states this is a promising research direction and not a ready-made solution.”
What was wrong with it. The source’s title claim, that no doubly robust estimator exists for aggregate-only targets with survival outcomes, is false and was unattributed. Both auditors found Park et al. 2024 (doi:10.1016/j.jval.2023.11.011), co-authored by Phillippo, which proposes and applies exactly that estimator, plus drMAIC 0.1.0 on CRAN which ships it; the claim is now sourced. The entry’s own claims_to_check already contained the line that doubly robust work for time-to-event indirect comparison exists, contradicting its title.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The title claim is contradicted by a paper that David Phillippo co-authored. Park, Campbell, Towle, Yuan, Jansen, Phillippo & Cope, Value Health 2024;27(3):278-286 (PMID 38135212) proposes and applies a doubly robust estimator for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparison with TIME-TO-EVENT outcomes in the IPD-versus-AGGREGATE-DATA setting, i.e. precisely the combination of limited target data, survival outcomes and aggregate-only reporting that the entry says has no usable estimator. drMAIC 0.1.0 (CRAN, 2026-03-29) then ships a DR-MAIC estimator whose stated scope includes binary and time-to-event (hazard ratio) outcomes against aggregate comparator summaries. What survives is narrower and worth keeping: no TMLE with a transport clever covariate, no cross-fitted nuisance estimation, no targeting of RMST or net benefit, and no formal handling of INCOMPLETE aggregate covariate reporting. Note the entry’s own claims_to_check already contains ‘Doubly robust work for time-to-event indirect comparison already exists in the literature’, which is inconsistent with its title. Cites doi:10.1016/j.jval.2023.11.011 (PMID 38135212): Proposes and demonstrates a doubly robust PAIC estimator for survival outcomes in the IPD-to-aggregate-data setting, contradicting the entry’s title and its first claim.. Cites cran:drMAIC 0.1.0: Reference implementation of augmented doubly robust MAIC against aggregate comparator summaries, with stated support for binary and time-to-event (hazard ratio) outcomes.. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106 (arXiv:2505.00113): Extends a doubly robust augmented MAIC estimator to the setting with unavailable individual participant data for the external control, i.e. an aggregate-only target..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C2 overstates the absence by sliding between ‘aggregate-only’ and ‘incompletely reported.’ A doubly robust time-to-event PAIC method already covers IPD versus aggregate-data targets when the required summaries are available, so C5 is true and the broad title is false; missing required moments remains a narrower unsolved identification problem. C3 is not resolved by cpaic: at 9d150e9 its NAMESPACE exports cmaic(), cstc(), and cmlnmr() but no AIPW or TMLE function. C4 is feasible in principle, but risks, survival probabilities, RMST, and net benefit require parameter-specific efficient influence functions and, for survival, treatment, event, and censoring nuisances rather than one generic clever covariate. C7’s ‘one of two’ summary is therefore incomplete outside the simplest setting. C8 is correct. C6 and C9 are maturity assessments rather than technical propositions. The important remaining gap is a ready-made targeted or cross-fitted method for incomplete target summaries and absolute-scale survival or decision estimands; that is a roadmap item, not evidence that no usable doubly robust survival PAIC exists. Cites doi:10.1016/j.jval.2023.11.011: Provides and applies a doubly robust PAIC estimator for time-to-event outcomes with an aggregate-data comparator, contradicting the broad no-estimator claim.. Cites CRAN:drMAIC: Provides software for doubly robust MAIC, including stated time-to-event support, while not supplying the broader TMLE, RMST, net-benefit, or incomplete-summary framework..

title: No post-selection inference for model choice in population adjustment
text: MOD-04 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: No post-selection inference for model choice in population adjustment
text:
Statement
When an ITC or PAIC model is chosen or tuned adaptively and the reported interval conditions on that choice, unconditional coverage can be understated, and no post-selection or shrinkage-propagation machinery has been adapted to population adjustment; both auditors searched and found nothing PAIC-specific. The stronger form does not hold, because regularization is not the same as omitted uncertainty: a Bayesian fit that carries posterior draws through to the transported effect does propagate shrinkage, as the development source choxos/cpaic@9d150e9 does, so what is actually omitted is discrete model-selection uncertainty and the choice of prior scale. The word ‘commonly’ is an empirical claim the source did not support; the nearest evidence is a methodological review of PAIC publications finding that key methodological aspects were reported inconsistently, with appropriate uncertainty measures among the less-followed recommendations (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004).

title: No post-selection inference for model choice in population adjustment
text:
Why it is open
Post-selection inference and honest sample splitting exist in general statistics but have not been adapted to population adjustment, where selection happens in the IPD trial while the estimand lives in a different population and further uncertainty enters through estimated weights and reported target moments. Splitting a single HTA-scale trial to buy honest inference costs precision these analyses cannot spare, so the same data keep being used for discovery, tuning, estimation and uncertainty. Bayesian implementations are not automatically safe either: carrying posterior draws through covers shrinkage under a fixed prior, but not the discrete model choice or the prior scale that was itself selected.

title: No post-selection inference for model choice in population adjustment
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Serret-Larmande et al. 2023, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (PMID 37717707)
Methodological review of published PAIC analyses reporting that key methodological aspects were reported inconsistently, with only three articles adequately reporting all aspects and appropriate uncertainty measures among the less-followed recommendations. This is the closest real evidence for the source’s unsourced ‘commonly’.


cpaic development source at commit 9d150e9 (choxos/cpaic)
Source-code counter-evidence cited by GPT-5.6 Sol: regularizing interaction priors are recorded in the fitted object and posterior draws are carried through to target-population effects and quantiles, so shrinkage uncertainty does reach the transported effect. cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN.

title: No post-selection inference for model choice in population adjustment
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Port existing machinery instead of inventing it: stacking or model averaging over scientifically plausible modifier sets, projection-predictive selection from a rich reference model, shrinkage priors with the full posterior carried into the transported effect, and honest splitting or cross-fitting where sample size permits. Do not present cross-fitting as the only valid route, since valid selective inference, resampling that repeats the selection step, debiasing and full Bayesian model averaging are alternatives with their own conditions. The PAIC-specific gap is that no coverage assessment of an effect-modifier selection procedure has been run with the selection step included, which is where the work should start.

title: No post-selection inference for model choice in population adjustment
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “Selection and shrinkage uncertainty absent from transported effects” The title says shrinkage uncertainty is absent from transported effects, which the audit rejected since a Bayesian fit carrying posterior draws through does propagate shrinkage.
The source said. “When a population-adjustment outcome model is chosen by variable selection or fitted with regularization, the reported standard errors and intervals condition on the selected model, so shrinkage and selection uncertainty never reach the transported effect. The report lists regularization or selection not reflected in uncertainty as a distinct STC bias source.”
What was wrong with it. The source said shrinkage and selection uncertainty ‘never reach the transported effect’. GPT-5.6 Sol found that false for a full Bayesian fit that carries posterior draws through to the target effect (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub that an auditor confirmed is not on CRAN), and the literature auditor could not verify the word ‘commonly’, pointing instead to doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004 on inconsistent uncertainty reporting in PAIC.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C2-C3 are correct for unconditional coverage of an adaptive procedure. C1 and C5 are correct only when model, modifier, or tuning selection is performed and the reported interval conditions on that choice; the word ‘commonly’ is an empirical claim not established here. Regularization is not synonymous with omitted uncertainty. At cpaic@9d150e9, cmlnmr() uses explicitly regularizing interaction priors and relative_effects.cpaic_mlnmr() carries posterior draws through target effects and quantiles, directly refuting the claim that shrinkage uncertainty never reaches a transported effect. Prior-scale choice or discrete model-selection uncertainty can still be omitted. C4 is also too absolute: reusing data without cross-fitting is not inherently invalid under parametric or Donsker conditions, selective-inference or debiasing theory, full Bayesian model averaging, or a bootstrap that repeats selection. The PAIC-specific practice and coverage problem remains open, but it is high priority only for analyses that actually select or tune adaptively and then ignore that process.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Searched PubMed and the web for post-selection or shrinkage-uncertainty propagation adapted to population adjustment and found nothing PAIC-specific, so the core ‘not adapted to population adjustment’ claim survives. But two caveats. First, the empirical claim that conventional STC analyses ‘commonly’ fail to reflect selection uncertainty is not sourced anywhere in the entry and I could not verify the word ‘commonly’; the nearest real evidence is Serret-Larmande et al. 2023 (PMID 37717707), which found that across 133 PAIC publications ‘Key methodological aspects were reported inconsistently, with only three articles adequately reporting all aspects’ and that appropriate uncertainty measures were among the less-followed recommendations. Second, prior_work is empty although the entry’s whole proposed_direction (stacking, projection-predictive selection, horseshoe and spike-and-slab priors, honest splitting, cross-fitting) is off-the-shelf general Bayesian methodology with mature software; nothing in the entry acknowledges that the machinery exists and only the adaptation is missing. Claims 2 and 3 are uncontested general statistical facts.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2-C3 are correct for unconditional coverage of an adaptive procedure. C1 and C5 are correct only when model, modifier, or tuning selection is performed and the reported interval conditions on that choice; the word ‘commonly’ is an empirical claim not established here. Regularization is not synonymous with omitted uncertainty. At cpaic@9d150e9, cmlnmr() uses explicitly regularizing interaction priors and relative_effects.cpaic_mlnmr() carries posterior draws through target effects and quantiles, directly refuting the claim that shrinkage uncertainty never reaches a transported effect. Prior-scale choice or discrete model-selection uncertainty can still be omitted. C4 is also too absolute: reusing data without cross-fitting is not inherently invalid under parametric or Donsker conditions, selective-inference or debiasing theory, full Bayesian model averaging, or a bootstrap that repeats selection. The PAIC-specific practice and coverage problem remains open, but it is high priority only for analyses that actually select or tune adaptively and then ignore that process.

title: Convenience functional forms and untested flexible alternatives
text: MOD-02 Not supported Very high priority Promising

title: Convenience functional forms and untested flexible alternatives
text:
Statement
Functional form and interaction structure in population-adjusted outcome models are chosen for convenience, and conventional STC can be biased when that structure is wrong, particularly where transport requires extrapolation; unanchored MAIC can be biased when important adjustment variables are omitted from the matching. The simulation evidence the source invoked does not say what the source said. Hatswell, Freemantle and Baio (doi:10.1016/j.jval.2020.02.008) evaluated unanchored MAIC only and never STC, and found MAIC unbiased across a range of misspecification scenarios, biased only when important characteristics were left out of the matching and degraded when matched characteristics had low explanatory power or overlap was poor. The defensible open part is that flexible outcome models such as splines, BART, Gaussian processes, causal forests, super learner and TMLE have not been benchmarked against parametric baselines in PAIC under adversarial data-generating mechanisms.

title: Convenience functional forms and untested flexible alternatives
text:
Why it is open
Extrapolation to a target population probes the outcome model where the source data are sparse, which is where a wrong functional form does the most damage and where residual diagnostics have the least power, so poor overlap and misspecification compound. Not every omission bites: a common prognostic nonlinearity or covariate-covariate interaction need not bias a randomized identity-link treatment contrast, although it can bias nonlinear-link or standardized predictions. Flexible alternatives need an explicit route to valid inference and enough events to estimate an interaction surface, and single HTA-scale trials rarely have either, so flexibility can trade transparent misspecification for opaque misspecification. With no shared adversarial benchmark, each paper defines its own comparison and the interpretability cost of flexible models has no offsetting evidence.

title: Convenience functional forms and untested flexible alternatives
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Hatswell, Freemantle & Baio 2020, The Effects of Model Misspecification in Unanchored Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison: Results of a Simulation Study, Value in Health (PMID 32540233)
The study the source cited without a locator. Simulates unanchored MAIC against propensity score weighting and finds MAIC unbiased under a variety of misspecification scenarios, biased only when important characteristics are omitted from the matching. STC is not evaluated.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Statistics in Medicine (PMID 33015906)
Large anchored simulation study in which ML-NMR and STC eliminated bias when the requisite assumptions were met, while MAIC performed poorly in nearly all scenarios. Cuts against the source’s ‘especially in STC’ framing.

title: Convenience functional forms and untested flexible alternatives
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run head-to-head comparisons of parametric STC, flexible STC, BART and TMLE-style hybrids and doubly robust estimators on adversarial data-generating mechanisms containing splines, thresholds, nonlinear effect modification and covariate-covariate interaction, reporting misspecification robustness, calibration and the interpretability trade-off rather than friendly-mechanism performance. Pair any flexible fit with an explicit route to valid inference, but do not state cross-fitting as a universal requirement: parametric or Donsker nuisance classes, valid selective inference, debiasing and resampling that repeats the full tuning procedure are alternatives with their own conditions. Treat a flexible fit as a nuisance estimator with causal structure imposed rather than learned, never as a source of causal effect-modifier claims.

title: Convenience functional forms and untested flexible alternatives
text:
Verification

Verdict. Not supported. No accessible source substantiates the claim as stated.
The source said. “Population-adjusted outcome models typically assume linear prognostic terms and a small set of simple treatment-by-covariate interactions, which are convenience assumptions rather than scientific claims, and the transported effect inherits whatever form is imposed. Omitted treatment interactions, nonlinear prognostic effects, nonlinear effect modification, covariate-covariate interactions, non-proportional hazards, and an incorrect target joint distribution are distinct routes by which the convenience model biases the answer, and simulation evidence indicates unanchored MAIC and STC are highly vulnerable when the model is wrong.”
What was wrong with it. The source said simulation evidence indicates unanchored MAIC and STC are highly vulnerable to misspecification, attributing it to ‘Hatswell and colleagues’ with no locator. Both auditors judged it misattributed: the study is doi:10.1016/j.jval.2020.02.008, it evaluates MAIC and not STC, and its conclusion is that MAIC performed well; the largest anchored simulation study (doi:10.1002/sim.8759) likewise found that STC and ML-NMR eliminated bias when assumptions held and reserved its concerns for MAIC. The claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced.

Literature and prior-art check

open / misattributed. Retrieved the only Hatswell paper matching the description: Hatswell, Freemantle & Baio, ‘The Effects of Model Misspecification in Unanchored Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison: Results of a Simulation Study’, Value Health 2020 (PMID 32540233). Two problems. First, it studies unanchored MAIC only, against propensity score weighting; STC is not evaluated anywhere in it, so attributing an STC vulnerability finding to it is wrong. Second, its headline conclusion is the opposite of ‘highly vulnerable’: MAIC was unbiased across a variety of misspecification scenarios and only became biased when important characteristics were omitted from the matching. Separately, the largest anchored simulation study in the field (Phillippo et al. 2020, Stat Med) found STC and ML-NMR eliminated bias when assumptions held and reserved its ‘serious concerns’ for MAIC, which cuts directly against ‘especially in STC’. The flexible-model claim (BART/causal forests/TMLE not systematically benchmarked against parametric baselines in PAIC under adversarial DGMs) I could not falsify and vote open.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / misattributed. C1 is a provenance placeholder, not a technical claim. C2 is misattributed and conflates models: standard unanchored MAIC is a weighting estimator, not an outcome model, and the cited Hatswell study is about unanchored MAIC rather than STC. C3-C4, C6, C8, C10, C17-C19 describe real conditional risks, especially when extrapolation is material. C7 and C9 are only potential bias routes: omitted common prognostic nonlinearity or covariate interactions need not bias a randomized identity-link treatment contrast, although they can bias nonlinear-link or standardized predictions. C11 concerns marginally standardized outcome regression, not the conventional mean-centered STC estimand itself. C16 is false as an absolute: cross-fitting relaxes overfitting and empirical-process conditions, but valid inference can instead rest on parametric or Donsker nuisance classes, external training, selective inference, valid debiasing, or resampling that repeats the full tuning procedure. C12-C15 and the claim that existing comparisons are uniformly friendly are literature and priority assertions outside this audit lens. Functional-form risk remains open, but very-high severity is analysis-specific rather than universal.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R6:counter-quote-uncontested

title: Model and bridge selection uncertainty never enters the interval
text: MIS-04 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Model and bridge selection uncertainty never enters the interval
text:
Statement
When the same data select a PAIC model or bridge and ordinary conditional intervals are then reported, nominal coverage is generally not guaranteed, although the distortion can run in either direction and a prespecified or externally chosen model does not create the problem at all. Model averaging as the response is established in evidence synthesis generally (Rover, Wandel and Friede 2019; Bartos et al., arXiv:2110.01076) but has not been applied to PAIC, and predictive stacking needs a held-out unit aligned with the prediction target and dependence structure, so patient, study, and contrast level prediction are different estimands to choose between rather than an ambiguity that blocks the method. For bridges the difficulty is narrower than the source claimed: likelihood-based weights can be formed when candidate bridges imply different observed-data likelihoods or predictions, and are unavailable only for observationally equivalent identifying assumptions, which need prior elicitation or sensitivity analysis instead. No PAIC software feeds model or bridge averaging into the reported effect interval; in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, loo() is observation-level and warns that it does not validate cross-gap prediction, while prior_sensitivity() and bridge_fragility() remain diagnostics.

title: Model and bridge selection uncertainty never enters the interval
text:
Why it is open
Selection happens on the same data used for estimation, so the reported interval is conditional on a choice it does not price. The standard remedy needs a predictive unit at which the stacking weights are meaningful, and in a network the choice among patient, study, and contrast has to be made deliberately as a statement of the prediction target rather than inherited from a default. Projection predictive selection controls predictive loss and does not by itself deliver valid post-selection intervals, and robust Bayes covers only the model and prior classes actually represented, so neither is a finished answer and neither has been tried in PAIC. For bridges that are observationally equivalent no fit statistic can separate them, and the only honest input is a prior on assumption plausibility, which nobody has elicited.

title: Model and bridge selection uncertainty never enters the interval
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Rover, Wandel and Friede 2019, Statistics in Medicine (locator not supplied by the auditor)
heavy-tailed mixture priors for effect estimation in meta-analysis, which effectively result in a model-averaging technique robust to prior-data conflict; established for meta-analysis, not applied to population-adjusted comparisons


Bartos et al., Bayesian Model-Averaged Meta-Analysis in Medicine
Bayesian model averaging over meta-analytic models so that model uncertainty enters the reported estimate; again for meta-analysis rather than for population-adjusted or network settings


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
provides prior_sensitivity() and bridge_fragility() diagnostics and an observation-level loo() that warns it does not validate cross-gap prediction; no model or bridge averaging enters the reported effect interval

title: Model and bridge selection uncertainty never enters the interval
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The machinery exists outside PAIC, so the task is to port and test rather than to invent. Apply Bayesian model averaging as practiced in meta-analysis to population-adjusted networks, and state which predictive unit the stacking weights target, since that choice defines the estimand. Test whether projection predictive selection and robust Bayesian analysis over model and prior classes actually restore coverage here rather than assuming they do. For bridges, build likelihood-based weights where candidates imply different observed-data predictions, reserve elicited priors over assumption plausibility for the observationally equivalent case, and feed existing diagnostics such as bridge fragility into the reported interval instead of reporting them beside it.

title: Model and bridge selection uncertainty never enters the interval
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Results are reported from one selected model or one selected bridge as if the selection step had not happened, so the interval omits the variability that the selection itself contributes.”
What was wrong with it. The source said reporting a single selected model understates uncertainty and that likelihood-based weights for bridge selection are not available at all. The code auditor narrowed both: post-selection distortion can run in either direction and does not arise for prespecified or externally chosen models, and likelihood-based weights do exist when candidate bridges imply different observed-data likelihoods or predictions, failing only for observationally equivalent assumptions; the literature auditor added that the entry carried no prior work despite an established model-averaging literature in evidence synthesis (Rover, Wandel and Friede 2019; Bartos et al., arXiv:2110.01076), and found no projection-predictive or robust-Bayes application to PAIC.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The entry carries no prior_work at all, which understates a mature adjacent literature. Model averaging as a response to selection uncertainty in evidence synthesis is established: Rover, Wandel & Friede (2019), Stat Med, describe ‘heavy-tailed mixture priors for effect estimation in meta-analysis, which effectively results in a model-averaging technique… robust in the sense that a potential prior-data conflict… is explicitly anticipated’; also Bartos et al., ‘Bayesian Model-Averaged Meta-Analysis in Medicine’ (arXiv 2110.01076). So ‘Reporting a single selected model understates uncertainty’ is supported but generic, not a PAIC finding. I could not retrieve any source stating the second claim, that model averaging in network settings requires choosing a valid predictive unit for stacking weights; it is defensible on general grounds about leave-one-out stacking in hierarchical data, but I found nobody writing it for NMA, so treat it as the authors’ own argument rather than a sourced one. I found no projection-predictive or robust-Bayes application to PAIC. The bridge half is the genuinely novel and correct part: candidate bridges are competing identifying assumptions rather than nested models, so likelihood-based weights do not exist and averaging would need a prior on assumption plausibility. I found no work doing that.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 is too categorical. If the same data select a model and ordinary conditional intervals are reported, nominal coverage is generally not guaranteed, but distortion may be in either direction; externally chosen or prespecified models do not create this post-selection problem. C2 is correct for predictive stacking: the held-out unit and dependence structure must match the intended prediction task. It is not a requirement of every form of model averaging, and patient-, contrast-, or study-level prediction are different estimands rather than an irresolvable ambiguity. C3 is plausible as a research direction, but projection predictive selection controls predictive loss rather than automatically delivering valid post-selection intervals, and robust Bayes addresses only the model or prior classes actually represented. Likelihood-based bridge weights are not universally unavailable: they can be formed when bridge models imply different observed-data likelihoods or predictions. They cannot learn the plausibility of observationally equivalent identifying assumptions, for which prior elicitation or sensitivity analysis is appropriate. At cpaic 9d150e9, loo() is explicitly observation-level and warns that it does not validate cross-gap prediction; prior_sensitivity() and bridge_fragility() provide diagnostics, but no model or bridge averaging enters the reported effect interval. The interval problem therefore remains open, but it is decision-critical mainly after material data-adaptive selection or when conclusions are sensitive to the bridge.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: No robustness theory for censoring-weighted survival transport
text: MIS-02 Unverifiable High priority Emerging

title: No robustness theory for censoring-weighted survival transport
text:
Statement
For survival outcomes, censoring that depends on covariates adds a weighting or modeling layer on top of transport adjustment. Yan et al. (2025, doi:10.1002/pst.70029) built that estimator: TADA multiplies time-varying inverse-probability-of-censoring weights by method-of-moments participation weights and estimates variance by nonparametric bootstrap, evaluated in an ADEMP simulation study, so the construction is done for the unanchored survival transport case under conditionally independent censoring, positivity, and correctly specified nuisance models. What is not done is the robustness characterization, which the paper itself lists as future work: sandwich variance under heavy censoring, non-proportional-hazards censoring models, and doubly robust protection against partial misspecification of either weighting component. Sampling error in the published target moments is also not propagated, because the method of moments conditions on them, and censoring driven by unmeasured event prognosis stays unidentified without a sensitivity parameter.

title: No robustness theory for censoring-weighted survival transport
text:
Why it is open
Survival PAIC has to reweight to a target covariate distribution and correct for covariate-dependent censoring at the same time, and the estimator that does both is one paper old. Its behavior under censoring-model misspecification, heavy censoring, and non-proportional hazards is unmapped, and overlap is not examined anywhere in the source paper. The censoring mechanism is usually unverifiable from published data, and the covariates driving censoring are often not the ones reported for the target population, so the censoring model cannot be calibrated to the target. Censoring that depends on unmeasured prognosis is not identified from observed data at all, so it needs an assumption or a sensitivity parameter rather than a better model.

Work

Yan, Vuong, Metcalfe, Guan, Shi and Park 2025, Target Aggregate Data Adjustment Method for Transportability Analysis Utilizing Summary-Level Data From the Target Population
TADA, a two-stage weighting framework whose final weights are the product of time-varying inverse-probability-of-censoring weights and participation weights derived by the method of moments, with nonparametric bootstrap variance and an ADEMP simulation study; it states that aggregate-data transportability methods under informative censoring remain underexplored, and it does not identify censoring driven by unmeasured event prognosis, does not propagate sampling error in the supplied target summaries, and leaves sandwich variance, non-proportional-hazards censoring models, and doubly robust extensions to future work
