text:
Probable solution or research direction
The estimator exists, so the work is characterization rather than construction. Run TADA under censoring-model misspecification, weak overlap, and non-proportional hazards, and compare bootstrap variance against sandwich or stacked M-estimation under heavy censoring, which the authors name as their own next step. Add doubly robust or semiparametric versions that survive partial misspecification of either weighting component, and extend the variance to carry sampling error in the published target summaries instead of conditioning on them. Supply an explicit sensitivity parameter for censoring that depends on unmeasured prognosis.

title: No robustness theory for censoring-weighted survival transport
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “Informative censoring compounds transport weighting in survival PAIC” The title presents the compounding of censoring and transport weights as unsolved, but TADA already builds, bootstraps and evaluates that estimator.
The source said. “For survival outcomes, informative censoring adds a further weighting or modeling layer on top of transport weighting and imputation, and the combined variance has to account for the estimation of both weight systems plus the estimated target summaries. Combining target-summary calibration with censoring adjustment is recent rather than settled.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no standard variance formula covers the product of the two weight systems and treated the joint approach as recent rather than settled. Both auditors rejected the variance claim: TADA (doi:10.1002/pst.70029) already estimates variance by nonparametric bootstrap, and stacked M-estimation or sandwich influence functions can also cover product weights; the code auditor added that TADA is an operational solution under its stated assumptions rather than an untested attempt, and what genuinely goes unpropagated is the sampling error in the published target moments.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Read the full text of Yan, Vuong, Metcalfe, Guan, Shi & Park (2025) via PMC12326296. Every attribution is accurate. TADA is a ‘two-stage weighting framework named Target Aggregate Data Adjustment (TADA) that can simultaneously adjust for both censoring bias and distributional imbalances of effect modifiers… the final weights are the product of the time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights and participation weights derived using the method of moments.’ The paper itself asserts the absence the entry describes: ‘AgD-based transportability methods in the presence of informative-censoring remain underexplored.’ Two corrections to the entry’s why_open. First, TADA does propagate uncertainty across both weight systems: ‘We are estimating the variance of [the log hazard ratio] using a nonparametric bootstrap method’, so ‘no standard variance formula covers the product’ is too strong; what is not propagated is the sampling error in the published target moments, which the method of moments treats as fixed. Second, the entry’s claimed uncharacterized behaviors are confirmed by the paper’s own discussion: sandwich variance under heavy censoring, non-PH censoring models, and doubly robust or semiparametric protection against ‘partial misspecification of either weighting component’ are all listed as future work, and the word overlap does not appear anywhere in the text. codex dissented (supported-with-caveat): C1 is technically correct when censoring is conditionally independent only after adjustment for observed variables: an IPCW factor may multiply the transport weight, or the two mechanisms may be handled through outcome or joint modeling. C2 is correct: TADA combines method-of-moments participation weights with time-varying censoring weights. C3 is proportionate only as a statement about remaining scope. TADA is an operational solution under conditional independent censoring, positivity, correct nuisance-model specification, and its defined target; it is not merely an untested attempt. Arbitrary dependent censoring remains unidentified without additional assumptions or sensitivity parameters. The claim that no standard variance method covers product weights is false: stacked M-estimation, sandwich influence functions, and a bootstrap that re-estimates both nuisance systems can do so. Target-summary sampling variability additionally matters when the estimand is defined for a superpopulation rather than conditional on the supplied summaries. cpaic does not solve informative censoring: its survival likelihood uses censoring contributions but does not model the censoring process. This is high priority only where censoring is plausibly informative and consequential.

title: Identification, estimation, computation and decision are conflated
text: IDN-14 Partially addressed Very high priority Established

title: Identification, estimation, computation and decision are conflated
text:
Statement
Identification, estimation, computation and decision relevance are distinct, and every specific claim the source makes is true: a faster sampler adds no identifying information, double robustness still requires positivity for its target, measured balance does not address unmeasured effect modification, a component model imposes rather than proves additivity, and a narrow interval says nothing about whether the target population was the right one. The classification itself is not missing. Petersen and van der Laan (doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000000078) set out the staged separation of causal question, identification and statistical estimation and named the confusions that follow from conflating them, and the Causal Roadmap (doi:10.1017/cts.2023.635) operationalizes it as an itemized, prespecified process developed with regulators and industry. What has not been done is the ITC and PAIC instantiation: no published mapping of MAIC, STC, ML-NMR, node-splitting and disconnected-network methods onto the four problem classes.

title: Identification, estimation, computation and decision are conflated
text:
Why it is open
Progress in the field is delivered mainly as new estimators and faster samplers, which are estimation and computation advances, while the binding constraint in most applied comparisons is identification or decision relevance. A more sophisticated estimator produces a more polished output, so the appearance of improvement is decoupled from whether the causal quantity was identified at all. The general roadmap exists but is not written in the vocabulary of indirect comparisons, so an analyst choosing between MAIC, STC and ML-NMR gets no help from it in naming which class the binding constraint belongs to. Two qualifications survive: identification is always relative to explicit structural assumptions, and practical near-positivity is not the same thing as structural positivity.

title: Identification, estimation, computation and decision are conflated
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Petersen and van der Laan 2014, Causal models and learning from data: integrating causal modeling and statistical estimation, Epidemiology
presents a systematic approach integrating causal modeling with statistical estimation and highlights the common points of confusion that occur when the stages are conflated in practice


Dang et al. 2023, A causal roadmap for generating high-quality real-world evidence, Journal of Clinical and Translational Science
operationalizes the separation of causal question, estimand and identifying assumptions from estimation and from sensitivity analysis as an explicit, itemized, iterative prespecification process; not yet specialized to ITC or PAIC

title: Identification, estimation, computation and decision are conflated
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Instantiate the existing roadmap for ITC and PAIC rather than propose a new classification: map MAIC, STC, ML-NMR, node-splitting and disconnected-network methods onto identification, estimation, computation and decision relevance, and state for each what it can and cannot repair. Require an analysis to name the class its binding constraint falls in before a method is chosen, and accept added model structure only when it is scientifically defensible and adequately informed by data. Since the framework is already endorsed elsewhere, the deliverable is a specialization and a reporting checklist, not a new conceptual apparatus.

title: Identification, estimation, computation and decision are conflated
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Identification, estimation, computation and decision problems are logically distinct, and treating a problem in one class with a solution from another is a systematic error in the ITC literature. A faster sampler does not cure non-identification, a doubly robust estimator does not cure positivity failure, and a narrow interval does not establish that the target population was the right one.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented the four-way separation as absent from the field. The literature auditor found it standardized outside indirect comparison since 2014 (doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000000078) and operationalized in the Causal Roadmap (doi:10.1017/cts.2023.635), leaving only the ITC instantiation, and the source-code auditor went further and voted that this is established analysis hygiene and a reporting checklist rather than an unresolved research problem.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Every claim_to_check here is definitionally true and I found nothing contradicting any of them. But the entry frames the four-way separation as a missing classification, and a mature, widely adopted framework already does exactly this outside the ITC literature. Petersen and van der Laan (Epidemiology 2014) present ‘A systematic approach for the integration of causal modeling with statistical estimation’ and explicitly ‘highlight some common points of confusion that occur when causal modeling techniques are applied in practice’. The Causal Roadmap paper (Dang et al., J Clin Transl Sci 2023, 26 authors including Dahabreh, Stuart, FDA and industry statisticians) operationalizes it as ‘an explicit, itemized, iterative process that guides investigators to prespecify study design and analysis plans’, with the causal question, estimand and identifying assumptions in steps 1-3, estimation in step 4 and sensitivity analysis in step 5. That is the entry’s proposed direction, already standardized and endorsed. What is not done is the ITC/PAIC instantiation: no published mapping of MAIC, STC, ML-NMR, node-splitting and disconnected-network methods onto the four problem classes. Publish it as that narrower gap, citing the Roadmap, not as an unaddressed conceptual hole. Cites 10.1097/EDE.0000000000000078: Establishes the separation of causal question, identification and statistical estimation as an explicit staged framework and names the confusions that follow from conflating them. Cites 10.1017/cts.2023.635: Provides the standardized, regulator-engaged process that separates estimand and identification from estimation and from decision relevance, i.e. the classification the entry proposes; not yet specialized to ITC/PAIC.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

not-a-problem / supported-with-caveat. C1-C4 correctly distinguish identification, finite-sample estimation, computation, and decision relevance relative to a stated estimand and assumption set. C5-C10 are also correct: faster sampling does not add identifying information; double robustness still requires positivity for its target; measured balance does not address unmeasured effect modification; a component model imposes rather than proves additivity; precision does not establish target-population relevance; and complexity does not imply dominance. The qualifications are that identification is always relative to explicit structural or model assumptions and practical near-positivity differs from structural positivity. This is established analysis hygiene and a useful reporting checklist, not an unresolved methodological research problem. Claims about how often the ITC literature commits these errors and the asserted priority are outside the technical lens.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Five mechanisms of cross-study effect variation are lumped together
text: IDN-12 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: Five mechanisms of cross-study effect variation are lumped together
text:
Statement
Cross-study effect variation can come from patient biology, treatment delivery, adherence, trial engagement and outcome ascertainment, and these transport differently, since a biological modifier travels with the patient while delivery, engagement and ascertainment travel with the care system. The five-way split is the source’s own taxonomy and the categories are not mutually exclusive: engagement can change implementation and adherence, and ascertainment changes the observed endpoint rather than necessarily the underlying outcome. Identification results already exist for two categories outside the ITC literature, engagement in Ung, VanderWeele and Dahabreh (doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863) and adherence-mediated effects separated from assignment effects in Dahabreh, Robertson and Hernan (arXiv:2211.04876). The ITC-specific part is what is open: when mechanism-specific variables and crossed variation are absent, which is the normal situation for aggregate-data indirect comparisons, the mechanisms share one statistical signature and the heterogeneity cannot be attributed.

title: Five mechanisms of cross-study effect variation are lumped together
text:
Why it is open
Aggregate publications do not carry the mediation-style information on adherence, exposure intensity, ascertainment schedules and care pathways that separating the mechanisms requires, so the aggregate treatment contrast is often the only signal and it mixes all of them. Conflating them gives the wrong prediction in the target setting, because the transport rule differs by mechanism. No population-adjustment implementation currently encodes the distinction: in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, the component ML-NMR fit uses a single interaction matrix for all component by covariate terms, and the STC path separates prognostic main effects from modifiers with no mechanism roles at all. Moving to realistic-strategy estimands to fix this forfeits the protection of randomization, adds adherence and treatment-version assumptions of its own, and yields a quantity that HTA reference cases may not accept without a parallel conventional analysis.

title: Five mechanisms of cross-study effect variation are lumped together
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ung, VanderWeele and Dahabreh 2025, Generalizing and Transporting Causal Inferences From Randomized Trials in the Presence of Trial Engagement Effects, Epidemiology
defines engagement-aware transport estimands and gives identification results under a no participation-by-treatment-assignment interaction condition, under which the identifying observed-data functionals are the same as those obtained under the stronger conditions invoked in prior work


Dahabreh, Robertson and Hernan, arXiv:2211.04876

title: Five mechanisms of cross-study effect variation are lumped together
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Import the identification results that exist for engagement and for adherence-mediated effects into the ITC setting first, and treat implementation and ascertainment as the categories still needing estimand definitions. Require analyses to state which mechanism a claimed effect modifier belongs to so the correct transport rule is applied, and design evidence sets that supply crossed variation or mechanism-specific variables rather than assuming attribution is possible from aggregate contrasts. Where realistic-strategy estimands are used, report them alongside assignment-based effects so decision models retain a comparable conventional quantity.

title: Five mechanisms of cross-study effect variation are lumped together
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Biological treatment modification, implementation modification, adherence-mediated modification, trial-engagement effects and outcome-ascertainment effects are all reported as undifferentiated effect modification or heterogeneity, although they transport differently. Separating them may require ITC/PAIC estimands defined under realistic treatment strategies rather than assignment-only effects.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no identification results or estimand definitions exist for the non-biological categories and that the mechanisms cannot be distinguished. The literature auditor found engagement formalized in the paper the entry already cites and adherence-mediated effects handled in arXiv:2211.04876, and the source-code auditor narrowed non-separability to the case where mechanism-specific variables and crossed variation are absent, since arm-level adherence, protocol, exposure and ascertainment data can distinguish some mechanisms.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is a useful causal taxonomy, but the categories are not automatically distinct or mutually exclusive: trial engagement can change implementation and adherence, and ascertainment changes the observed endpoint rather than necessarily the underlying outcome. C2 holds only when an aggregate treatment contrast is the sole information and mechanism indicators or crossed variation are absent; arm-level adherence, protocol, exposure, and ascertainment data can distinguish some mechanisms. C3 is correct. C4 is a universal absence claim outside source-code ground truth. For cpaic specifically at 9d150e9, the claim holds: cmlnmr() uses one Gamma for all component-by-covariate interactions and cstc() separates prognostic main effects from modifiers but has no five-mechanism roles. C5 is relevant to adherence and treatment versions but is not automatically required for engagement or ascertainment; a target assignment effect may remain the decision estimand. Caveat two: ‘No current PAIC method distinguishes these five mechanisms’ is an absence claim I cannot verify, and it is too broad given work the entry misses. Dahabreh, Robertson and Hernan (arXiv 2211.04876) already separate assignment effects from adherence-mediated effects for generalizability and transportability, treating ‘a trial engagement effect via adherence’ as a distinct identification obstacle, which covers two of the five categories in the neighbouring literature. What is genuinely open, and what I would lead with, is the ITC-specific part: for aggregate-data indirect comparisons the mechanisms share one statistical signature, and the mediation and ascertainment data needed to separate them are not in the publications ITCs rely on. The claims about realistic-strategy estimands forfeiting randomization protection are logically sound and I found nothing contradicting them.

title: Transported control-arm outcomes are uncalibrated where it matters
text: IDN-10 Partially addressed Very high priority Promising

title: Transported control-arm outcomes are uncalibrated where it matters
text:
Statement
Comparing transported control-arm outcomes with observed ones tests the absolute-outcome transport model rather than only the relative effect, and it is available wherever a suitable validation control outcome exists, which can come from a masked or external validation dataset rather than from the target analysis itself. It is unavailable in the single-arm comparator case that motivates much unanchored population adjustment, although unanchored means only that there is no common randomized anchor and does not by itself imply single-arm evidence. Gupta et al. (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152) show that a hidden-randomized-truth benchmark is feasible, setting aside the randomized control arms of 14 advanced non-small-cell lung cancer trials, substituting Flatiron Health external controls, and reporting mean absolute log hazard ratio differences of 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 after measured-confounder adjustment and 0.098 after external adjustment for unmeasured confounding. That design is retrospective and benchmarks relative effects, so it does not calibrate transported absolute control-arm outcomes and does not establish transfer to control-free targets.

title: Transported control-arm outcomes are uncalibrated where it matters
text:
Why it is open
Where the check is possible, agreement of absolute control-arm outcomes conflates prognostic transport, outcome definition, follow-up length, censoring and care context, so a pass can arise from offsetting errors across several mechanisms, and agreement is neither necessary nor sufficient for an unbiased relative effect. No accepted tolerance states how close a transported control outcome must be before the transport model is accepted. The arm-level quantities the check needs are usually not published, because analyses report relative effects, and extrapolating a favorable verdict from settings that have a control arm to the control-free comparisons that need it remains an untested assumption.

title: Transported control-arm outcomes are uncalibrated where it matters
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gupta et al. 2025, Quantitative Bias Analysis for Single-Arm Trials With External Control Arms, JAMA Network Open
sets aside the randomized control arms of 14 advanced non-small-cell lung cancer trials (15 experimental arms), substitutes Flatiron Health external controls, and benchmarks against the randomized answer: mean absolute log hazard ratio difference 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 after measured-confounder adjustment, 0.098 after external adjustment for unmeasured confounding. It is retrospective and compares relative effects, not transported versus observed absolute control-arm outcomes

title: Transported control-arm outcomes are uncalibrated where it matters
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the existing hidden-truth benchmark rather than propose it: run it beyond one disease area and outcome, across data sources and bias mechanisms, and add the absolute control-arm comparison the published example did not make. Masked or external validation control outcomes suffice, so prospective withholding is not a precondition and should not gate the work. Require reporting of bias-adjusted arm-level outcomes alongside relative effects so the check is possible at all, and extend it from point outcomes to survival curves and restricted mean survival time.

title: Transported control-arm outcomes are uncalibrated where it matters
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Comparing transported (predicted) control-arm outcomes with observed control-arm outcomes tests the absolute-outcome transport model rather than only the relative effect. The check is available only where a randomized control arm exists, which is precisely not the single-arm setting in which unanchored PAIC is used.”
What was wrong with it. The entry attached Gupta et al. 2025 to a check the paper does not perform. Both auditors found it a retrospective benchmark of relative effects with quantitative bias analysis rather than the prospective withholding the entry described or a comparison of transported against observed absolute control-arm outcomes, and the source-code auditor also rejected the equation of unanchored population adjustment with single-arm evidence.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is correct for the literal observed-versus-predicted check, but the observed validation outcome need not come from the target analysis itself; masked or external validation datasets suffice. C2 is false as a definition: unanchored means no common randomized anchor, not necessarily single-arm evidence, although the common high-risk single-arm use case lacks a target control outcome. C3 is correct. Absolute-outcome agreement is neither sufficient nor necessary for an unbiased relative treatment effect because offsetting prognostic, measurement, follow-up, and censoring errors can coexist with treatment-effect misspecification. C4 is a reasonable validation program, but prospective hiding is not essential. C5 supports feasibility of a hidden-randomized-truth benchmark for external-control relative-effect and QBA analyses; it does not directly establish calibration of transported absolute control-arm outcomes.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I retrieved the cited paper. DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152 is Gupta et al., ‘Quantitative Bias Analysis for Single-Arm Trials With External Control Arms’ (JAMA Netw Open 2025). The design description in prior_work is broadly fair but misstates the paper’s contribution and its temporal design. The paper set aside the randomized control arms of 14 Roche-sponsored advanced NSCLC RCTs (15 experimental arms), substituted Flatiron Health external controls (43,302 patients), and benchmarked against the randomized answer; but that benchmarking design is the vehicle, not the finding. The finding is that QBA for residual confounding is feasible and moves estimates toward the randomized truth (mean absolute log hazard ratio difference 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 after measured-confounder adjustment, 0.098 after external adjustment for simulated unmeasured confounders). It is retrospective benchmarking, not the prospective withholding the proposed_direction describes, and it compares relative effects, not transported versus observed absolute control-arm outcomes, which is the check this entry is actually about. So the citation is one step removed from the claim it is attached to. The underlying problem is open.

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is correct for the literal observed-versus-predicted check, but the observed validation outcome need not come from the target analysis itself; masked or external validation datasets suffice. C2 is false as a definition: unanchored means no common randomized anchor, not necessarily single-arm evidence, although the common high-risk single-arm use case lacks a target control outcome. C3 is correct. Absolute-outcome agreement is neither sufficient nor necessary for an unbiased relative treatment effect because offsetting prognostic, measurement, follow-up, and censoring errors can coexist with treatment-effect misspecification. C4 is a reasonable validation program, but prospective hiding is not essential. C5 supports feasibility of a hidden-randomized-truth benchmark for external-control relative-effect and QBA analyses; it does not directly establish calibration of transported absolute control-arm outcomes. title: No curated benchmark validates bridged cross-gap comparisons
text: IDN-08 Overstated Very high priority Promising Tractability 5/5

title: No curated benchmark validates bridged cross-gap comparisons
text:
Statement
Bridge deletion has been done. Beliveau et al. (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1256) took two publicly available connected networks, disconnected them in several ways, compared the recovered contrasts against the connected analysis, and released code so other datasets can be run. It is also not the only empirical route: Rucker et al. (doi:10.1002/bimj.201900339) appraised a bridged comparison in a genuinely disconnected multiple myeloma network by re-analyzing it with RCT-only component network meta-analysis and comparing against a matching-based bridge, and later randomized direct evidence or masked and held-out validation designs are further options, with cross-method concordance counting as triangulation rather than validation. What is genuinely missing is a curated public benchmark with factorial scenarios, full-IPD gold standards and independent replication, together with evidence that performance on an artificially cut link transfers to a real gap.

title: No curated benchmark validates bridged cross-gap comparisons
text:
Why it is open
In a real disconnected network a cross-gap contrast has no direct or overidentifying evidence, so its bridging restriction cannot be tested from that dataset and validation has to be borrowed from connected networks where the answer is known. Whether that transfers depends on the deleted link being representative in population and design of the gap being bridged, which has not been shown. Connected networks carrying the IPD and bridging covariates needed to run the exercise are scarce and none have been assembled into a public benchmark, so methods are demonstrated on bespoke synthetic examples that establish no external operating characteristics. Fit-based checks do not fill the gap: in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, additivity_test() checks only the observed evidence and can be vacuous, returning Q = 0 on zero degrees of freedom.

title: No curated benchmark validates bridged cross-gap comparisons
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Beliveau et al. 2017, Network meta-analysis of disconnected networks: how dangerous are random baseline treatment effects?, Research Synthesis Methods
performs empirical bridge deletion on two publicly available connected networks, disconnecting them in multiple ways and benchmarking the recovered contrasts against the connected analysis, with code released


Rucker et al. 2020, Component network meta-analysis compared to a matching method in a disconnected network: a case study, Biometrical Journal

cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, additivity_test()

title: No curated benchmark validates bridged cross-gap comparisons
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the benchmark rather than the exercise: curate connected networks that carry IPD, apply factorial deletion scenarios, and require that direct and reconstructed estimates share an estimand and target population and that removed evidence is excluded from fitting. Register the two existing empirical routes as the starting point, reporting both deletion-based recovery and cross-method concordance while labeling the latter as triangulation. Report the degrees of freedom behind any additivity or fit-based check so a vacuous pass is visible, and pair the benchmark with independent replication before treating a disconnected-network method as decision-grade.

title: No curated benchmark validates bridged cross-gap comparisons
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Empirical bridge deletion has been demonstrated (Beliveau et al. 2017, two public connected networks disconnected multiple ways, with code released), but no curated public benchmark suite with factorial scenarios, full-IPD gold standards and independent replication exists, and it is not the only empirical route: cross-method concordance on real disconnected networks (Rucker et al. 2020) is another.
The source titled this. “Bridge deletion is the only empirical check on bridged comparisons” The title says bridge deletion is the only empirical check, but the audit found it already published and found cross-method concordance on real disconnected networks as another route.
The source said. “Deleting an existing bridge from a connected network and testing whether a disconnected-network method reconstructs the removed contrast is the only empirical route to validating bridged comparisons, because the bridging assumption in a genuinely disconnected network has no cross-gap evidence to test it against. No public benchmark suite for such bridge-deletion validation exists.”
What was wrong with it. The source said empirical bridge deletion is the only route to validating bridged comparisons, cited no one and rated the exercise’s novelty at 3. The literature auditor found it published in 2017 on public data with code released (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1256) and a second route that requires no deletion at all (doi:10.1002/bimj.201900339), so the surviving gap is the benchmark suite rather than the design.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The entry has no prior_work and rates novelty 3, but the exercise it describes was published in 2017 with public data and released code. Beliveau et al. (Res Synth Methods) took two publicly available connected networks, disconnected them in multiple ways, analyzed each disconnected version, and compared the recovered contrasts against the original connected analysis, then wrote ‘We provide code, so other datasets can be investigated.’ That is empirical bridge deletion with a reproducible public starting point. Separately, ‘empirical bridge deletion is the only route’ is false: Rucker et al. (Biom J 2020) validated a bridged comparison by re-analyzing a genuinely disconnected multiple myeloma network with RCT-only component NMA and comparing against Schmitz et al.’s matching-based bridge, a cross-method concordance route requiring no deletion. What survives is narrower but still worth publishing: no curated, factorial, IPD-bearing benchmark suite with independent replication exists, and whether performance on an artificially cut link transfers to a real gap remains untested. Cites 10.1002/jrsm.1256: Performs empirical bridge deletion on public connected networks and benchmarks the recovered contrasts against the connected analysis, with code released. Cites 10.1002/bimj.201900339: Demonstrates a second empirical route to appraising a bridged comparison: RCT-only component NMA re-analysis of a real disconnected network, compared against a matching-based bridge.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 is a legitimate held-out prediction and falsification design only if the removed evidence is not used in fitting, the direct and reconstructed estimates share an estimand and target population, and the deletion mechanism is relevant to the intended gaps. C2 is false: later or external randomized direct evidence, masked-arm or held-out-network validation, and independent validation designs with known truth are other empirical routes; mere cross-method concordance is only triangulation. C3 is true for an unsupported cross-gap contrast in an exactly identified disconnected likelihood, but bridge models can have testable observable implications when replicated component contrasts or other overidentifying restrictions exist. Passing those checks still does not validate the missing contrast. C5 is correct about external operating characteristics. C4 is a literature-absence claim outside this audit. At cpaic@9d150e9, additivity_test() is explicitly only an observed-evidence fit check and can be vacuous at Q = 0 on 0 degrees of freedom. A benchmark is useful, but neither necessary nor sufficient by itself for decision-grade credibility.

Decision path

title: ML-NMR interactions can rest solely on aggregate-data variation
text: IDN-06 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: ML-NMR interactions can rest solely on aggregate-data variation
text:
Statement
In mixed IPD and aggregate-data ML-NMR, interaction directions without adequate within-study IPD support may be weakly identified or nonidentified and are then sensitive to aggregate-study variation, shared-interaction restrictions and priors, and one coefficient forced to carry both within-study and between-study variation conflates individual-level effect modification with an ecological gradient. How far this bites is design- and parameter-specific rather than a categorical property of the method. The auditors disagreed on scope and the disagreement stands: the literature auditor found each claim confirmed almost verbatim by the ML-NMR authors, who report that the secukinumab interaction estimates rest solely on aggregate data and that the shared-interaction restriction was required to identify the model (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162), while the source-code auditor judged the diagnostic void overstated, because cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that cannot be installed from CRAN, already labels whether a row is identified by IPD, by between-study gradients or by neither, and flags posteriors that simply reproduce their priors.

title: ML-NMR interactions can rest solely on aggregate-data variation
text:
Why it is open
Studies contributing only aggregate data inform covariate effects mainly through between-study contrasts, so when the model imposes one coefficient for both sources an ecological gradient is read as individual-level modification and the fit still looks good. Flags help but do not identify: labeling a parameter as aggregate-informed or as prior-driven tells a reader where to distrust the estimate without supplying the missing within-study information. The remedy the source proposes, splitting interactions by treatment, is described by the ML-NMR authors as possible given sufficient data and an interesting avenue for further research, so it has not been evaluated, and the general-likelihood extension (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169) leaves the integration-distribution requirement intact.

title: ML-NMR interactions can rest solely on aggregate-data variation
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes

Phillippo et al. 2025, Multilevel network meta-regression for general likelihoods (arXiv:2401.12640), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A

title: ML-NMR interactions can rest solely on aggregate-data variation
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not rebuild the flags; make them standard and test them. Evaluate in simulation whether identified-by labeling, prior-to-posterior contraction and prior-data conflict checks actually detect the within-versus-between conflation when the truth is known, and report them next to estimates rather than on request. Fit within-study centered specifications that separate within-study from between-study coefficients, and treatment-specific interactions with hierarchical shrinkage, the avenue the ML-NMR authors flag as unexplored, then characterize how much IPD each interaction needs before its posterior stops tracking its prior.

title: ML-NMR interactions can rest solely on aggregate-data variation
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “ML-NMR interaction parameters are only partially identified” The title states partial identification as a categorical property of the method, which the audit found to be design- and parameter-specific.
The source said. “ML-NMR relies on conditional constancy of relative effects, a correct individual-level model, a specified integration distribution, and shared-interaction restrictions where needed. Partial identifiability of its interaction parameters and conflation of within-study with between-study effect modification remain unresolved weaknesses.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated partial identifiability as a categorical weakness and said nothing in standard output separates a parameter learned from data from one supplied by the prior. The source-code auditor found identifiability parameter- and design-specific and found both flags already implemented in cpaic at commit 9d150e9, while the literature auditor found the claims confirmed by the ML-NMR authors themselves; the entry is published as unverifiable because both readings carry evidence, and it is now sourced to doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162, for which it previously cited nothing.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 and C2 are technically sound: ML-NMR transports conditional relative-effect models and must integrate aggregate-study likelihood contributions over specified covariate distributions. C3 is too categorical. Interaction identifiability is parameter- and design-specific: interactions may be well identified by adequate within-trial IPD variation, weakly identified, or nonidentified. Aggregate arms can identify model-dependent integrated functionals and sometimes interaction combinations, rather than supplying only a generic ecological gradient. C4 is correct as a possibility when one coefficient is forced to represent both within-study and between-study variation. The report also overstates the diagnostic void for cpaic at 9d150e9: estimable_effects_at() labels whether information is from IPD, aggregate gradients, or neither, while plot_prior_posterior() exposes parameters whose posteriors reproduce their priors. These diagnostics flag rather than solve the underlying identification problem.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. This entry has no prior_work at all, yet every one of its four claims is confirmed almost verbatim by a paper by the ML-NMR authors themselves, which I read in full. On partial identifiability: in the psoriasis network the secukinumab interaction estimates ‘are much more uncertain than for the ixekizumab regimens, as the secukinumab parameters are based solely on AgD, and the ixekizumab data largely drive the interaction estimates in the common interaction model’, and the shared-interaction restriction was ‘required to identify the model’. On within-versus-between conflation, Phillippo et al. state the ecological-bias mechanism explicitly and flag the entry’s own proposed remedy as unexplored: ‘it is possible to fit ML-NMR models where the interaction terms are split in this manner (given sufficient data), and this is an interesting avenue for further research.’ That is a source asserting the gap, which is the strongest evidence a ‘this is open’ claim can have. The integration-distribution requirement is intrinsic to ML-NMR and restated in the general-likelihood extension (arXiv 2401.12640 / JRSS-A 10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169). I recommend the catalog attach Phillippo et al. 2023 as prior_work rather than publishing this entry unsourced.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C2 are technically sound: ML-NMR transports conditional relative-effect models and must integrate aggregate-study likelihood contributions over specified covariate distributions. C3 is too categorical. Interaction identifiability is parameter- and design-specific: interactions may be well identified by adequate within-trial IPD variation, weakly identified, or nonidentified. Aggregate arms can identify model-dependent integrated functionals and sometimes interaction combinations, rather than supplying only a generic ecological gradient. C4 is correct as a possibility when one coefficient is forced to represent both within-study and between-study variation. The report also overstates the diagnostic void for cpaic at 9d150e9: estimable_effects_at() labels whether information is from IPD, aggregate gradients, or neither, while plot_prior_posterior() exposes parameters whose posteriors reproduce their priors. These diagnostics flag rather than solve the underlying identification problem.

title: Recorded-covariate adjustment cannot remove unmeasured modifier bias
text: IDN-04 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging

title: Recorded-covariate adjustment cannot remove unmeasured modifier bias
text:
Statement
Absent randomization, valid proxies or instruments, validation data or other structural information, weighting and outcome regression built on recorded covariates cannot guarantee removal of bias from unmeasured effect modifiers or unmeasured prognostic causes of study selection, and balance on measured covariates does not establish comparability. The stronger claim that no estimator can address such bias is wrong: proximal identification with valid proxies and bridge conditions, instruments, or validation data can identify effects without observing the latent variable, and balancing measured covariates can reduce, preserve or amplify omitted-variable bias depending on the causal structure. Quantitative bias analysis is operable here rather than aspirational: across 15 emulated advanced non-small-cell lung cancer comparisons, adjustment for measured confounders cut the mean absolute log hazard ratio difference from 0.247 to 0.139 and external adjustment for unmeasured confounders to 0.098 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152), which narrows the gap without closing it and takes its sensitivity parameters from outside the data.

title: Recorded-covariate adjustment cannot remove unmeasured modifier bias
text:
Why it is open
Balancing, weighting and outcome modeling operate on recorded covariates, so a variable that drives both study membership and outcome is outside their reach by construction; this is an identification failure, so better algorithms and larger samples do not reduce it. Every diagnostic the field reports is a function of the measured covariates, so a perfectly balanced covariate table is compatible with large residual bias, and design and care differences sit in the unmeasured node precisely because no function of the measured covariates blocks that path. The alternatives that do identify carry further untestable structure of their own: proximal methods need proxy independence, completeness and bridge conditions rather than merely a plausible proxy, and quantitative bias analysis characterizes sensitivity without licensing a causal reading. Overlap is a second identification requirement, not only a weight-stability nuisance.

title: Recorded-covariate adjustment cannot remove unmeasured modifier bias
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE
official guidance stating that unanchored MAIC and STC assume all effect modifiers and prognostic factors are accounted for, an assumption it calls very strong and largely considered impossible to meet, and that anchored approaches are preferred whenever a connected network exists


Phillippo et al. 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis, Medical Decision Making
assesses population-adjustment assumptions inside a nine-study network: splits the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, checks conditional constancy through residual heterogeneity and inconsistency in sufficiently large networks, and reports that the shared-interaction restriction was required to identify the model where a treatment was informed only by aggregate data


Gupta et al. 2025, Quantitative Bias Analysis for Single-Arm Trials With External Control Arms, JAMA Network Open
sets aside the randomized control arms of 14 advanced non-small-cell lung cancer trials (15 experimental arms), substitutes Flatiron Health external controls, and benchmarks against the randomized answer: mean absolute log hazard ratio difference 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 after measured-confounder adjustment, 0.098 after external adjustment for unmeasured confounding. It is retrospective and compares relative effects, not transported versus observed absolute control-arm outcomes

title: Recorded-covariate adjustment cannot remove unmeasured modifier bias
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Replace routine covariate-balancing language with an assumption map drawn from a causal DAG that names the unmeasured design and care node, and pair every balancing analysis with bias analysis aimed at that node rather than with balance tables alone. Use quantitative bias analysis with explicit, externally elicited sensitivity parameters, partial identification that reports bounds, negative controls, and proximal methods where proxy independence and bridge conditions can actually be defended. Benchmark these against hidden randomized truth as Gupta et al. did, so the residual gap after adjustment is reported rather than assumed away.

title: Recorded-covariate adjustment cannot remove unmeasured modifier bias
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “Unmeasured modifiers and design differences are beyond adjustment” The title says such bias is beyond adjustment, which the audit rejected since proximal, instrumental and validation-data designs can identify effects without observing the latent variable.
The source said. “No adjustment method can balance a variable that was not measured, so unmeasured effect modifiers and, in unanchored comparisons, unmeasured prognostic factors and unmeasured design or care differences leave a residual bias that no estimator can address. Weighting or outcome regression cannot rescue such a comparison and at best disguises the bias more elegantly.”
What was wrong with it. The source cited nothing and said the residual bias is beyond every estimator. The source-code auditor found that too strong, since proximal, instrumental and validation-data designs can identify effects without observing the latent variable and measured balancing can amplify as well as reduce bias; the literature auditor supplied the references the entry lacked, so it is now sourced to NICE DSU TSD 18, Phillippo et al. 2023 on overlap acting through weight stability and extrapolation, and Gupta et al. 2025 on quantitative bias analysis at this exact task.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. This unsourced entry’s claims are structurally true rather than empirical, and I found no work that contradicts them. NICE DSU TSD 18’s judgement that the unanchored assumption is ‘largely considered impossible to meet’ is the guidance-level version of the same point. Phillippo et al. 2023 independently supports the overlap claim I was asked to check: ‘unlike MAIC, ML-NMR does not require full overlap between populations for stable estimation and remains unbiased under the usual extrapolation assumptions’ - i.e. overlap acts through weight stability and extrapolation, not through balance alone. On the entry’s normative claim that QBA and partial identification are the appropriate response, Gupta et al. 2025 (JAMA Netw Open) is direct empirical evidence that QBA is operable at this exact task: across 15 emulated aNSCLC comparisons, adjustment for measured confounders cut the mean absolute log hazard ratio difference from 0.247 to 0.139, and external adjustment for unmeasured confounders to 0.098. That demonstrates QBA’s usefulness, not identification: the residual gap is still not zero and the sensitivity parameters are supplied externally. The problem is unsolvable by any paper and correctly listed as open.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. Measured-covariate weighting or ordinary outcome regression cannot guarantee removal of bias caused by an unmeasured study-selection variable, and perfect balance on measured covariates does not establish exchangeability. The report improperly expands that result to ‘no estimator can address’ the bias. Randomization, valid instruments, validation data, proximal identification with valid proxies and bridge conditions, or other structural information can identify effects without directly observing the latent variable. C6 is not a general theorem: balancing measured variables can reduce, preserve, or amplify bias from an unmeasured variable, depending on the causal structure. C7 understates overlap because positivity is also an identification condition, not merely a weight-stability issue. Credible proxies are necessary but not sufficient for proximal methods; proxy-independence, completeness, and bridge assumptions are also needed. QBA and bounds are appropriate responses when point identification fails, but they are not the only responses.

Decision path

title: No assumption map spans identification, transport and consistency
text: IDN-02 Overstated Very high priority Emerging

title: No assumption map spans identification, transport and consistency
text:
Statement
‘Similarity’, ‘transitivity’, ‘exchangeability’, ‘conditional constancy’ and ‘shared effect modification’ are used loosely and often interchangeably in applied ITC and PAIC writing, and no single agreed assumption map ties within-study identification, cross-study transport, target positivity, treatment and outcome consistency and network coherence together for a given estimator. Formal notation for the individual restrictions already exists: Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) write conditional constancy and the shared effect modifier assumption as explicit restrictions tied to a named estimator and a declared target population. The five headings proposed here are one useful non-exhaustive taxonomy rather than an exact decomposition, since the categories overlap and they subsume or omit sampling exchangeability, positivity, interference, censoring, missingness, measurement and model or integration assumptions.

title: No assumption map spans identification, transport and consistency
text:
Why it is open
In applied writing the terms function as slogans, so an analysis can satisfy one restriction while silently violating another and a reader cannot tell which restriction the estimator actually needs. The restrictions also sit at different levels, inside one trial, between two trials and across a whole network, and are protected by different design features, so a single verbal claim that transitivity holds cannot be stated precisely enough to refute. The two works the source cited state the anchored and unanchored assumption asymmetry but not a level-by-level map, so nothing currently obliges a submission to say which restriction each part of its analysis leans on.

title: No assumption map spans identification, transport and consistency
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2018, Medical Decision Making
sets out population-adjustment methods for HTA and distinguishes anchored from unanchored comparisons according to whether a common comparator arm is used, stating that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions that are widely regarded as infeasible


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE
official guidance stating that unanchored MAIC and STC assume all effect modifiers and prognostic factors are accounted for, an assumption it calls very strong and largely considered impossible to meet, and that anchored approaches are preferred whenever a connected network exists


Phillippo et al. 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis, Medical Decision Making
assesses population-adjustment assumptions inside a nine-study network: splits the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, checks conditional constancy through residual heterogeneity and inconsistency in sufficiently large networks, and reports that the shared-interaction restriction was required to identify the model where a treatment was informed only by aggregate data

title: No assumption map spans identification, transport and consistency
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Since the notation for individual restrictions is settled, the task is assembly and adoption rather than invention: build a map that lists, for each estimator, which restriction it requires, at which level, and against which declared target population and effect scale, treating the five headings as a checklist that must also carry positivity, missingness, measurement and interference. Test it as a reporting device on real submissions and check whether readers using it identify the binding restriction more reliably than prose does. Attach negative controls, held-out-trial falsification and bias functions to each restriction separately rather than to the analysis as a whole.

title: No assumption map spans identification, transport and consistency
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. The ITC/PAIC literature uses ‘similarity’, ‘transitivity’, ‘exchangeability’, ‘conditional constancy’ and ‘shared effect modification’ loosely and often interchangeably in applied writing, and no single agreed assumption map ties within-study identification, across-study transport, target support, treatment-version consistency and network consistency together for a given estimator; formal notation for individual restrictions (notably conditional constancy and shared effect modification, each tied to a declared target population) does already exist.
The source titled this. “Assumption vocabulary conflates five distinct causal restrictions” The title asserts an exact decomposition into five restrictions, which both auditors rejected as an overlapping, non-exhaustive taxonomy.
The source said. “Similarity, transitivity, exchangeability, conditional constancy and shared effect modification are used in the ITC/PAIC literature as if interchangeable, when they denote different causal restrictions. The report proposes writing assumptions instead as an explicit five-part decomposition: within-study causal identification, across-study effect transport, target support, outcome and treatment-version consistency, and network consistency.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed the assumptions decompose into exactly five restrictions and that no standard formal notation maps a restriction to an estimator and a target population. Both auditors rejected that: the notation exists for conditional constancy and shared effect modification (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162), and the five boxes overlap while leaving out positivity, interference, missingness and measurement, so what is genuinely absent is a single map spanning all levels rather than notation as such.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. Both cited works check out. Phillippo et al. 2018 (abstract, retrieved): ‘We describe the assumptions required for population-adjusted indirect comparisons, and demonstrate how these may be used to generate comparisons in any given target population. We distinguish between anchored and unanchored comparisons according to whether a common comparator arm is used or not.’ NICE DSU TSD 18 is the guidance companion. Neither states a five-part decomposition, so both citations are decorative with respect to the five-restriction taxonomy, which is the entry’s own proposal. Two claims overreach. ‘Exactly these five restrictions’ is a taxonomy assertion no retrieved source makes. ‘There is currently no standard formal notation in the ITC/PAIC literature that maps each of these restrictions to a specific estimator and target population’ is too strong: Phillippo et al. 2018 and 2023 both write conditional constancy of relative effects and the shared effect modifier assumption as explicit restrictions tied to a named estimator and a named target population, and the transportability literature does the same for S-indexed estimands. What is genuinely absent is a single agreed assumption map spanning all five levels.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The proposed five-part map is a useful reporting device, not an exact mathematical decomposition. Its categories overlap and compress multiple restrictions, while omitting or subsuming sampling exchangeability, positivity, interference, censoring, missingness, measurement, and model or integration assumptions. Similarity, transitivity, and exchangeability are also overlapping or synonymous under some formalizations, unlike conditional constancy and shared effect modification, which are more clearly distinct. C3 is estimand-dependent: randomization identifies an assigned-treatment effect without an extra intercurrent-event assumption under a treatment-policy strategy when outcomes are complete; additional assumptions arise for hypothetical strategies or missing outcomes. C4 also needs consistency and target positivity. C5 describes nonparametric positivity but mixes identification with finite-sample precision. C7 is a literature-wide absence claim outside the assigned lens. Explicit assumption mapping remains useful, but the exact five-box taxonomy is a roadmap convention rather than a very-high-priority identification result.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text: HET-04 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Statement
Standard aggregate-data node splitting, as implemented in netmeta and gemtc, compares direct and indirect evidence without standardizing either path to a common target population, so a population difference between the paths and a genuine loop conflict arrive as a single number. Node splitting is local to a comparison rather than a global test of the network, and it can already be fitted inside a population-adjusted regression: multinma has supported consistency = ‘nodesplit’ since 0.4.0 and the same call accepts a regression formula and integration points, so both paths can be compared after adjustment (Phillippo et al. 2022, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162 assess inconsistency inside a population-adjusted psoriasis model with estimates produced for three external target populations). Two things remain undone: that adjusted split reports a conditional inconsistency factor rather than one standardized to a named target population on the marginal scale, and no study has quantified how often the unadjusted diagnostic flags population mismatch as inconsistency or misses true inconsistency that a compensating mismatch has masked. Whether consistency is population-indexed at all needs care, because marginal effects on non-collapsible measures are population-dependent (Chandler and Ishak, arxiv:2602.17041) but a loop whose every effect is defined in the same population telescopes algebraically, so population-varying inconsistency requires different populations along the evidence paths, design-specific effect surfaces, or an inconsistency-by-covariate interaction.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Why it is open
Unadjusted node splitting takes the direct estimate from the studies that made that comparison and the indirect estimate from a different set of studies, so the two paths carry different covariate distributions; a population difference registers as inconsistency, a real conflict can be cancelled by a compensating population difference, and one number is returned for both explanations. Fitting the split inside a population-adjusted regression removes that confounding at the conditional level, but only under the usual transport conditions: consistent estimands, positivity, measured effect modifiers, and correctly specified outcome and transport models. Even then the output is a conditional inconsistency factor, so no diagnostic is reported at a named target population on the marginal scale a decision uses. And the false-positive and masking rates of the unadjusted test, which is the one applied work actually runs, have never been measured, so nobody knows how much reported inconsistency in the literature is population mismatch.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The immediate work is measurement rather than method: run the simulation that quantifies how often unadjusted node splitting flags population mismatch as inconsistency and how often a compensating mismatch masks a real conflict, since that number decides whether the adjusted version is worth its cost. Beyond that, marginalize the ML-NMR node split so the inconsistency factor is reported at a named target population on the decision scale rather than at a covariate profile, and treat population-indexed inconsistency parameters as the harder remaining case. Any such diagnostic inherits the transport assumptions and cannot separate genuine inconsistency from unmeasured population or design differences, so it should be reported with that limit stated. In cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, neither piece exists at commit 9d150e9: relative_effects() evaluates a conditional contrast at a single covariate profile without marginal standardization, and no node-splitting or design-by-treatment diagnostic is exported.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Consistency is population-indexed but tested as a global property” The title calls consistency tested as a global property, but node splitting is local to a comparison and can already be fitted inside a population-adjusted regression.
The source said. “A network loop can be consistent in one population and inconsistent in another, so consistency is a population-indexed property; standard node splitting and design-by-treatment interaction models nonetheless test it as a global property of the network.”
What was wrong with it. The source said node splitting and design-by-treatment models test consistency as a global property with no population standardization; the literature auditor found node splitting can already be fitted inside a covariate-adjusted ML-NMR (multinma since 0.4.0; Phillippo et al. 2022, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162), and the code auditor noted that node splitting is local to a comparison rather than global, and that non-collapsibility on its own does not make consistency population-dependent because a loop defined in one population telescopes algebraically. The auditors split on whether the entry is open or partly solved, and it is published at the weaker claim.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Claim 1 is supported. Chandler & Ishak (arXiv 2602.17041, in this corpus) state: ‘even when effect modifiers are shared across treatments, marginal effects are generally population-dependent for commonly used non-collapsible measures, including hazard ratios and odds ratios.’ If the effects being compared are population-dependent, then so is any consistency relation among them. Claim 2 needs a qualifier. It is true of aggregate-data node splitting in netmeta and gemtc, but false as stated for multinma: node-splitting was added in multinma 0.4.0 (consistency=‘nodesplit’) and the same nma() call accepts a regression formula and integration points, so a node-split can be fitted inside a covariate-adjusted ML-NMR where direct and indirect paths are compared at a common covariate profile and estimates can be produced in any target population. Phillippo et al. (2022) do exactly this: ‘We examine residual heterogeneity and inconsistency and relax the shared effect modifier assumption for each covariate in turn.’ What is genuinely open is the evaluation the entry asks for. I found no study quantifying how often standard node splitting flags population mismatch as inconsistency, or how often a compensating mismatch masks true inconsistency, and ML-NMR node splitting reports a conditional inconsistency factor, not a target-population-standardized marginal one. Cites cran:multinma 0.9.1: Node splitting can already be fitted within a covariate-adjusted, population-adjusted ML-NMR, so the two evidence paths are compared after adjustment rather than on raw aggregate contrasts. Feature added in multinma 0.4.0 (2022-01-18).. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162: Demonstrates assessment of inconsistency inside a population-adjusted model with estimates produced for three external target populations..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 is possible, but non-collapsibility alone does not make consistency switch across populations. If each effect is coherently defined as delta_jk(P) = g(mu_k(P)) - g(mu_j(P)) in the same population P, loop consistency telescopes algebraically for every P. Population-varying inconsistency requires different populations along the evidence paths, design-specific effect surfaces, or an inconsistency-by-covariate interaction. C2 is correct for ordinary node splitting, which generally compares estimates from their contributing study populations rather than transporting both paths to an explicit common target. Node splitting is local to a comparison, however, so describing it as a global test is inaccurate. C3 is promising only under consistent estimands, positivity, measured effect modifiers, and correctly specified outcome and transport models; it cannot separate genuine inconsistency from unmeasured population or design differences. At cpaic 9d150e9, relative_effects() evaluates a conditional contrast at one covariate profile and explicitly does not marginally standardize over a target distribution, while NAMESPACE exposes no node-splitting or design-by-treatment diagnostic. The proposed diagnostic therefore remains open in the package.
