title: Component ML-NMR integration has no parallel or adaptive scheme
text: CMP-25 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Component ML-NMR integration has no parallel or adaptive scheme
text:
Statement
Bayesian component ML-NMR integrates an individual-level outcome model over aggregate covariate distributions with fixed Sobol quasi-Monte Carlo points, a cost structure inherited from ML-NMR rather than invented for component models, and its survival work scales as the number of aggregate rows times the number of integration points. The Stan likelihood loops serially over that grid with no within-chain parallelization, and no adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo scheme is implemented in component or non-component packages. Two of the proposed remedies are already in place: noncentered random effects are the default and a prior-sensitivity refit under tighter and looser priors is provided. Divergences arise from posterior geometry and weak identification rather than from the integration alone, and the claim that the cost precludes broad simulation studies is not backed by a benchmark.

title: Component ML-NMR integration has no parallel or adaptive scheme
text:
Why it is open
The aggregate likelihood requires a numerical integral inside every likelihood evaluation, so cost grows with integration points, aggregate studies, and posterior draws simultaneously, and survival likelihoods with flexible baselines and censoring make each evaluation expensive. Divergences concentrate in weakly identified interaction and drift parameters, which is exactly where the prior matters most, so computational failure and prior dominance are entangled and hard to diagnose separately even with a prior-sensitivity refit available. The remaining computational levers, adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo and within-chain parallelization through mechanisms such as Stan’s reduce_sum, are absent from component and non-component implementations alike.

title: Component ML-NMR integration has no parallel or adaptive scheme
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2020
proposes the general quasi-Monte Carlo numerical integration approach for the ML-NMR aggregate likelihood, from which the component version inherits its cost structure


multinma 0.6.0 NEWS, default integration points
lowered the default number of integration points from 1000 to 64 on the grounds that the previous default was excessive, showing the cost is real and managed upstream


cmdstanr
optional Stan backend for the component ML-NMR models, which are fitted with rstan by default


cpaic 0.1.0 (development version, choxos/cpaic@9d150e9)
unreleased development R package on GitHub, not on CRAN; integrates the aggregate likelihood over fixed Sobol quasi-Monte Carlo points with a serial Stan loop and no within-chain parallelization, and provides noncentered random effects by default plus prior_sensitivity()

title: Component ML-NMR integration has no parallel or adaptive scheme
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Add adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo integration and within-chain parallelization, which are the two proposed items that are genuinely missing, and benchmark the result so the claim about simulation feasibility rests on measurement rather than assertion. Keep the noncentered parameterization and prior-sensitivity refit as defaults and extend them with a diagnostic that separates divergence caused by posterior geometry from prior dominance in the weakly identified directions. Surrogate or emulator models with validation are worth exploring only once a benchmark shows where the cost actually binds.

title: Component ML-NMR integration has no parallel or adaptive scheme
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Aggregate-likelihood integration is slow and prior-entangled” The title asserts the integration is slow and prior-entangled, but the audit found no benchmark behind the runtime claim and traced divergences to posterior geometry rather than integration.
The source said. “Bayesian component ML-NMR integrates an individual-level outcome model over aggregate covariate distributions by quasi-Monte Carlo; for complex survival likelihoods this can diverge or be too slow to permit broad simulation studies, and results can be sensitive to priors.”
What was wrong with it. The source proposed noncentered parameterizations and prior-sensitivity diagnostics as future work; GPT-5.6 Sol found both already implemented at choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, with noncentered as the default for random effects, and noted the runtime claim has no benchmark behind it. The literature auditor added that the quasi-Monte Carlo cost is inherited ML-NMR structure (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579) and is actively managed upstream, where multinma 0.6.0 lowered the default number of integration points from 1000 to 64.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The computational structure is as described and inherited from ML-NMR rather than invented here: Phillippo et al. 2020 state ‘Motivated by the complexity of the closed form integration, we propose a general numerical approach using quasi-Monte-Carlo integration’, so the nested-integral cost is a property of the method, not of cpaic. Evidence that the cost is real and actively managed upstream: multinma 0.6.0 lowered the default number of integration points from 1000 to 64 on the grounds that the old default ‘was excessive’. I found no mention of within-chain parallelisation or adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo anywhere in the multinma changelog either, so that gap generalises beyond cpaic; Stan’s reduce_sum makes it available in principle. The entanglement argument (divergences concentrate in weakly identified interaction and drift parameters, which is where the prior matters most) is plausible and I found nothing addressing it. Claims about cpaic’s own runtime behaviour are for the code auditor; cpaic is not publicly available.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C2 is source-confirmed: aggregate covariates use fixed Sobol quasi-Monte-Carlo points. C3 is also correct: the Stan likelihood loops serially over a fixed n_int grid and contains no reduce_sum or other within-chain parallelization; parallel chains are not within-chain parallelism. C1 is plausible and explicitly acknowledged by the package: survival work scales as nrow(agd) times n_int, and random-effects survival fits can produce divergences. The claim that this precludes broad simulations is not supported by a benchmark, however, and HMC divergences arise from posterior geometry and weak identification rather than from QMC integration alone. The problem is partially mitigated already: noncentered random effects are the default, integration-error diagnostics exist, and prior_sensitivity() refits under tighter and looser priors. Adaptive QMC and within-chain parallelization remain open. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: The proposed noncentered parameterization is already the default for random effects.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Provides explicit refitting under tighter and looser priors to separate prior-driven movement from a single fitted result..

title: ML-NMR integration cost is unaddressed for flexible survival models
text: CMU-01 Overstated Medium-high priority Promising

title: ML-NMR integration cost is unaddressed for flexible survival models
text:
Statement
Multilevel network meta-regression integrates the individual-level model over each aggregate study’s covariate distribution, and that integration error is now quantified and separated from Markov chain Monte Carlo error rather than left unmanaged: multinma has checked it automatically since version 0.6.0 (2024-01-24), running half the chains at n_int and half at n_int/2 so an R-hat failure can be ascribed either to the sampler or to too few integration points, an algorithm formalized in Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169). What is not resolved is cost and coverage. For general likelihoods, and flexible survival models in particular, each aggregate-study individual carries its own integral, cumulative integration-error plots are unsupported there, and adaptive integration, calibrated variational approximation, GPU or parallel Stan, and likelihood emulation have never been evaluated for ML-NMR. No single reported summary covers sampler convergence, integration accuracy, hierarchical shrinkage, and population-specific predictive accuracy at once.

title: ML-NMR integration cost is unaddressed for flexible survival models
text:
Why it is open
Cost is driven by likelihood and gradient evaluations rather than by the number of saved draws, and it grows with integration points, studies, covariates, and the flexibility of the outcome model, so analysts cut integration points and convert a visible runtime cost into an invisible bias in the likelihood. The premise that the aggregate-data likelihood never has a closed form is false for Gaussian identity-link models; the burden is real for the non-Gaussian and survival cases. The diagnostics that do exist are layer-specific: sampler checks interrogate the chains, int_check interrogates the grid, and neither speaks to hierarchical shrinkage or to whether population-specific predictions are accurate, so a reviewer must assemble several checks and no software assembles them. In cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, the integration diagnostic compares quasi-Monte Carlo prefixes against the same finite grid, is unavailable for survival, and does not quantify residual full-grid error or runtime.

title: ML-NMR integration cost is unaddressed for flexible survival models
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A
defines ML-NMR with quasi-Monte Carlo integration, reports empirical integration-error rates of order N^-1 over the whole posterior, and reports runtime of around 5 minutes for the plaque psoriasis example


Phillippo et al. 2025, Multilevel network meta-regression for general likelihoods (arXiv:2401.12640), JRSS-A
gives the split-chain algorithm that separates numerical integration non-convergence from MCMC non-convergence when per-individual aggregate-data integrals make cumulative-error plots infeasible, and documents its implementation in multinma


multinma 0.6.0 release notes (2024-01-24), commit dmphillippo/multinma@6be4758
adds int_check, enabled by default, which runs half the chains at n_int and half at n_int/2 and ascribes R-hat or ESS warnings to either sampler non-convergence or insufficient integration accuracy; lowers the default to 64 points and stops saving cumulative integration points by default


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
implements a quasi-Monte Carlo stability plot (estimate at the first N points minus the estimate at all points) for non-survival models and automatic checks of divergences, tree depth, E-BFMI, R-hat and ESS across every sampled parameter block

title: ML-NMR integration cost is unaddressed for flexible survival models
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The integration-error diagnostic exists, so the work is to lower the cost it prices and to widen the checks it does not cover. Benchmark adaptive integration, calibrated variational approximation, GPU and parallel Stan backends, and likelihood emulation against exact ML-NMR fits, since none has been evaluated in this setting. Extend cumulative integration-error reporting to general likelihoods and survival models, where it is currently unsupported, and report runtime next to residual integration error so the trade-off is made knowingly. Add hierarchical cross-validation and level-specific PSIS diagnostics for the shrinkage and population-prediction layers that no current check reaches.

title: ML-NMR integration cost is unaddressed for flexible survival models
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 3 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. For flexible survival ML-NMR with one integral per aggregate-study individual, runtime is a real burden and methods to reduce it (adaptive integration, calibrated variational approximation, GPU/parallel Stan, emulation) have not been evaluated; and no single reported summary simultaneously covers sampler convergence, integration accuracy, hierarchical shrinkage, and population-specific prediction accuracy.
The source titled this. “ML-NMR integration cost and integration error are unquantified” The title says integration error is unquantified, but multinma has separated integration error from Monte Carlo error by default since version 0.6.0.
The source said. “Fitting multilevel network meta-regression requires numerical integration of the individual-level model over the covariate distribution of every aggregate study, which makes the model expensive and introduces an integration error that is distinct from Monte Carlo sampling error. Neither the runtime nor the integration error is routinely managed or quantified, and no single diagnostic covers the several layers on which such a fit can go wrong.”
What was wrong with it. The source said integration error is neither routinely managed nor quantified nor separable from Monte Carlo error. All three auditors found that outdated: multinma has made exactly that separation by default since 0.6.0 (2024-01-24, the int_check argument), and Phillippo et al. 2020 (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579) already reported empirical integration-error rates over the whole posterior and a runtime of about 5 minutes for its worked example.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. I read the full text of Phillippo et al. 2020 (Europe PMC PMC7362893) and the general-likelihoods ML-NMR preprint PDF (arXiv 2401.12640, now JRSS-A 10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169). Both contradict the framing. The 2020 paper states the QMC error rate, demonstrates empirical integration error over the whole posterior, and reports runtime (‘around 5 min’; ‘not markedly increased over an equivalent full IPD network meta-regression’). The general-likelihoods paper has a dedicated section 2.3 ‘Assessing integration error’ giving an algorithm that splits chains across n_int and n_int/2 and uses R-hat to separate MCMC non-convergence from integration non-convergence, and states multinma implements it. multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24) confirms this is on by default via int_check, and plot_integration_error() exists (test-plot_integration_error.R in the repo). So integration error is quantified, separated from MC error, and automated. Genuinely open: runtime reduction (adaptive integration, calibrated variational approximation, GPU/parallel Stan, emulation) for which I found no ML-NMR evaluation, and coverage of hierarchical shrinkage and population-specific prediction in one diagnostic. Cites arxiv:2401.12640: Provides an operational diagnostic that separates numerical integration error from MCMC error and is implemented by default in multinma; also published as JRSS-A doi 10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169.. Cites cran:multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24): Integration-accuracy checking is automatic and enabled by default, and attributes warnings to either sampler non-convergence or insufficient integration accuracy..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is correct subject to identification, correct model specification, and adequate AgD covariate distributions. C2 is conditional: integrating an individual-level model avoids the usual aggregate plug-in bias, but AgD-only interaction information can remain ecological. C3 inflates severity because identification and transportability may be more fundamental than computation. C4-C6 are correct for non-Gaussian and flexible survival paths. C5 correctly distinguishes error in the approximated posterior target from MCMC error conditional on that target. C7 is defensible only as saying no single scalar validates every layer; a dashboard can summarize multiple diagnostics. C8 is plausible but workload-dependent. The universal no-closed-form premise is false for Gaussian identity models and some analytic moments, and cost scales with likelihood and gradient evaluations rather than saved draws. At 9d150e9, cpaic already exposes integration and sampler diagnostics. Its integration plot compares QMC prefixes with the same finite full grid at fixed posterior draws, is unavailable for survival, and does not quantify residual full-grid posterior error or runtime. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Provides an implemented diagnostic for stability as the number of Sobol integration points increases, partially resolving the claim that integration accuracy is wholly unmanaged.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Automatically checks and stores several major sampler diagnostics across all sampled parameter blocks..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / overstated. The core claim that ML-NMR integration error is neither managed nor separable from MCMC error is outdated for the multinma implementation path. Since multinma 0.6.0 (CRAN 2024-01-24), default int_check runs half the chains at n_int and half at n_int/2 and ascribes R-hat/ESS failures either to MCMC non-convergence or to insufficient integration points; plot_integration_error already existed for cumulative QMC error. Phillippo (2025/2026 JRSSA general-likelihoods paper, section 3.3) formalizes this split-R-hat algorithm, notes the older cumulative-error plots become untenable for per-individual AgD integrals, defaults n_int=64, and documents multinma warnings when N-tilde is insufficient. Claims that ML-NMR yields population-specific effects and avoids ecological bias remain faithful to Phillippo et al. 2020. What remains open is not basic integration-error diagnostics but: (i) a single review-facing summary that also covers hierarchical shrinkage and population-specific predictive accuracy; (ii) adaptive integration, variational approximations with calibration, GPU/parallel Stan, likelihood emulation, and sparse designs as routine cost reducers; (iii) survival models, where cumulative integration points are not saved and plot_integration_error is unsupported. Searches of arXiv/medRxiv and multinma NEWS through 2026 found no shipped adaptive/VI/GPU ML-NMR solver. Cites dmphillippo/multinma@6be475898729f1ccdf88e275c99bbd1f9a143e81: Ships default automatic separation of integration insufficiency from MCMC non-convergence via split n_int vs n_int/2 chains and R-hat/ESS warnings; lowers default n_int to 64; disables cumulative integration saving by default.. Cites doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169: Formalizes assessing integration error with a split-chain R-hat algorithm when per-individual AgD integrals make cumulative-error plots infeasible; documents multinma implementation.. Cites doi:10.1111/rssa.12579: Defines ML-NMR as hierarchical IPD+AgD synthesis with QMC integration; earlier source for empirical integration-error plots and for C1–C2 method claims..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=3) → R8:overstated-majority(n=3)

title: Bayesian component ML-NMR and bridge models lack SBC validation
text:
Statement
Simulation-based calibration checks that an implementation recovers its own generative model: draw parameters from the exact fitted prior, simulate data, refit, and test rank uniformity of the true value among posterior draws (Talts et al., arXiv:1804.06788). No such study has been found for Bayesian component ML-NMR or bridge models; the code auditor confirmed that cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub and not on CRAN, has no SBC harness in its tracked source, and the literature and recency auditors searched and found nothing published, which is unrefuted absence rather than proof. The criterion itself needs updating: Modrak et al. (arXiv:2211.02383) show that rank uniformity of parameter draws alone cannot detect a posterior equal to the prior, which is precisely the failure mode of CMU-02, so data-dependent test quantities such as the joint log-likelihood have to be added. Passing SBC in any form validates code and computation, not the scientific assumptions.

title: Bayesian component ML-NMR and bridge models lack SBC validation
text:
Why it is open
SBC requires drawing from the exact prior used in fitting, which is awkward when that prior is hierarchical and constrained; the integration scheme, contrary to the source, belongs to the likelihood computation rather than to an implicit prior, so it is not what obstructs the draw. The real deterrent is cost: a simulate-and-refit loop over hundreds of replicates of a model that is already expensive to fit once. And because SBC detects only coding and computational error, a study that runs it can present a pass as scientific validation, which leaves the misspecification question untouched while appearing to have answered it.

title: Failed fits are deleted rather than classified and reported
text:
Statement
Dropping failed or non-converged replicates makes every reported performance figure conditional on the method having worked, and when failure depends on scenario difficulty or on the size of the estimation error those figures can favor the more fragile method. The general solution is already published: Pawel et al. (arXiv:2409.18527; The American Statistician, doi:10.1080/00031305.2025.2540002) review 482 simulation studies, find that only 23% mention missingness at all, 19% report its frequency and 14% report how it was handled, propose a classification of failure types with handling options, and state the direction of the bias explicitly. What remains open is adoption in ITC and PAIC, where no equivalent review or typed failure reporting was found, plus one extension: their taxonomy does not separate a principled refusal to estimate a non-estimable contrast from a numerical convergence failure, and in this field that distinction carries scientific content.

title: Failed fits are deleted rather than classified and reported
text:
Why it is open
Failures are not missing at random with respect to the truth: separation, non-overlap, weak identification and sampler breakdown occur in the same cells that produce the largest errors, so deleting the failing method’s replicates while keeping the others’ flatters the method that failed. Software defaults reinforce the practice by returning NA values that pipelines drop without comment, and reviewers cannot detect the deletion because the per-cell replicate count is usually not reported. A conceptual problem also remains in what ‘reporting performance including failures’ means: an absent estimate has no bias and no interval coverage, so failure rates and conditional performance have to sit side by side unless a prespecified loss or worst-case rule combines them.

text:

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Simulation studies silently drop non-converged or failed replicates instead of publishing a classification of the failures, so every reported performance figure is conditional on the method having worked. What was wrong with it. The source proposed a failure classification as new work. It states explicitly that deleting only the failing method’s replicates biases results in favor of that method, and cites the Peduzzi ‘ten events per variable’ rule as an influential result later shown to be driven by non-convergence handling. So the general-methodology solution now exists (2025) and the residual gap is adoption in ITC/PAIC, where I found no equivalent review. If failures are omitted, bias, RMSE, and coverage describe performance conditional on successful estimation rather than unconditional operational performance. C2 requires an explicit condition: the failure mechanism must depend on scenario difficulty, the latent estimation error, or both. The direction and effect on method ranking are not guaranteed mathematically. title: Published PAIC analyses do not record the choices that drive them
text: CMU-07 Unverifiable High priority Emerging

title: Published PAIC analyses do not record the choices that drive them
text:
Statement
The choices that determine a population-adjusted estimate (covariate selection and exclusion, weight trimming, priors, target population definition, survival curve reconstruction settings) are frequently not reported, and this is now documented rather than asserted: Truong et al. (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1653) reviewed 106 articles and 157 PAIC analyses and found conduct and reporting ‘remarkably heterogeneous and suboptimal in current practice’, Farinasso et al. (doi:10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088) found 3 of 117 oncology MAICs met all NICE recommendations with weight distributions and effect-modifier evidence among the least reported items, and Phillippo et al. 2019 (PMID 31190671) documents covariate selection in NICE appraisals resting variously on availability, expert opinion, effective sample size, statistical significance or cross-validation. No released PAIC package emits a standalone analysis manifest or model card; cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, stores priors, targets, selected covariates, seed and integration settings inside its fitted objects but exports no manifest and records neither the covariate-selection rationale nor upstream survival reconstruction. Shared executable code can recover many of these choices, so the failure is one of disclosure and machine-readability rather than of absolute irrecoverability.

title: Published PAIC analyses do not record the choices that drive them
text:
Why it is open
The decisive choices are made before any model is fitted and leave no trace in the printed estimate, so a reviewer has only the analyst’s narration to check and no artifact to check it against. Package defaults fill the gaps silently, which turns scientific decisions into settings chosen by the package author, and because the analysis looks complete without disclosure there is no error signal prompting it. Fitted objects can hold much of this, as cpaic shows, but nothing exports it in a form a reviewer can read without running R, and the upstream choices (how a survival curve was reconstructed, why a covariate was in or out) sit outside the fitted object entirely. HTA timelines reward a defensible-looking number over an auditable pipeline, so the documentation effort is unrewarded exactly where the stakes are highest.

title: Published PAIC analyses do not record the choices that drive them
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Truong et al. 2023, Population adjusted-indirect comparisons in health technology assessment: a methodological systematic review, Research Synthesis Methods
reviews 106 articles and 157 PAIC analyses and concludes that conduct and reporting are remarkably heterogeneous and suboptimal, with model-fitting results adequately reported in 3 of the 18 analyses that required an outcome model

title: Published PAIC analyses do not record the choices that drive them
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The fitted objects already carry much of the specification, so the near-term work is an export: a machine-readable manifest or model card generated from the fit, covering the covariate set with the reason for each inclusion and exclusion, any trimming rule, the priors, the target definition, the reconstruction settings and the diagnostics. Extend it upstream to survival curve reconstruction and to the covariate-selection rationale, which no fitted object currently holds. Require environment capture in some form, with a container as one implementation rather than as the requirement itself, and pair the manifest with a registry-style pre-specified analysis plan so what was done can be compared with what was planned.

title: Deciding which covariates are true effect modifiers
text: COV-01 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising

title: Deciding which covariates are true effect modifiers
text:
Statement
There is no agreed default for choosing the effect-modifier set: the right set depends on the treatment contrast, estimand, effect scale, design and available support, and in the small samples typical of these analyses significance screening is unstable while balancing on every available covariate can destroy overlap and exhaust the information available for interaction terms. Reviews document what applied work does: NICE technology appraisals selected covariates by availability, expert opinion, effective sample size, statistical significance or cross-validation (Phillippo et al. 2019, doi:10.1017/S0266462319000333); of 117 oncology MAICs only 3 met all NICE recommendations, with evidence of effect-modifier status among the least reported items (Farinasso 2025, doi:10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088); and no study among 27 CAR-T indirect comparisons described its identification methodology (Neumann 2026, doi:10.57264/cer-2026-0033). Adjustment sets are not uniformly small: those reviews report anywhere from no adjustment to 19 covariates, and a median of 6 (range 1 to 13) for unanchored analyses. A formal causal covariate-selection procedure does exist for transporting experimental results (Egami and Hartman, arxiv:1909.02669), but it assumes richer target data than an aggregate-data comparator supplies, and it has not been benchmarked for this setting.

title: Deciding which covariates are true effect modifiers
text:
Why it is open
Interaction terms carry far less information than main effects, so a data-driven modifier set fluctuates across resamples and the downstream interval is conditional on a selection event that is never reported. Balancing on everything trades that instability for a support problem: extra balancing constraints usually make the weights harder to satisfy and cut effective sample size, though not monotonically, and extra interaction terms consume information the network may not hold. Clinical elicitation, the remaining route, is incomplete and not free of the analyst’s interest in the result. Because the rationale is seldom documented the same evidence base yields different adjustment sets in different submissions, and getting the set wrong has measured consequences: all population adjustment methods incur bias when an effect modifier is missing (Phillippo et al. 2020, doi:10.1002/sim.8759).

title: Deciding which covariates are true effect modifiers
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al., 2019
Reviews population adjustment in NICE technology appraisals and records that covariates were included ‘based on: availability, expert opinion, effective sample size, statistical significance, or cross-validation’; the audit uses it to source the ad hoc and significance-screening claims, and it reports a median of 6 covariates (range 1 to 13) for unanchored analyses.


Farinasso, 2025
Scoping review of 117 oncology MAICs focused on reporting quality; only 3 fulfilled all NICE recommendations, and evidence of effect-modifier status and the distribution of weights were among the least reported items.


Neumann, 2026
Systematic review of 27 CAR-T indirect comparisons; covariates were chosen from clinical expertise or literature review but ‘no study provided a detailed description of the identification methodology’, and adjustment ranged from none to 19 covariates.


Egami and Hartman, 2021
Formal causal covariate-selection procedure based on estimated separating sets for generalizing experimental results; adjacent prior art that assumes richer target data than an aggregate-data comparator provides.


Phillippo et al., 2020
Simulation study of anchored population adjustment methods; all methods incur bias when an effect modifier is missing, which is the consequence of getting the modifier set wrong.

title: Deciding which covariates are true effect modifiers
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Prespecify the selection process and record it: causal and clinical knowledge, cross-trial interaction evidence, prognostic strength where the design is unanchored or the strategy is precision-oriented, measurement comparability, expected imbalance between source and target, support and estimability consequences, and predeclared sensitivity sets over alternative modifier lists. The gap to fill is not a way to encode nonlinear covariate effects, which splines and basis expansions already do, but a way to choose and estimate them when interaction information is sparse. Adapt and benchmark the existing separating-set procedure (arxiv:1909.02669) for the case where the target is known only through published summaries, and report uncertainty for the whole procedure including selection, whether by sample splitting, cross-fitting, resampling the entire selection procedure, selective inference, shrinkage or model averaging. Minimum covariate reporting sets for aggregate-data publications would make any of this auditable.

title: Deciding which covariates are true effect modifiers
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Effect-modifier transport is the entire reason population adjustment exists, yet there is no defensible default for choosing the modifier set: significance-based screening rests on underpowered interaction tests, adjusting for every available covariate destroys overlap and can leave the interaction model unidentified, and clinical elicitation is incomplete. Applied work uses small ad hoc covariate sets with weak overlap diagnostics and poorly reported selection rationale.”
What was wrong with it. The claim was unattributed in the source, which also said applied work uses ‘small ad hoc covariate sets’; the literature auditor supplied real references, so the ad hoc-selection, weak-diagnostic and poor-rationale claims are now sourced to three reviews (doi:10.1017/S0266462319000333, doi:10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088, doi:10.57264/cer-2026-0033), the last of which contradicts ‘small’ by reporting adjustment sets that range from none to 19 covariates. The code auditor struck two further claims: splines and basis expansions already encode nonlinear covariate effects, so only their selection and estimation under sparse data is unresolved, and honest sample splitting is one valid inferential strategy among several rather than a necessity.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Retrieved three empirical reviews that source this entry’s unsourced claims. Phillippo 2019 (NICE TAs) reports covariates ‘included based on: availability, expert opinion, effective sample size, statistical significance, or cross-validation’ — sourcing both the significance-screening and ad hoc claims. Farinasso 2025 (117 oncology MAICs) reports only 3 met all NICE recommendations and that ‘the least reported aspects were the adjustment for all effect modifiers and prognostic variables…, evidence of effect modifier status, and distribution of weights’ — sourcing the poor-rationale and weak-diagnostics claims. Neumann 2026 (27 CAR-T ITCs) states ‘no study provided a detailed description of the identification methodology’ and that standardized approaches are ‘urgently needed’. Caveat: the same review contradicts ‘small’ covariate sets (range: none to 19 covariates); Phillippo 2019 gives median 6, range 1-13 for unanchored. The ‘no benchmarked pipeline’ claim is an absence claim I cannot verify; a formal separating-set selection algorithm exists for generalization (Egami & Hartman), just not benchmarked with an aggregate-data target. Cites doi:10.1017/S0266462319000333: Sources the claims that applied PAIC selects covariates ad hoc and partly by statistical significance. Cites doi:10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088: Sources the weak-diagnostics and poor-reporting-of-rationale claims with numbers (117 studies, 3 compliant). Cites doi:10.57264/cer-2026-0033: A source that itself asserts the absence of a standardized covariate-identification approach. Cites arxiv:1909.02669: A formal causal covariate-selection procedure (estimated separating sets) for transporting effects; adjacent prior art the entry does not cite, though it assumes richer target data than a PAIC aggregate-data comparator provides. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.8759: Sources the consequence of getting the modifier set wrong.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The underlying selection problem is genuinely open because the needed adjustment set is specific to the treatment contrast, estimand, effect scale, design, and available support. The compound claim is nevertheless too broad. C3-C6 and C8 are prevalence or consensus claims with no supplied evidence. C7 is false as written: splines, basis expansions, and prespecified interactions already encode nonlinear effects; choosing and estimating them under sparse data is the unresolved part. C9 and C11 are common finite-sample risks, not universal facts. C12 holds when selection is ignored, and C15 is false as a necessity because cross-fitting, resampling the full selection procedure, selective inference, shrinkage or model averaging, and external prespecification are alternatives. Added balance constraints often worsen feasibility and ESS but need not reduce ESS monotonically. At cpaic@9d150e9, no modifier-selection pipeline is exported; cstc() and cmaic() accept analyst-specified sets and default to all IPD covariates. Very-high priority is warranted only when plausible modifier omission and weak support can materially move the target contrast.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Design-dependent roles of prognostic covariates
text: COV-03 Overstated High priority Established

title: Design-dependent roles of prognostic covariates
text:
Statement
Whether a strong prognostic non-modifier should be adjusted for depends on the estimand and the design, not on the variable alone. For a conditional or collapsible effect in an anchored comparison, balancing such a variable spends effective sample size without removing bias, although including it in an outcome model can improve precision. For non-collapsible measures such as the odds ratio or hazard ratio, a variable that is purely prognostic on the conditional scale can still change the marginal effect, so cross-study imbalance in it can bias an anchored marginal comparison even when marginal covariate moments are balanced (Remiro-Azocar 2024, doi:10.1002/sim.10111). In unanchored comparisons, omitting prognostic variables biases the cross-study contrast on any scale.

title: Design-dependent roles of prognostic covariates
text:
Why it is open
Covariate role is a function of the estimand, the effect scale and the evidence structure, and the clean split between anchored and unanchored designs holds only on collapsible or conditional scales; once the target is a marginal odds ratio or hazard ratio, prognostic distributions matter for transport too. Applied analyses and guidance still carry one covariate list across both designs, so either the effective-sample-size cost or the bias is paid without being noticed. Software support is uneven rather than absent: the cSTC interface in the development package cpaic already separates prognostic main effects from treatment interactions while its cML-NMR path has no prognostic-only role, and cpaic is an unreleased GitHub development version, commit 9d150e9, not installable from CRAN. The numbers that exist cover a transported risk difference, so the trade-off has not been quantified where non-collapsibility makes it hardest.

title: Design-dependent roles of prognostic covariates
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Webster-Clark, 2024
Variable selection when estimating effects in external target populations; quantifies in one simulation the precision penalty of adjusting for non-effect-measure-modifiers and the bias from omitting modifiers when transporting a risk difference.


Campbell and Remiro-Azocar, 2025
Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect comparisons; uses prognostic covariates through the outcome model rather than through balancing constraints, with higher precision than non-augmented weighting.


Remiro-Azocar, 2024
Counter-evidence to the source’s first claim: unadjusted anchored indirect comparisons can be biased even when marginal covariate moments are balanced, so adjustment for purely prognostic variables may be necessary for non-collapsible marginal estimands.


cpaic, commit 9d150e9
Unreleased development R package on GitHub, not on CRAN; its cSTC function already separates prognostic main effects from treatment interactions, while its cML-NMR function has no prognostic-only covariate role, so the proposed software separation is partly present already.

title: Design-dependent roles of prognostic covariates
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Index covariate role by estimand and scale in guidance and in software, keeping the modifier set required for bias removal separate from the prognostic set used for precision, and complete that separation in the code paths that lack it rather than designing it from scratch. Extend the existing simulation evidence from a transported risk difference (doi:10.1093/aje/kwae048) to non-collapsible measures, so the anchored penalty and the unanchored bias are quantified where the design-based rule breaks down. Extend the augmented weighting approach (arxiv:2505.00113), which already uses prognostic covariates without balancing constraints, from the single-source unanchored case to anchored comparisons and to networks.

title: Design-dependent roles of prognostic covariates
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. On a collapsible effect scale, or for a conditional estimand, balancing strong prognostic variables that are not effect modifiers in an anchored comparison reduces effective sample size without removing bias; for non-collapsible measures such as the odds ratio or hazard ratio, purely prognostic variables can modify the marginal effect, so cross-trial imbalance in them can bias even an anchored marginal comparison and adjustment may be warranted. In unanchored comparisons, omitting prognostic variables biases the cross-study contrast on any scale.
The source said. “Whether a strong prognostic variable that is not an effect modifier should be adjusted for depends on the design: in anchored analyses balancing it can reduce effective sample size without reducing bias, whereas in unanchored analyses omitting prognostic variables can directly bias cross-study contrasts. Precision-oriented methods may use such variables differently again.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors judged the source’s first claim too strong: it holds on a collapsible scale or for a conditional estimand, but under non-collapsibility purely prognostic variables can modify the marginal effect, so an anchored comparison can be biased even with balanced marginal moments and adjustment may be warranted (doi:10.1002/sim.10111). The source also said no guidance covers the precision-oriented intermediate case; Campbell and Remiro-Azocar 2025 (arxiv:2505.00113) give an augmented estimator that uses prognostic covariates through an outcome model without imposing balance constraints on them, and Webster-Clark 2024 (doi:10.1093/aje/kwae048) already quantifies the precision penalty of adjusting for non-modifiers and the bias from omitting modifiers in one simulation.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The first and fifth claims are false as stated for non-collapsible measures. Remiro-Azocar 2024 (Stat Med, read verbatim) concludes that ‘Unadjusted anchored indirect comparisons can be biased in the absence of individual-level treatment effect heterogeneity, or when marginal covariate moments are balanced across studies’, and that adjustment ‘may be necessary to account for cross-study imbalances in joint covariate distributions involving purely prognostic variables’. So balancing a purely prognostic variable in an anchored comparison does not merely cost effective sample size; on the odds-ratio or hazard-ratio scale it can remove real bias in the marginal estimand. Separately, the precision half of the problem is partly answered: Webster-Clark 2024 quantifies in one simulation both the precision cost of including non-modifiers and the bias from omitting modifiers, and Campbell & Remiro-Azocar 2025 give an augmented estimator that uses prognostic covariates in an outcome model for precision without imposing balance constraints on them, reporting ‘higher precision than all non-augmented weighting estimators’. Cites doi:10.1093/aje/kwae048: Quantifies, in a single simulation, the precision penalty of adjusting for non-effect-measure-modifiers and the bias from omitting modifiers when transporting a risk difference. Cites arxiv:2505.00113: Shows how prognostic covariates can be used for precision through the outcome model rather than through balancing constraints, i.e. the ‘intermediate case’ the entry says has no guidance.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is correct for a conditional or collapsible target contrast when the variable truly is not an effect modifier on that scale: balancing it can spend ESS without removing bias, while including it as an outcome-model main effect may improve precision. It is not generally correct for a marginal odds ratio or hazard ratio, because a purely prognostic variable on the conditional scale can change the marginal contrast through non-collapsibility. C2-C4 are broadly correct for unanchored absolute-outcome comparisons, provided the prognostic factor differs between studies and is otherwise uncontrolled. C5 confuses modifier selection with inclusion as a prognostic nuisance variable and its word ‘only’ misses non-collapsibility and proxy-variable cases. cpaic@9d150e9 already lets cstc() separate prognostic main effects from treatment interactions, while cmlnmr() explicitly lacks a prognostic-only role. Thus the software-design part is only partially open; the unanchored identification issue is decision-critical, while the anchored efficiency issue is a roadmap item. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9: cstc() already implements separate treatment-interaction and prognostic-main-effect roles; cmlnmr() does not, so only part of the proposed software separation is present..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Legitimate versus dangerous roles for flexible learners
text: COV-05 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Legitimate versus dangerous roles for flexible learners
text:
Statement
Flexible learners such as BART, causal forests, Gaussian processes, neural additive models and super learner can estimate nuisance functions, outcome surfaces or heterogeneous effects inside an identified PAIC analysis, but numerically well-behaved predictions do not repair missing overlap or missing information about the target distribution, and generic predictive feature importance is not evidence of effect modification. Neither auditor found a PAIC-specific protocol separating the roles where these learners help from the roles where they mislead. Two of the source’s prohibitions do not hold as written: causal forests are constructed for causal heterogeneity under assumptions rather than for prediction alone, and variable importance can be defined on the CATE itself with inference (PermuCATE, arxiv:2408.13002), so what is disqualified is predictive importance from an outcome model, not importance measures in general.

title: Legitimate versus dangerous roles for flexible learners
text:
Why it is open
Whether a flexible fit is legitimate depends on an identified target estimand, adequate joint support, suitable target data, nuisance-rate conditions and an uncertainty procedure, and none of those is delivered by predictive accuracy; many learners return smooth predictions outside the region where the causal quantity is identified, which is exactly where an answer is most wanted. The event counts available for treatment interactions in typical trials are far below what nonparametric interaction estimation needs, so an apparently rich fit can be estimating noise. Reusing one sample for discovery, tuning, estimation and uncertainty breaks the guarantees of most procedures unless the inference explicitly accounts for the adaptivity. What is missing is a PAIC-specific protocol tying each role to the conditions under which it is defensible.

title: Legitimate versus dangerous roles for flexible learners
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Paillard et al. (PermuCATE)
Conditional permutation importance for the conditional average treatment effect, giving statistically rigorous global variable importance defined on the CATE; counter-evidence to the blanket claim that machine-learning importance can never be read causally.

title: Legitimate versus dangerous roles for flexible learners
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write the protocol conditionally rather than as a list of bans: name the target estimand and the support and target-data conditions that must hold, then state which use of a flexible learner is licensed under them, covering nuisance estimation inside AIPW, TMLE or DML, discovery of candidate nonlinear modifiers for later confirmation, flexible standardization, and support diagnostics or outcome-model stress testing. Replace the blanket prohibition on feature importance with a requirement that any importance claim use a causally defined estimand such as the CATE-based measure in arxiv:2408.13002. Require an inference procedure that accounts for adaptive fitting, with cross-fitting as one accepted route alongside external training, independent splitting and a bootstrap that repeats tuning and estimation, and require support diagnostics before any extrapolation to an unsupported target.

title: Legitimate versus dangerous roles for flexible learners
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Flexible learners such as BART, causal forests, Gaussian processes, neural additive models and super learner can estimate complex outcome or participation models in PAIC, but their useful roles are narrow and their misuses are common. The report enumerates four legitimate roles and four dangerous ones, with no protocol enforcing the distinction.”
What was wrong with it. The source said interpreting machine-learning feature importance as causal effect modification is invalid, and that using one sample for discovery, tuning, estimation and uncertainty without cross-fitting invalidates the inference. The literature auditor cited PermuCATE (arxiv:2408.13002), a conditional-permutation importance measure defined directly on the CATE with inference, and the code auditor noted that valid inference can also rest on parametric or empirical-process restrictions, external training data, independent sample splitting, or a bootstrap that repeats tuning and estimation.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Most of the enumerated claims are standard causal-machine-learning knowledge rather than contested propositions: flexible learners as nuisance estimators inside AIPW/TMLE/DML and the cross-fitting requirement are the defining features of double machine learning, and extrapolation to unsupported regions is a general property of predictive fits. I found no PAIC-specific protocol separating legitimate from dangerous roles, but ‘no protocol exists’ is an absence claim I cannot verify, so I do not credit it. One claim is too blunt as worded. ‘Interpreting machine-learning feature importance as causal effect modification is invalid’ is right about predictive importance, but Paillard et al. (PermuCATE) develops conditional-permutation variable importance defined directly on the CATE with inference, i.e. a causally-defined importance measure for exactly this question. The defensible version is that predictive feature importance from an outcome model is not evidence of effect modification, not that no importance measure can be causal.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1-C5 describe technically possible uses, but legitimacy depends on an identified target estimand, adequate joint support, suitable target data, nuisance-rate conditions, and an uncertainty procedure. Causal forests are specifically constructed for causal heterogeneity under assumptions, so the blanket statement that these learners are optimized only for prediction is inaccurate. C6 is right for generic predictive feature importance, but a formally defined causal variable-importance estimand is a different object. C7 is context-dependent, and C8 should say that many learners can return numerically smooth predictions outside support, not that extrapolation is inevitable. C9 is categorically false: cross-fitting is often valuable for flexible nuisance estimation, but valid inference can instead rest on parametric or empirical-process restrictions, external training, independent sample splitting, or a bootstrap that repeats tuning and estimation. At cpaic@9d150e9 none of the named learners is implemented; the exported forest() is a forest-plot function, not a causal forest. A PAIC-specific protocol remains open, but this is conditional guidance and validation rather than a universally critical missing method.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Unknown target joint covariate distribution
text:
Statement
For marginal standardization of a nonlinear or nonseparable outcome model, published marginal summaries do not identify the features of the target joint covariate law that the estimand needs, and different compatible dependence structures can give materially different answers. The reconstruction step is not missing: multilevel network meta-regression has built the aggregate-data joint distribution with a Gaussian copula matched to IPD correlations since 2020 (Phillippo et al. 2020, doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), and multinma::add_integration() ships it, creating quasi-Monte Carlo integration points from a Gaussian copula and Sobol sequences with user-supplied or IPD-derived correlations (cran:multinma). What is missing is a standard way to carry the non-identification of the dependence structure into the reported interval, and PAIC-specific work on the alternatives the source lists: maximum-entropy reconstruction, distributionally robust standardization and multiple synthetic target populations. The problem also does not touch every estimand, since an additive identity-link model depends only on the target means and moment-calibration weighting can be defined from reported moments without reconstructing the joint law.

title: Unknown target joint covariate distribution
text:
Why it is open
Published marginals constrain only the one-dimensional margins, so an infinite family of joint laws is compatible with them, and standardization of a nonlinear model is not a function of the margins alone. The shipped fix is an assumption rather than a solution: importing correlations from the IPD trial presumes exactly the cross-trial stability that population adjustment exists to question, and the assumption does not appear in the output. No standard machinery propagates that structural uncertainty into the reported interval, and any covariate not reported at all cannot be balanced, so the achievable adjustment is bounded by the comparator publication rather than by the method.

title: Unknown target joint covariate distribution
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al., 2020
Multilevel network meta-regression: reconstructs the aggregate-data joint covariate distribution with a Gaussian copula whose correlations come from the IPD studies while retaining the published marginals, and integrates the individual-level model over it.


multinma (R package, version 0.9.1)
add_integration() ‘creates Quasi-Monte Carlo numerical integration points using a Gaussian copula and Sobol sequences’, taking a weighted correlation matrix from the IPD studies when none is supplied, with a cor_adjust option; the shipped implementation of the reconstruction the source treats as a candidate direction.

title: Unknown target joint covariate distribution
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on the shipped copula machinery instead of proposing it: add sensitivity analysis over the dependence parameters and a route for the resulting structural uncertainty to reach the reported interval. Develop partial-identification or distributionally robust standardization that reports the range of the effect over joint distributions compatible with the published moments, and test maximum-entropy reconstruction against the copula default on the same networks. Multiple synthetic target populations qualify as multiple imputation only when they are draws from a specified posterior predictive imputation model; otherwise report them as sensitivity scenarios rather than combining them with Rubin’s rules. Privacy-preserving release of richer summaries, including cross-moments and quantiles, would shrink the problem at its source.

title: Unknown target joint covariate distribution
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “ML-NMR, g-computation and weighting all require the target joint covariate distribution, but aggregate-data publications typically report only marginal means, standard deviations or proportions, and the joint law is not identified by those summaries. Assuming independence or borrowing correlations from the IPD source can materially change nonlinear standardized effects.”
What was wrong with it. The source listed copulas among candidate directions to pursue; copula reconstruction has been the operating default of ML-NMR for six years and ships in multinma::add_integration() with a correlation-adjustment option (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579, cran:multinma), which the literature auditor documented. The code auditor narrowed the scope: the claim that ML-NMR, g-computation and weighting all require the target joint distribution is false as a blanket statement, so the problem belongs to nonlinear marginal standardization rather than to every PAIC estimand.
Dissent. codex dissented (open): C1 is correct for marginal ML-NMR or g-computation standardization, but cpaic’s cML-NMR output at 9d150e9 is a conditional contrast at x, not a marginal standardized effect. The blanket statement about weighting is false: calibration weighting can be defined from reported moments without reconstructing the full joint law, subject to its density-ratio and balance assumptions. C2-C3 are unsourced prevalence claims. C4-C7 are correct for nonlinear or nonseparable standardized response functions: with at least two covariates, marginals do not identify the copula, and equal marginals can yield materially different effects. They are not universal; an additive identity-link model depends only on means. C8, C10, and C11 are candidate assumptions, sensitivity analyses, or partial-identification methods, not recovery of an unidentified joint law. C12 is valid as multiple imputation only if synthetic populations are draws from a specified posterior predictive imputation model; arbitrary dependence scenarios are sensitivity analyses and Rubin-style combining rules are not justified. C13-C14 are sound. cpaic already implements Gaussian-copula QMC integration with a user-supplied correlation and otherwise borrows pooled within-IPD correlation, but it does not identify the target correlation or propagate that structural uncertainty. This is very high priority for nonlinear marginal standardization from sparse AgD, not for every PAIC estimand.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The non-identification claim is correct and the problem is real, but the entry treats copulas as a candidate direction when copula reconstruction has been the operating default of the leading method for six years. Phillippo et al. 2020 (JRSS-A) constructs the joint covariate distribution for aggregate-data studies with a Gaussian copula so that the correlation matrix matches the IPD studies while retaining the published marginals, and multinma’s add_integration() implements this: it ‘creates Quasi-Monte Carlo numerical integration points using a Gaussian copula and Sobol’ sequences’, taking a weighted correlation matrix from all IPD studies when cor is NULL, with cor_adjust for Spearman/Pearson/copula correlations. So ‘Copulas and maximum entropy are promising tools’ reads as decorative: for copulas it is implemented, documented and default, and the ML-NMR literature has examined varying the assumed correlation structure. The genuinely open parts are the ones the entry states well: propagating the non-identification into the reported interval, and the max-entropy, distributionally-robust and multiple-synthetic-target alternatives, for which I found no PAIC-specific work. Cites doi:10.1111/rssa.12579: Reconstructs the aggregate-data joint covariate distribution with a Gaussian copula and IPD-derived correlations, and integrates the individual-level model over it. Cites cran:multinma: Shipped implementation of copula-based joint-distribution reconstruction with user-supplied or IPD-derived correlations.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 is correct for marginal ML-NMR or g-computation standardization, but cpaic’s cML-NMR output at 9d150e9 is a conditional contrast at x, not a marginal standardized effect. The blanket statement about weighting is false: calibration weighting can be defined from reported moments without reconstructing the full joint law, subject to its density-ratio and balance assumptions. C2-C3 are unsourced prevalence claims. C4-C7 are correct for nonlinear or nonseparable standardized response functions: with at least two covariates, marginals do not identify the copula, and equal marginals can yield materially different effects. They are not universal; an additive identity-link model depends only on means. C8, C10, and C11 are candidate assumptions, sensitivity analyses, or partial-identification methods, not recovery of an unidentified joint law. C12 is valid as multiple imputation only if synthetic populations are draws from a specified posterior predictive imputation model; arbitrary dependence scenarios are sensitivity analyses and Rubin-style combining rules are not justified. C13-C14 are sound. cpaic already implements Gaussian-copula QMC integration with a user-supplied correlation and otherwise borrows pooled within-IPD correlation, but it does not identify the target correlation or propagate that structural uncertainty. This is very high priority for nonlinear marginal standardization from sparse AgD, not for every PAIC estimand.

title: Measurement non-equivalence of covariates across trials
text: COV-09 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Measurement non-equivalence of covariates across trials
text:
Statement
Nominally identical covariates may be recorded on different assays, scales, thresholds, timings, assessors or definitions, so unless measurement invariance or a source-to-target crosswalk is established, balancing the recorded summaries does not guarantee balance of the underlying construct. Classical nondifferential additive error attenuates a linear treatment-by-covariate interaction, but differential error, Berkson error, misclassification, correlated error, nonlinear links and non-collapsible estimands can bias the interaction in either direction. Machinery exists for adjacent cases: correction strategies for covariate-balancing weights under measurement error in the individual-level single-sample setting (Wen and Yan 2024, arxiv:2406.09163), and multiple-imputation harmonization of non-commensurate measures using external calibration studies that administered both instruments (Siddique et al. 2015, doi:10.1002/sim.6562). Neither covers the PAIC case, where the mismeasurement can differ between source and target and the target is a published summary.

title: Measurement non-equivalence of covariates across trials
text:
Why it is open
Balancing and standardization operate on the recorded number, so a systematic measurement difference passes through as if it were a real difference in patient characteristics, and reports usually give a variable name and a summary statistic without the assay, cut-point or timing that would reveal the discrepancy. Without metadata, bridge information or defensible mapping assumptions, balance on the latent covariate and the transported effect are not identified from ordinary PAIC inputs, which makes this decision-critical when the variable is a strong effect modifier. The existing corrections need linking data that PAIC usually lacks, and even where calibration studies exist, imputation-based harmonization can fail to recover accurate values (counter-evidence in the audit record, doi:10.1007/s11121-017-0760-x).

title: Measurement non-equivalence of covariates across trials
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wen and Yan, 2024
Covariate balancing with measurement error: notes that covariate balancing assumes all covariates are accurately measured and proposes correction strategies for the individual-level single-sample observational case, which is the machinery closest to MAIC weights.


Siddique et al., 2015
Multiple imputation for harmonizing longitudinal non-commensurate measures in individual participant data meta-analysis, using external calibration studies in which both versions of the measure were administered; the linking-study route the source proposes, already implemented.


Counter-evidence in the audit record, 2017
Cited by the literature auditor as evidence that imputation-based harmonization can fail: ‘Even after reducing the scale of our application, we were still unable to produce accurate imputations of the missing values.’ The audit record supplies no title for this reference.

title: Measurement non-equivalence of covariates across trials
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the two existing lines to this setting: covariate-balancing corrections under measurement error (arxiv:2406.09163) assume one individual-level sample, and imputation-based harmonization (doi:10.1002/sim.6562) assumes access to both instruments, so both need a version in which the target is an aggregate summary and the error may be differential between source and target. Where no linking information exists, report explicit sensitivity ranges over the measurement mapping rather than treating calibration equations or paired bridge studies as prerequisites, and run cut-point sensitivity analysis where a continuous variable has been dichotomized differently. Reporting the assay, cut-point and timing alongside the covariate summary is a cheap partial fix that would at least make the discrepancy detectable.

title: Measurement non-equivalence of covariates across trials
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Covariates carrying the same name across trials are frequently measured on different assays, scales, timings or definitions, so a target mean of nominally the same variable is not a meaningful balancing constraint and adjusting for it does not balance the same underlying construct. Measurement error in an effect modifier usually attenuates interaction estimates and may leave substantial residual transport bias.”
What was wrong with it. The source said measurement error ‘usually’ attenuates interaction estimates and that balancing a mismeasured covariate can leave more residual imbalance than not adjusting at all; the code auditor restricted the attenuation result to classical nondifferential additive error in a linear interaction model, and neither auditor could verify the worse-than-nothing claim, which is plausible only under systematic study-specific scale, offset or classification differences. The literature auditor sourced the calibration and linking-study elements to arxiv:2406.09163 and doi:10.1002/sim.6562, and the code auditor rejected the framing that calibration equations, linking studies and cut-point sensitivity analysis are requirements rather than options.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The mechanism claims are sound and one is now directly sourced. Wen & Yan 2024 states that covariate balancing’s validity ‘relies on an implicit assumption that all covariates are accurately measured, which is frequently violated’, that ‘the impact of measurement error on covariate balancing is unclear, and there is no existing work on balancing mismeasured covariates adequately’, and then proposes correction strategies; since MAIC weights are entropy-balancing weights, this is the closest existing machinery to the entry’s problem, in the single-sample observational case. The linking-study claim is also already realized: Siddique et al. 2015 harmonize non-commensurate measures across trials by multiple imputation using ‘external calibration studies in which both depression measures were used’. Two caveats. Neither covers the PAIC-defining case, where the mismeasurement is differential between source and target and the target is a published summary. And the strongest claim, that balancing a mismeasured covariate can leave more residual imbalance than not adjusting at all, I could not verify against any retrieved source; treat it as unevidenced. Cites arxiv:2406.09163: Measurement-error correction strategies for covariate balancing weights, the same estimating machinery MAIC uses, in the individual-level single-sample case. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.6562: Sources the linking-study and calibration claims: an implemented cross-study harmonization method using external calibration studies measuring both versions of a variable.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C3-C8 describe valid forms of operational non-equivalence, although C7 concerns outcome-measure heterogeneity unless the assessment is used as a baseline covariate. Formally, if study s records W_s = a_s + b_s X + U_s, equality of recorded means does not imply equality of the latent X means without measurement invariance or a known crosswalk. C2 is nevertheless too categorical: differing procedures do not invalidate a target mean when their equivalence or transformation is established. C9 holds for classical, nondifferential additive error in a correctly specified linear treatment-by-covariate model, where the interaction is attenuated by a reliability factor. Differential error, Berkson error, misclassification, correlated error, nonlinear links, and non-collapsible estimands can bias interactions in either direction. C10 is therefore possible but conditional. C11 is possible under systematic study-specific scale, offset, or classification differences; simple classical attenuation alone ordinarily yields partial correction rather than greater bias than no adjustment. C12, C14, and C15 overstate necessity. What is required is identifying information or assumptions about the cross-study measurement mapping, or an explicit sensitivity analysis when it remains unidentified. A dedicated paired linking study and cut-point sensitivity analysis are useful routes, not universal requirements. Calibration and latent-variable models address C13 only to the extent their mapping assumptions are supported. Without metadata, bridge information, or defensible mapping assumptions, latent covariate balance and the transported effect remain unidentified from ordinary PAIC inputs, so the core problem remains open and can be decision-critical when the variable is a strong effect modifier.

Decision path
