title: No factorial study ranks which choice most often flips a decision
text: DEC-02 Overstated Very high priority Emerging

title: No factorial study ranks which choice most often flips a decision
text:
Statement
No study has crossed bridge type, prior specification, target-population definition and outcome model in a factorial design scored on decision reversals, so there is no ranking of which structural choice most often flips a recommendation. Individual factors have been examined: Jiang et al. 2025 (10.1017/rsm.2025.10) construct a MAIC paradox in which switching which trial supplies IPD reverses which drug is judged superior, and Cassidy et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001) show across 80 comparisons that MAICs shift estimates toward the treatment whose IPD is held. The four choices are also not equivalent in kind: changing the target population changes the estimand and changing the bridge changes the identifying assumptions, whereas a prior changes regularization and the posterior and an outcome-model specification usually changes the estimator, not the estimand.

title: No factorial study ranks which choice most often flips a decision
text:
Why it is open
The four choices are made at different points in the workflow by different people, so no single analysis varies them jointly and their interactions are never observed. Conventional sensitivity analysis varies a parameter inside a fixed structure and so does not reach choices that change the identifying assumptions or the target population. The factorial study is feasible with ordinary scenario or simulation methods, so what is missing is that nobody has run it, not a missing identification principle; the design must hold a common decision target and use only coherent combinations, because a reversal between two target populations can mean two different decision questions rather than sensitivity of one.

title: No factorial study ranks which choice most often flips a decision
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Jiang et al. 2025
Shows that the target-population choice alone can reverse which treatment is judged superior in MAIC, quantifying one of the four factors.


Cassidy et al. 2023
Compares 80 MAIC estimates with the corresponding standard anchored ITCs across 17 publications and finds MAICs systematically favor the IPD holder’s treatment.

title: No factorial study ranks which choice most often flips a decision
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run the factorial simulation with a common decision target held fixed and only coherent factor combinations crossed, reporting the frequency and direction of decision reversals attributable to each factor and to their interactions. Separate factors that redefine the estimand, meaning target population and bridge, from those that change identification or estimation, meaning prior and outcome model, and report them on that footing rather than as one undifferentiated sensitivity. Use the resulting ranking to decide which structural choices must be prespecified in a protocol.

title: No factorial study ranks which choice most often flips a decision
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No study has jointly varied bridge type, prior specification, target-population definition and outcome model in a factorial design scored on decision reversals, so there is no ranking of which structural choice most often flips a recommendation. Individual factors have been examined: target-population choice has been shown to reverse MAIC conclusions, and estimator choice (MAIC vs standard anchored ITC) has been shown empirically to shift estimates in a consistent direction.
The source titled this. “Decision sensitivity to bridge, prior, target and model unmeasured” The title says this sensitivity is unmeasured, but the audit found target-population choice and estimator choice each already shown to change conclusions.
The source said. “How sensitive a reimbursement decision is to the analyst’s choice of bridge, prior, target population and outcome model has never been quantified. There is therefore no evidence about which structural modeling choice most often flips a recommendation, and no basis for ranking which choices must be pre-specified.”
What was wrong with it. The source said this sensitivity has never been quantified and that all four choices change the estimand. The literature auditor found two of the four already quantified (Jiang et al. 2025 for target population, Cassidy et al. 2023 for estimator choice), and GPT-5.6 Sol found the estimand claim false for prior and outcome-model specification, which change estimation rather than the estimand.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. No factorial study crossing bridge type, prior, target population and outcome model and scoring decision reversals exists, so the proposed direction is genuinely unoccupied. But ‘has never been quantified’ is too strong for one of the four factors. Jiang et al. 2025 (Res Synth Methods, doi 10.1017/rsm.2025.10, full text read) constructs an explicit ‘MAIC paradox’ in which the comparative-effectiveness conclusion reverses purely by switching which trial supplies IPD, i.e. by changing the target population, and notes NICE DSU TSD 18 already documented a real secukinumab/adalimumab case where two MAICs reached opposing conclusions. Cassidy et al. 2023 (doi 10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001) empirically compared 80 MAIC estimates against the corresponding standard anchored ITCs and found MAICs systematically favor the IPD-holder’s treatment, quantifying the estimator-choice factor. Phillippo et al. 2018 threshold analysis quantifies how far evidence must move before the recommendation flips, though for data perturbations rather than structural choices. So target population and estimator choice have each been shown to flip or shift conclusions; what is missing is the joint factorial evaluation and the prior and outcome-model arms. Cites 10.1017/rsm.2025.10: Demonstrates that the target-population choice alone can reverse which treatment is judged superior, partially quantifying one of the four factors.. Cites 10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001: Empirically quantifies the estimator-choice factor across 80 comparisons from 17 publications..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

not-a-problem / overstated. The proposed sensitivity exercise is feasible using ordinary scenario, posterior-predictive, or factorial simulation, so no new statistical identification principle is missing. More importantly, C3 is false as a blanket statement. Changing the target population changes the estimand; changing a bridge usually changes the identifying assumptions or information path; changing a prior changes regularization and the posterior, not the estimand; and changing an outcome-model specification ordinarily changes the estimator or model, not the estimand, unless the outcome, horizon, or effect measure also changes. Factors cannot always be crossed independently because some combinations are incoherent. A decision reversal between different target populations may reflect a different decision question rather than sensitivity of one estimand. The claim that this has never been quantified is an uncited literature claim outside the technical evidence supplied.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: No PAIC-specific reporting standard or credibility appraisal tool
text:
Statement
There is no risk-of-bias or credibility scoring instrument built for population-adjusted indirect comparisons. Farinasso et al. 2025 (10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088) state this and find only 3 of 117 oncology MAICs met all NICE recommendations, and Truong et al. 2023 (10.1002/jrsm.1653) find conduct and reporting remarkably heterogeneous and suboptimal. The domains themselves are not unaddressed: NICE DSU TSD 18 already requires an explicit target population, assessment of covariate distributions, evidence of effect-modifier status and the distribution of weights, TSD 7 supplies a pro forma reviewer checklist covering the decision problem, disconnected networks, assumptions, sensitivity and uncertainty, and CINeMA (10.1371/journal.pmed.1003082) gives per-comparison credibility judgments for network meta-analysis, though with no items for target population, overlap, weighting moments or bridge assumptions. What is missing is a scored PAIC-specific instrument and a consolidated standard adding estimand classification, reproducibility, assumption stress tests and documented provenance for any quantitative bias analysis.

title: No PAIC-specific reporting standard or credibility appraisal tool
text:
Why it is open
Existing guidance states requirements but does not score them, so an assessor has no instrument that turns a domain judgment into a comparable credibility rating and compliance is visible only through retrospective review. Each HTA agency issues its own template, so there is no cross-jurisdiction standard and no shared vocabulary for these items. The items that would expose an analysis as assumption-driven impose a cost on the submitting party, so voluntary adoption is unlikely without a requirement.

title: No PAIC-specific reporting standard or credibility appraisal tool
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Farinasso et al. 2025
Scoping review of 117 oncology MAICs; states that no risk-of-bias tool specific to MAIC exists and reports that only 3 fulfilled all NICE recommendations, 72% were unanchored and 78% did not report the IPD source.


Truong et al. 2023
Methodological systematic review of PAICs in HTA; finds conduct and reporting heterogeneous and suboptimal, with quality or bias of individual studies assessed in 9.3% of analyses.


Cassidy et al. 2023
Supplies the reporting-bias evidence: MAICs in connected networks reported more favorable estimates for the IPD holder’s treatment than the corresponding anchored ITCs.


CINeMA framework (2020)
Per-comparison credibility framework for network meta-analysis across six domains, built on the contribution matrix; has no items for target population, overlap, weighting moments or bridge assumptions.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18 (2016)
PAIC-specific recommendations covering target population, covariate overlap, effect-modifier evidence, distribution of weights, uncertainty and systematic error. Read by the code auditor from a document corpus at the given commit.

title: No PAIC-specific reporting standard or credibility appraisal tool
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on TSD 18 and TSD 7 rather than start from scratch: add the domains they do not cover, namely explicit estimand classification, reproducibility, assumption stress tests and documented rationale and provenance for any quantitative bias analysis, and turn the result into an instrument an assessor can score. Follow CINeMA in keeping domain-level judgments separate rather than collapsing identification judgments into one aggregate score, and require quantitative bias analysis only where it is relevant and supportable. Validate the instrument on a sample of submitted analyses.

title: No PAIC-specific reporting standard or credibility appraisal tool
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Published population-adjusted indirect comparisons are reported inconsistently and there is no risk-of-bias or credibility instrument built for them. Nor is there a reporting standard covering the nine areas that decide whether a submission is interpretable: decision question and estimand, evidence graph, population adjustment, overlap and extrapolation, model specification, uncertainty, assumption stress tests, quantitative bias analysis and reproducibility.”
What was wrong with it. The source said existing tools contain no items for target population, overlap, weighting moments or bridge assumptions, so those features are never assessed. GPT-5.6 Sol found NICE DSU TSD 18 already requires exactly those disclosures and TSD 7 supplies a reviewer checklist, and the literature auditor added CINeMA as an existing per-comparison credibility framework for network meta-analysis, so the surviving gap is a scored PAIC-specific instrument rather than an absence of appraisal criteria.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The central claim is asserted by a source, which is the strongest form of evidence available for an absence claim. Farinasso et al. 2025 (Value Health Reg Issues, doi 10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088) state: ‘There is no risk of bias tool specific for MAICs, which can hinder their applicability in the health technology assessment (HTA) process. Without the risk of bias assessment, it is also not possible to apply the Grading of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria.’ Their scoping review of 117 oncology MAICs found only 3 fulfilled all NICE recommendations, 72% were unanchored, 78% did not report the IPD source and 66% ran no systematic review. Truong et al. 2023 (doi 10.1002/jrsm.1653) independently concludes reporting is ‘remarkably heterogeneous and suboptimal’. Cassidy et al. 2023 supplies the reporting-bias evidence. Caveat: the why_open text says existing RoB tools were built for RCTs and conventional meta-analysis; that omits CINeMA (doi 10.1371/journal.pmed.1003082), a per-comparison credibility framework for NMA built on the contribution matrix. CINeMA still has no items for target population, overlap, weighting moments or bridge assumptions, so the PAIC gap stands. codex dissented (overstated): The inspected guidance directly defeats the claim that target population, overlap, weights, uncertainty, and bridge assumptions are never assessed. TSD 18 gives PAIC-specific reporting recommendations for those domains, while TSD 7 supplies a reviewer checklist covering the decision problem, disconnected networks, assumptions, sensitivity analysis, and uncertainty. Neither document is a formal PAIC-specific risk-of-bias scoring instrument or a complete modern nine-domain standard, and both leave room for an updated framework. C1-C3 still require a current literature review. C4-C6 are therefore universal negatives stated too strongly. C7 is broadly sound, but QBA should be required when relevant and supportable, and identification judgments should not be collapsed into a misleading aggregate score. C8 accurately describes a proposal.

Literature and prior-art check

Farinasso et al. 2025 (Value Health Reg Issues, doi 10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088) state: ‘There is no risk of bias tool specific for MAICs, which can hinder their applicability in the health technology assessment (HTA) process. Without the risk of bias assessment, it is also not possible to apply the Grading of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria.’ Their scoping review of 117 oncology MAICs found only 3 fulfilled all NICE recommendations, 72% were unanchored, 78% did not report the IPD source and 66% ran no systematic review. title: Estimand-first guidance exists but is not enforced in PAIC practice
text: DEC-06 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: Estimand-first guidance exists but is not enforced in PAIC practice
text:
Statement
Published PAIC practice is dominated by MAIC and by unanchored designs, with poor reporting of covariate handling and diagnostics: 89% (16/18) of NICE appraisals using population adjustment used MAIC and 89% were unanchored (10.1017/S0266462319000333), 72% of 117 oncology MAICs were unanchored with only 3 meeting all NICE recommendations (10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088), and quality or bias of individual studies was assessed in 9.3% of PAIC analyses with outcome-model fitting adequately reported in 3 of 18 (10.1002/jrsm.1653). That this pattern is caused by choosing the estimator before the estimand is an inference from those figures rather than a measured finding, and the eight-step sequence is the source’s own construction, not an externally validated standard. Guidance already implements part of the ordering: NICE DSU TSD 18 makes connectedness of the randomized evidence determine whether anchored or unanchored adjustment is admissible and requires the decision target population to be stated. The deficit is therefore adoption and enforcement of rules that exist, not an absent workflow.

title: Estimand-first guidance exists but is not enforced in PAIC practice
text:
Why it is open
Software, guidance documents and submission templates are organized around methods rather than estimands, so an estimator can be fixed before the decision question is stated and the target population inferred afterwards from whatever data are available. Nothing in review or reimbursement requires the earlier steps to be documented, so they can be skipped without consequence, and because covariate handling and diagnostics are poorly reported the drift is invisible in the published record and not self-correcting. The existing rule that connected evidence permits only anchored adjustment constrains the admissible estimator set; what is absent is any mechanism that checks it was applied.

title: Estimand-first guidance exists but is not enforced in PAIC practice
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Truong et al. 2023
Methodological systematic review of PAICs; sources MAIC dominance and quantifies poor covariate, diagnostic and bias reporting (quality or bias assessed in 9.3%; model fitting adequately reported in 3 of 18).


Farinasso et al. 2025
Sources the frequency of unanchored designs (72% of 117 oncology MAICs) and the poverty of covariate-handling and diagnostic reporting, with only 3 studies meeting all NICE recommendations.


Phillippo et al. 2019 (NICE technology appraisals review)
Independent NICE-submission figures: 89% (16/18) used MAIC and 89% were unanchored.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18 (2016)
Ties admissible population-adjustment methods to connectedness of the randomized evidence and requires an explicit decision target population, implementing part of the proposed ordering. Read by the code auditor from a document corpus at the given commit.

title: Estimand-first guidance exists but is not enforced in PAIC practice
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Enforce the ordering that guidance already implies: require the decision target, estimand, evidence graph, identification conditions and support assessment to be documented before the estimator is named, with the admissible estimator set tied to the evidence structure as TSD 18 already does for anchored versus unanchored adjustment. Make that documentation a mandatory reporting appendix so that skipping a step becomes visible rather than silent. Measure compliance empirically once the requirement exists, since current compliance is known only from retrospective reviews.

title: Estimand-first guidance exists but is not enforced in PAIC practice
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “Estimator is chosen before the estimand and the evidence structure” The title asserts a causal claim about how estimators are chosen, which the audit found to be an inference from prevalence figures rather than a measured finding.
The source said. “Applied practice selects an estimator first: most published PAICs still use MAIC, unanchored designs are common, and reporting of covariate handling, diagnostics and bias assessment is poor. The eight-step sequence that would begin with the target decision and estimand and end with evaluation of decision consequences remains a recommendation rather than the operational default.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated the practice pattern without attribution; the literature auditor sourced every figure (Phillippo et al. 2019, Farinasso et al. 2025, Truong et al. 2023) while GPT-5.6 Sol held the prevalence claims were not established by the material supplied to it, so the figures now appear with their locators. GPT-5.6 Sol also found the sequence is not wholly missing, since TSD 18 already ties admissible methods to connectedness, and rejected the claim that only a small subset of estimators stays credible when assumptions fail, since robustness is assumption-specific.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Every empirical claim in this entry checks out against retrieved reviews, and each has an exact figure. Jiang et al. 2025 (doi 10.1017/rsm.2025.10, full text read) reports ‘In a recent methodological systematic review, 88.9% (144 out of 162) of PAIC studies used MAICs’, citing Truong et al. 2023; Phillippo et al. 2019 found MAIC in 89% (16/18) of NICE TAs using population adjustment. On unanchored designs: Farinasso et al. 2025 found 72% of 117 oncology MAICs unanchored; Phillippo et al. 2019 found 89% (16/18). On poor reporting: Truong et al. 2023 found extensive heterogeneity assessment in only 37.0% of analyses and quality/bias assessment of individual studies in only 9.3%; Farinasso et al. found only 3/117 MAICs met all NICE recommendations, with the least-reported items being adjustment for all effect modifiers and prognostic variables in unanchored analyses, evidence of effect-modifier status, and the distribution of weights. The eight-step workflow and its ordering are the report’s own construction and cannot be validated against an external source; treat them as a proposal, not a finding. The gap is a practice and enforcement gap and is unresolved. codex dissented (overstated): The proposed order is methodologically sound, but it is not a wholly missing technical workflow. Existing PAIC guidance already makes evidence connectedness determine whether anchored or unanchored adjustment is admissible and requires an explicit target population. C2-C4 are current-practice prevalence claims for which no current source is supplied. C5 is undefined and technically misleading: robustness is assumption-specific, and no estimator remains credible after its required identification assumptions fail. C6 and C7 correctly describe the proposed eight-step sequence. C8 is appropriate for consequential untestable assumptions in a decision-grade analysis, although sensitivity analysis cannot validate those assumptions. C9 is appropriate when the stated aim is reimbursement decision support, not as a universal requirement for every statistical methods paper. The remaining issue is adoption and enforcement rather than absence of a statistical method.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Every empirical claim in this entry checks out against retrieved reviews, and each has an exact figure. Jiang et al. 2025 (doi 10.1017/rsm.2025.10, full text read) reports ‘In a recent methodological systematic review, 88.9% (144 out of 162) of PAIC studies used MAICs’, citing Truong et al. 2023; Phillippo et al. 2019 found MAIC in 89% (16/18) of NICE TAs using population adjustment. On unanchored designs: Farinasso et al. 2025 found 72% of 117 oncology MAICs unanchored; Phillippo et al. 2019 found 89% (16/18). On poor reporting: Truong et al. 2023 found extensive heterogeneity assessment in only 37.0% of analyses and quality/bias assessment of individual studies in only 9.3%; Farinasso et al. found only 3/117 MAICs met all NICE recommendations, with the least-reported items being adjustment for all effect modifiers and prognostic variables in unanchored analyses, evidence of effect-modifier status, and the distribution of weights. The eight-step workflow and its ordering are the report’s own construction and cannot be validated against an external source; treat them as a proposal, not a finding. The gap is a practice and enforcement gap and is unresolved. Cites 10.1002/jrsm.1653: Sources MAIC dominance (88.9%, 144/162 per Jiang et al.’s reading of it) and quantifies poor covariate/diagnostic/bias reporting.. Cites 10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088: Sources the frequency of unanchored designs and the poverty of covariate-handling and diagnostic reporting.. Cites 10.1017/S0266462319000333: Independent NICE-submission figures for MAIC dominance and unanchored prevalence..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. The proposed order is methodologically sound, but it is not a wholly missing technical workflow. Existing PAIC guidance already makes evidence connectedness determine whether anchored or unanchored adjustment is admissible and requires an explicit target population. C2-C4 are current-practice prevalence claims for which no current source is supplied. C5 is undefined and technically misleading: robustness is assumption-specific, and no estimator remains credible after its required identification assumptions fail. C6 and C7 correctly describe the proposed eight-step sequence. C8 is appropriate for consequential untestable assumptions in a decision-grade analysis, although sensitivity analysis cannot validate those assumptions. C9 is appropriate when the stated aim is reimbursement decision support, not as a universal requirement for every statistical methods paper. The remaining issue is adoption and enforcement rather than absence of a statistical method. title: No provenance label separates bridged from prior-driven contrasts
text: DEC-08 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: No provenance label separates bridged from prior-driven contrasts
text:
Statement
For connected networks, contrast-specific evidence provenance is already computable and shipped in standard software: the proportion contribution matrix (10.12688/f1000research.14770.3) shows how much each direct comparison contributes to each network estimate, it is available as netmeta::netcontrib and drives CINeMA’s per-comparison judgments, it has been applied across 213 published network meta-analyses, and the shortest-path approach has now been extended to component networks (10.1186/s12874-026-02766-8). What no convention or software produces is a provenance label separating structurally bridged from purely prior-driven contrasts across a disconnection, or an explicit ledger naming what carries information over each gap. Contrast-specific estimability is the right check rather than global rank, since a contrast is estimable exactly when its vector lies in the row space of the design; that check is implemented in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that an auditor confirmed is not on CRAN.

title: No provenance label separates bridged from prior-driven contrasts
text:
Why it is open
A network diagram draws a randomized comparison and one manufactured by a structural assumption identically, and contribution-matrix methods are defined for connected networks, so they say nothing about a contrast that exists only because of a bridge. Across a gap the information may be carried by several component parameters or by a linear subspace rather than by one named parameter, so a ledger with one row per gap is a reporting convention still to be defined rather than a quantity waiting to be read off a fit. Global rank of the design matrix continues to be reported as evidence that a network is estimable, which hides that a specific decision contrast may lie outside the estimable space.

title: No provenance label separates bridged from prior-driven contrasts
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Papakonstantinou et al. 2018
Derives the proportion contribution matrix showing how much each direct treatment effect contributes to each network estimate, giving contrast-specific evidence provenance for connected networks.


netmeta::netcontrib (R package netmeta)
Ships the contribution matrix as standard software output: rows are network treatment effects, columns are the contributions of direct treatment effects.


Papakonstantinou et al. 2020
Applies the contribution matrix to 213 published network meta-analyses, finding 33% of information from direct evidence, 47% from length-2 paths and 20% from length-3.


Yang et al. 2026
Adapts the shortest-path approach to component network meta-analysis, tracing evidence contributions to component-level estimates.


cpaic (development package, audited at commit 9d150e9)
Unreleased development package on GitHub, confirmed by an auditor not to be on CRAN. Implements treatment subnetworks and bridging-component discovery, an exact per-contrast row-space estimability check, suppression of non-estimable effects, and a network plot distinguishing IPD from aggregate-data studies; it does not implement the four-way provenance labels, a separate component graph, articulation and single-arm markings, or the bridge ledger.

title: No provenance label separates bridged from prior-driven contrasts
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend contribution-matrix reporting to the disconnected case rather than build per-contrast provenance from nothing: for each decision-critical contrast report the mixture of randomized, indirect, structural and prior information instead of a single label, alongside the row-space estimability check that cpaic already performs. Define the bridge disclosure as the assumptions plus the parameter loadings that carry information across the gap, which covers the case where no single parameter does. Add a separate component-network display with articulation edges and single-arm evidence marked, recognizing that component structure is often a design matrix or hypergraph rather than an ordinary graph.

title: No provenance label separates bridged from prior-driven contrasts
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. For connected networks, contrast-specific evidence provenance is already computable and shipped in standard software (the proportion contribution matrix in netmeta and CINeMA), and component-level evidence flow now exists too. What is not produced by any convention or software is a provenance label distinguishing structurally bridged from purely prior-driven contrasts in disconnected evidence, or an explicit bridge ledger naming the parameter carrying information across each gap.
The source titled this. “Contrast provenance and the bridge ledger are not reported” The title says contrast provenance is not reported, but the proportion contribution matrix has shipped in netmeta and CINeMA since 2018 and now extends to component networks.
The source said. “Evidence-graph reporting does not distinguish the provenance of each contrast. Reports do not show the treatment and component networks separately, do not identify connected components, articulation edges and single-arm evidence, do not state for each cross-treatment contrast whether it is randomized, indirectly randomized, structurally bridged or purely prior-driven, report global rank instead of contrast-specific estimability, and carry no bridge ledger for disconnected comparisons.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no convention or software output currently produces a per-contrast provenance label, so even a willing analyst has nothing to fill in. The literature auditor found the contribution matrix has been in netmeta and CINeMA since 2018 and now extends to component networks, leaving only the disconnected case; GPT-5.6 Sol added that a single four-way label can itself conceal a mixture of direct, indirect, structural and prior information, and that per-contrast estimability is already implemented in cpaic.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim ‘No convention or software output currently produces a per-contrast provenance label … so even a willing analyst has nothing to fill in’ is wrong for connected networks. Papakonstantinou et al. 2018 (F1000Research, doi 10.12688/f1000research.14770.3) derived the proportion contribution matrix showing ‘how much each direct treatment effect contributes to each treatment effect estimate from network meta-analysis’; it is shipped as netmeta::netcontrib, whose documentation I retrieved (‘generates the contribution of direct comparisons to every network treatment comparison … rows represent network treatment effects and columns represent the contribution of direct treatment effects’), and it is the engine behind CINeMA’s per-comparison within-study-bias and indirectness judgments. Papakonstantinou et al. 2020 (doi 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.04.009) applied it across 213 published NMAs, finding 33% of information from direct evidence, 47% from length-2 paths and 20% from length-3. Yang et al. 2026 (doi 10.1186/s12874-026-02766-8) extends evidence-flow tracing to component NMA via pseudo-paths, addressing the treatment-versus-component-network claim. What genuinely remains: labels distinguishing ‘structurally bridged’ from ‘prior-driven’ for disconnected evidence, and the bridge ledger itself. Cites 10.12688/f1000research.14770.3: Provides contrast-specific evidence provenance (direct vs indirect decomposition per network estimate) rather than a global rank statistic.. Cites cran:netmeta::netcontrib: Shows the per-contrast provenance output already exists as standard software output.. Cites 10.1186/s12874-026-02766-8: Extends contribution tracing to the component network, addressing the claim that treatment and component networks are different graphs with no tooling..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C2 is correct only with qualification: when X = BC is rank deficient, a contrast is estimable exactly when its contrast vector lies in row(X), so the rank number alone does not identify which contrasts survive. Full column rank of the correct estimand design does, however, certify every linear contrast. C3-C4 are useful reporting recommendations, although component information is often a design matrix, bipartite graph, or hypergraph rather than one ordinary graph. C5 is too categorical: cross-gap information may be carried by several component parameters or a linear subspace, and an equivalent assumption-and-loading report can replace a formal ledger. A single provenance label can also conceal mixtures of direct, indirect, structural, and prior information. C1’s frequency is not established here. At the requested cpaic commit, subnetworks, bridging components, contrast-specific estimability, IPD-versus-AgD plotting, and approximate edge influence already exist. The four-way provenance labels, separate component graph, articulation and single-arm markings, and bridge ledger remain absent. This is critical for cross-gap decision contrasts, but not uniformly a very-high-priority defect for every contrast. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Implements treatment subnetworks and bridging-component discovery, an exact row-space check for each treatment contrast, suppression of nonestimable effects, and a network plot distinguishing IPD from AgD. This resolves C2 and parts of C3-C4, but not the requested ledger or complete provenance taxonomy..

title: Trimming redefines the target population without naming it
text: DEC-10 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: Trimming redefines the target population without naming it
text:
Statement
Weight truncation and trimming shift the target population and therefore the estimand, and no reporting convention requires the resulting population to be named; Remiro-Azocar 2022 (10.1186/s12874-022-01692-9) states this for both and adds that the cutoffs are ad hoc. Reporting effective sample size alone is insufficient, and part of the remedy exists in prototype: cpaic reports weight entropy, coefficient of variation, maximum normalized weight, top-5-percent weight mass and residual balance alongside ESS, plus contrast-specific edge influence that its own source calls approximate for multi-arm trials; cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub and is not on CRAN. What remains missing is local support, out-of-distribution diagnostics for outcome-model methods, an explicit definition of the population created by trimming, and exact leave-one-study-out influence. The proportion of target mass outside source support is identifiable only where the target joint distribution and an operational definition of support are available, which published marginal summaries alone do not supply.

title: Trimming redefines the target population without naming it
text:
Why it is open
Trimming is presented as a technical stabilization step, so the population it creates is never named, and normalized truncated weights converge to an altered weighted distribution that may be data-adaptive and lack a simple population interpretation; truncation that vanishes with sample size is better read as finite-sample regularization for the original estimand. Support failure is a property of a region of covariate space whereas ESS is a scalar, so a report can satisfy the conventional diagnostic while the decision-relevant region of the target is unsupported. The diagnostics that do exist sit in an unreleased development package rather than in a reporting requirement, so they are absent from reports by default.

title: Trimming redefines the target population without naming it
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar 2022 (two-stage MAIC)
States that weight truncation shifts the target population or estimand definition and requires ad hoc cutoffs, that trimming changes the target population further, and that weight-dispersion displays are needed beyond ESS.


Serret-Larmande et al. 2025
Simulation study of covariate-distribution and positivity violations in weighting-based indirect comparisons; finds first-moment MAIC robust to moderate positivity violations while MAIC-2 and propensity-score weighting are more sensitive.


cpaic (development package, audited at commit 9d150e9)
Unreleased development package on GitHub, confirmed by an auditor not to be on CRAN. Computes ESS with entropy, coefficient of variation, maximum normalized weight, top-5-percent weight mass and residual balance per IPD study, and returns an influence weight for every study edge for a requested contrast, described in its own source as a screening approximation for multi-arm trials.

title: Trimming redefines the target population without naming it
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Require weight concentration, local support and balance to be reported alongside ESS, extrapolation and out-of-distribution diagnostics for outcome-model methods, and an explicitly redefined target population whenever trimming or truncation is applied. Because the concentration diagnostics and contrast-specific edge influence already exist in prototype, the work is to release, validate and standardize them, and to replace the approximate edge influence with exact leave-one-study-out influence for decision-critical contrasts. Report target mass outside support only where the target joint distribution and an operational support definition make it identifiable, and state what was assumed when they do not.

title: Trimming redefines the target population without naming it
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “Trimming silently redefines the target and ESS stands alone” The title says effective sample size stands alone, but the audit found weight entropy, concentration, residual balance and contrast-specific edge influence already implemented alongside it.
The source said. “Overlap reporting is incomplete: effective sample size is reported without weight concentration, local support or balance, extrapolation and out-of-distribution diagnostics are absent for outcome-model methods, the amount of target mass lying outside source support is not stated, the changed target population created by trimming is not defined, and study or edge influence on each decision-critical contrast is not reported.”
What was wrong with it. The source said study and edge influence on a decision contrast is not produced by standard software and that ESS stands alone in reports. GPT-5.6 Sol found weight-concentration diagnostics and contrast-specific edge influence already implemented in cpaic, an unreleased GitHub package that is not on CRAN, with the influence explicitly labeled approximate, and narrowed the target-mass claim to cases where the target joint distribution and a support definition are available.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The load-bearing claim is directly sourceable and I retrieved the verbatim text. Remiro-Azocar 2022 (BMC Med Res Methodol, doi 10.1186/s12874-022-01692-9, PMID 35941551; full text read) states of MAIC weights: ‘Limitations of weight truncation are that it shifts the target population or estimand definition, and that it requires arbitrary ad hoc decisions on cutoff thresholds’, and of trimming: ‘It involves excluding the subjects with outlying weights, thereby sharing many of the limitations of truncation: setting arbitrary cutoff points, and changing the target population even further.’ The same paper also supports the ‘ESS is not enough’ claim: ‘Density plots are likely helpful to assess the dispersion of the weights and identify an optimal cutoff point.’ Serret-Larmande et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.12241) is a recent simulation study of exactly the positivity/overlap violations the entry says are undiagnosed, and finds MAIC-2 and propensity-score weighting more sensitive to positivity violations than first-moment MAIC. So the methodological claims are established; what is open is that none of this is a required reporting element, and that study/edge influence on a specific decision contrast is not standard PAIC output. codex dissented (supported-with-caveat): C1 is broadly correct for fixed trimming or weight truncation: normalized truncated weights converge to an altered weighted distribution, although that distribution may be data-adaptive and may lack a simple population interpretation. Vanishing truncation can instead be viewed as finite-sample regularization for the original estimand. C2 is important but the exact target mass outside support is identifiable only when the target joint distribution and an operational definition of support are available; marginal summaries alone generally cannot supply it. C3 and C5 are technically sound. C4 is useful for decision-critical contrasts, but influence should distinguish exact leave-one-study-out changes from linearized edge weights. At the requested commit, cpaic already reports ESS with entropy, coefficient of variation, maximum normalized weight, top-5-percent weight mass, and residual balance. It also emits contrast-specific edge influence, although the source explicitly calls it approximate for multi-arm trials. Local support, target mass, trimming-induced estimands, outcome-model OOD diagnostics, and exact study-deletion influence remain open.

Literature and prior-art check

Remiro-Azocar 2022 (BMC Med Res Methodol, doi 10.1186/s12874-022-01692-9, PMID 35941551; full text read) states of MAIC weights: ‘Limitations of weight truncation are that it shifts the target population or estimand definition, and that it requires arbitrary ad hoc decisions on cutoff thresholds’, and of trimming: ‘It involves excluding the subjects with outlying weights, thereby sharing many of the limitations of truncation: setting arbitrary cutoff points, and changing the target population even further.’ The same paper also supports the ‘ESS is not enough’ claim: ‘Density plots are likely helpful to assess the dispersion of the weights and identify an optimal cutoff point.’ Serret-Larmande et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.12241) is a recent simulation study of exactly the positivity/overlap violations the entry says are undiagnosed, and finds MAIC-2 and propensity-score weighting more sensitive to positivity violations than first-moment MAIC. So the methodological claims are established; what is open is that none of this is a required reporting element, and that study/edge influence on a specific decision contrast is not standard PAIC output. title: Nothing requires showing how far a conclusion is assumption-driven
text: DEC-12 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: Nothing requires showing how far a conclusion is assumption-driven
text:
Statement
No rule requires a formal quantitative bias analysis or a minimum stress-test set for a decision-grade unanchored analysis, and there is no agreed minimum set, so any single sensitivity analysis can be presented as sufficient. The methods themselves are largely available: decision tipping points are computable and on CRAN (nmathresh, implementing 10.1111/rssa.12341), quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in unanchored PAIC was published in 2025 (10.1017/rsm.2025.13) with deterministic, probabilistic and tipping-point variants, and component-drift tipping plus prior sensitivity are implemented in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN. What is not computable from current tools is support and effective sample size across a whole bias region, joint evaluation of multiple interacting biases, and interaction-level drift sensitivity. A probability of recommendation reversal also requires a defensible joint distribution for the bias parameters and a fully specified decision rule before it can be reported.

title: Nothing requires showing how far a conclusion is assumption-driven
text:
Why it is open
Stress tests and bias analyses can only weaken a submission’s apparent strength, so a submitting party has no incentive to run them unless they are required, and appraisal templates ask for scenario analyses of economic inputs rather than of synthesis assumptions. Because there is no agreed minimum set, any single sensitivity analysis can be presented as sufficient, and the tools that exist are scattered across a CRAN package for network meta-analysis, a 2025 PAIC method paper and an unreleased development package rather than assembled into a standard. Support and effective sample size across a bias region and joint evaluation of interacting biases remain genuinely uncomputed, though support and ESS need re-evaluation only for scenarios that change the target distribution or the weighting problem.

title: Nothing requires showing how far a conclusion is assumption-driven
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2018
Derives decision-invariant bias-adjustment thresholds, the smallest changes to the data that change the treatment decision, which is the tipping-point computation the source described as unavailable.


nmathresh 0.1.6 (R package)
Released CRAN implementation of decision-invariant bias-adjustment thresholds and invariant intervals for network meta-analysis, showing tipping-point computation is standard software rather than custom work.


Ren et al. 2025
Quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparisons, with deterministic and probabilistic variants and tipping-point analysis.


Phillippo et al. 2019 (threshold analysis for guideline developers)
Presents threshold analysis to decision makers and guideline developers as a direct statement of how robust a treatment recommendation is to plausible changes in the evidence.


cpaic (development package, audited at commit 9d150e9)
Unreleased development package on GitHub, confirmed by an auditor not to be on CRAN. Its bridge_fragility() computes the component-main-effect drift needed to cross a specified decision threshold, with an optional posterior robustness probability, and it provides tighter and looser prior refits reporting contrast movement; it excludes interaction drift, joint biases, general quantitative bias analysis and reversal probability.

title: Nothing requires showing how far a conclusion is assumption-driven
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define a minimum stress-test set for decision-grade ITC and assemble it from existing components: threshold analysis for the decision tipping point, the published unanchored-PAIC quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding, and drift sensitivity for cross-subnetwork bridges. Require the disclosures that accompany a bias analysis, namely separated bias mechanisms, stated bias parameters with ranges and evidence sources, dependence assumptions, deterministic scenarios alongside probabilistic ones, and labeling of which quantities are data-identified, externally informed, elicited or purely bounded. Develop what is genuinely missing: joint evaluation of interacting biases, interaction-level drift, and support and ESS re-evaluated for the scenarios that change the weighting problem.

title: Nothing requires showing how far a conclusion is assumption-driven
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No rule requires a formal quantitative bias analysis or a minimum stress-test set for a decision-grade unanchored analysis, and there is no agreed minimum set, so any single sensitivity analysis can be presented as sufficient. The methods themselves are not all missing: decision tipping points are computable and on CRAN for network meta-analysis (nmathresh), and quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in unanchored PAIC was published in 2025. What remains uncomputed is support and effective sample size across an entire bias region, joint evaluation of multiple interacting biases, and cross-subnetwork drift sensitivity.
The source said. “The analyses that would show how much of a conclusion rests on assumptions are optional: omitted modifier and prognostic sensitivity, cross-subnetwork drift, component-interaction and target-distribution sensitivity, MNAR missingness, alternative outcome and effect-scale analyses, bridge-deletion or held-out validation, and the decision tipping point with the probability of recommendation reversal. No rule requires a formal quantitative bias analysis for a decision-grade unanchored analysis, nor the disclosures that accompany one: separated bias mechanisms, stated bias parameters with ranges, dependence assumptions and evidence sources, deterministic scenarios alongside probabilistic ones, support, feasibility and ESS across the whole bias region, joint evaluation of multiple biases, tipping surfaces, and labeling of which quantities are data-identified, externally informed, elicited or purely bounded.”
What was wrong with it. The source said tipping surfaces and drift sensitivity do not exist as standard software features. Tipping-point computation has been on CRAN since nmathresh 0.1.6 (2020) and quantitative bias analysis for unanchored PAIC was published in 2025 (10.1017/rsm.2025.13); GPT-5.6 Sol found component-drift tipping already implemented in cpaic and rejected the claim that omitting a bias analysis asserts residual bias is exactly zero, since it only leaves inference conditional on assumptions that fix modeled residual bias at zero.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The why_open text asserts that ‘several of the required computations do not exist as standard software features, including … tipping surfaces’, and that any single sensitivity analysis can be presented as sufficient. The first half is wrong. Phillippo et al. 2018 (doi 10.1111/rssa.12341) derive decision-invariant bias-adjustment thresholds, ‘the smallest changes to the data that result in a change of treatment decision’, shipped as the CRAN package nmathresh 0.1.6 (2020-06-11): ‘Calculation and presentation of decision-invariant bias adjustment thresholds and intervals for Network Meta-Analysis’. Phillippo et al. 2019 (doi 10.7326/M18-3542) proposed it to NICE guideline developers as an alternative to GRADE, and Holper 2020 (doi 10.1002/jrsm.1393) applied it with GRADE to 21 antidepressants. Separately, Ren et al. 2025 (doi 10.1017/rsm.2025.13, full text read) supplies formal QBA for unmeasured confounding in unanchored PAIC, covering multiple unmeasured covariates, deterministic and probabilistic variants, and tipping-point analysis. What is genuinely open: an agreed minimum stress-test set for PAIC, support and ESS evaluated across a whole QBA region, and joint evaluation of multiple biases. Cites 10.1111/rssa.12341: Provides decision tipping points and the revised recommendation, the exact computation the entry says is unavailable.. Cites cran:nmathresh 0.1.6: Shows tipping-point computation is a released, standard software feature, not custom work.. Cites 10.1017/rsm.2025.13: Supplies a published QBA method specific to unanchored PAIC, with deterministic and probabilistic variants and tipping-point analysis, and argues such analysis is necessary..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1-C2 are empirical practice claims not established by the supplied material. C3 is only partly right: tipping points are broadly interpretable, but a probability of recommendation reversal is unidentified without a defensible joint distribution for bias parameters and a fully specified decision rule. C4 requires care because changing effect scale generally changes the estimand; alternatives should be clinically meaningful, not presented as interchangeable answers. C5 is useful where deletion leaves the target contrast estimable, but held-out performance cannot validate an unobserved cross-gap assumption. C6 is proportionate for genuinely unanchored decision-grade analyses. C7 is too strong: omitting QBA leaves inference conditional on identifying assumptions that fix modeled residual bias at zero; it does not logically assert that actual residual bias is zero. C8-C10, C13, and C14 are sound transparency requirements. C11 is a category error for bias parameters that do not alter target moments or weights, because support and ESS then do not vary. C12 also overreaches: validation-data uncertainty may already be incorporated into sensitivity-parameter uncertainty, while numerical error should usually be bounded and reduced rather than probabilistically propagated. cpaic already implements component-main-effect drift tipping through bridge_fragility() and prior sensitivity, contradicting the claimed complete absence of drift sensitivity. It does not implement a general QBA, interaction drift, joint biases, or recommendation-reversal probability. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Partially resolves cross-subnetwork drift sensitivity and decision tipping by calculating the component-main-effect drift needed to cross a specified decision threshold, with an optional posterior robustness probability at a fixed drift bound. It excludes interaction drift and is not a general QBA.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Provides tighter and looser prior refits and reports contrast movement, partially addressing assumption-driven conclusions and prior dependence..

title: No diagnostic can falsify unmeasured effect modification in PAIC
text: DIA-01 Overstated Very high priority Emerging

title: No diagnostic can falsify unmeasured effect modification in PAIC
text:
Statement
Balance, support, fit and inconsistency diagnostics can falsify limited observable restrictions, but none of them can establish the absence of unmeasured effect modification or cross-study noncomparability, which is the part of the identifying assumption the analysis depends on. Residual heterogeneity and inconsistency checks, and covariate-by-covariate relaxation of the shared effect modifier assumption, are already available and are used inside ML-NMR target-population projections (Phillippo et al. 2022, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162), and a proof-of-concept falsification test built on partitioning a single arm’s IPD exists for measured-covariate sufficiency (Yi and Jiang 2025, doi:10.57264/cer-2024-0235). What has not been developed for PAIC is falsification of transport itself through held-out IPD or leave-one-study-out prediction.

title: No diagnostic can falsify unmeasured effect modification in PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Balance diagnostics are functions of measured covariates and fit statistics are functions of observed outcomes, so both speak to the measured, within-network part of the model and are silent on unmeasured effect modification and cross-study comparability. Under the classical two-trial configuration only one trial supplies IPD, so there is no second source from which observable implications of the transport assumption could be built. Held-out-study and deleted-edge designs do exist in disconnected NMA (Beliveau et al. 2017, doi:10.1002/jrsm.1256), but a failed reconstruction is not uniquely attributable to transport failure, so such procedures test a joint prediction procedure rather than the identifying assumption on its own.

title: No diagnostic can falsify unmeasured effect modification in PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2022, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis
Integrates residual heterogeneity and unrelated-mean-effects inconsistency checks with ML-NMR target-population projection and relaxes the shared effect modifier assumption one covariate at a time; contradicts the claim that residual inconsistency checks are not integrated with target-population projections.


Yi and Jiang 2025, A process to validate prognostic factors for unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison of single-arm trials in oncology: a proof-of-concept study
Splits a single arm into two risk-stratified groups with an imposed hazard ratio and tests whether reweighting on the candidate covariate set drives it back to one; a falsification-style test of measured-covariate sufficiency built on an IPD partition.


Jiang et al. 2025, A critical assessment of matching-adjusted indirect comparisons in relation to target populations
States that the shared effect modifier assumption is statistically untestable under the classical two-trial scenario; supplies the published attribution the source lacked.


Beliveau et al. 2017, Network meta-analysis of disconnected networks: How dangerous are random baseline treatment effects?
Disconnects real connected networks in multiple ways and scores the reconstructed cross-gap comparisons against the connected-network analysis, showing that synthetic bridge deletion is an established design rather than a new proposal.

title: No diagnostic can falsify unmeasured effect modification in PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the falsification designs that already exist rather than build new machinery: generalize the single-arm IPD-partition test to multi-covariate and anchored settings, and carry the leave-one-study-out and edge-deletion designs already used in disconnected NMA into PAIC where IPD sit on both sides of the deleted edge. State for each check what it can and cannot rule out, since rejection implicates the joint model rather than transport alone and acceptance cannot validate a genuinely missing gap. Where negative-control outcomes or falsification endpoints are available, add them as a second observable implication rather than as a substitute for the transport check.

title: No diagnostic can falsify unmeasured effect modification in PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No falsification test exists for the unmeasured-covariate component of PAIC identifying assumptions. Residual heterogeneity/inconsistency checks and shared-effect-modifier relaxation are available and are used within ML-NMR target-population projections, but they interrogate the measured, within-network part of the model; held-out-IPD and leave-one-study-out falsification of transport has not been developed for PAIC.
The source titled this. “Reported diagnostics cannot falsify the assumptions they rest on” The title says reported diagnostics cannot falsify the assumptions at all, but the audit found balance, fit and inconsistency checks do falsify limited observable restrictions.
The source said. “Covariate balance and model fit can look excellent in a population-adjusted comparison even under severe residual confounding, so the diagnostics that are routinely reported carry no evidential content for the assumption the analysis actually depends on. No formal falsification test of PAIC identifying assumptions, built on held-out IPD or aggregate-data partitions, currently exists.”
What was wrong with it. The source said routine diagnostics carry no evidential content and that residual inconsistency checks are not integrated with target-population projections; the literature auditor found them integrated in Phillippo et al. 2022 (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) and found a proof-of-concept IPD-partition falsification test in Yi and Jiang 2025 (doi:10.57264/cer-2024-0235). The core claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced to Jiang et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10), which states that under the classical two-trial scenario the shared effect modifier assumption is statistically untestable.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. Retrieved Phillippo et al. 2022 (Med Decis Making, psoriasis ML-NMR), which does exactly what the entry says is not done: it fits UME ML-NMR to test residual inconsistency and RE ML-NMR to test residual heterogeneity AFTER population adjustment, inside a framework that projects to arbitrary target populations, and relaxes the shared-effect-modifier assumption one covariate at a time. So ‘residual inconsistency checks are not currently integrated with target-population projections’ is false. I also retrieved Yi & Jiang 2025, a proof-of-concept falsification procedure for unanchored MAIC built on partitioning a single arm’s IPD, inducing a known hazard imbalance and asking whether reweighting on candidate covariates removes it. The core claim survives: nothing I found tests the unmeasured-confounding/conditional-constancy assumption itself, and Jiang et al. 2025 assert its untestability outright. Synthetic bridge deletion is already used in disconnected NMA (Beliveau 2017), so that sub-claim is not novel. Cites 10.1177/0272989X221117162: Integrates residual heterogeneity and residual inconsistency (UME) checks with ML-NMR target-population projection, and relaxes the shared effect modifier assumption covariate-by-covariate. Contradicts the claim that residual inconsistency checks are not integrated with target-population projections.. Cites 10.57264/cer-2024-0235: Proposes a formal falsification-style test built on an IPD partition: split a single arm into two risk-stratified groups with a known imposed hazard ratio, then test whether reweighting on the candidate covariate set drives it back to 1. Partially contradicts ‘no formal falsification test built on held-out IPD partitions currently exists’; it is a proof-of-concept covering measured-covariate sufficiency only.. Cites 10.1017/rsm.2025.10: Supplies a real published assertion of untestability for the shared effect modifier assumption, converting the unsourced core claim into a sourced one..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C5 and a limited form of C6 are correct: excellent measured balance or within-source fit can coexist with severe bias and cannot establish absence of unmeasured effect modification or cross-study constancy. However, “no evidential content” is false because balance, support, fit, and inconsistency checks can falsify observable necessary conditions. Synthetic bridge deletion and leave-one-study-out emulation test a joint prediction procedure only when the held-out unit is independent, relevant, and prespecified; failure is not uniquely attributable to transport, and success cannot validate a genuinely missing gap. The field-wide absence claims in C2 and C4 are unsourced and cannot be established within this audit. The identification limitation remains open, but the proposed procedures are not universal falsification tests of PAIC assumptions.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: PAIC diagnostics are not evaluated as classifiers of realized error
text: DIA-03 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: PAIC diagnostics are not evaluated as classifiers of realized error
text:
Statement
Apart from isolated work relating low effective sample size to error, PAIC diagnostics have not been evaluated as classifiers of realized error with reported discrimination and calibration. Two exceptions exist: a simulation reported at ISPOR Europe 2024 (abstract MSR65) found bias in unanchored MAIC once absolute ESS fell below roughly 30 to 35, and Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511) reports that the robust sandwich variance estimator underestimates variability where effective sample sizes are small. Cross-validation is also still reported at a hierarchical level that does not match the prediction task; in cpaic at commit 9d150e9, PSIS-LOO is observation-level and documented as incapable of validating cross-gap prediction, and grouped study-level leave-one-out is not implemented.

title: PAIC diagnostics are not evaluated as classifiers of realized error
text:
Why it is open
Diagnostics are computed from the same data and model that produced the estimate, which does not logically prevent them from predicting error but does mean the predictive value has to be demonstrated rather than assumed. Sensitivity, specificity and calibration are not intrinsic properties of a diagnostic; they are defined only relative to a specified distribution of scenarios and a prespecified threshold for material error, so establishing them requires a simulation program with an agreed scenario set, which the field has not built. Patient-level cross-validation measures within-study accuracy dominated by information the target task does not have, while the decision quantity is a prediction for a new population or study, and importance-sampling diagnostics behave differently at each hierarchical level and are rarely reported per level.

title: PAIC diagnostics are not evaluated as classifiers of realized error
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




MSR65 Can Low Effective Sample Size in Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons (MAICs) Lead to Bias? Findings From a Simulation Study, ISPOR Europe 2024 / Value in Health abstract
Simulates unanchored MAICs across sample size, event rate and overlap and reports bias once absolute ESS falls below roughly 30 to 35; quantifies one standard diagnostic against realized error. Conference abstract, retrieved at abstract level only.


Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021, Methods for population adjustment with limited access to individual patient data: A review and simulation study
Links a diagnostic quantity (small effective sample size) to a documented inferential failure, namely underestimation of variability by the robust sandwich variance estimator.


cpaic (development version), commit 9d150e9
Unreleased development package on GitHub, not available from CRAN. Its PSIS-LOO is observation-level and documented as incapable of validating cross-gap prediction; grouped study-level leave-one-out is not implemented, which is the mismatch the entry describes.

title: PAIC diagnostics are not evaluated as classifiers of realized error
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Specify a scenario distribution and a material-error threshold first, then score each diagnostic as a predictor of realized error against known truth and report its discrimination and calibration, taking the published ESS-to-bias findings as the starting calibration point rather than the endpoint. Separate descriptive from error-predictive diagnostics in reporting guidance and retain only the latter as evidence. Aggregate log-likelihood contributions at the deployment-relevant unit by adding grouped study-level, comparison-level and subnetwork-level leave-one-out to the observation-level PSIS-LOO that implementations currently provide, and report the diagnostics separately by level.

title: PAIC diagnostics are not evaluated as classifiers of realized error
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Apart from isolated work relating low effective sample size to bias, PAIC diagnostics have not been evaluated as classifiers of realized error with reported discrimination and calibration, and cross-validation for PAIC is not routinely performed at the hierarchical level matching the prediction task.
The source titled this. “PAIC diagnostics are never scored on whether they predict error” The title says diagnostics are never scored on predicting error, but the audit found two exceptions relating low effective sample size to bias and to variance underestimation.
The source said. “Whether the diagnostics used in PAIC (ESS, balance, overlap, influence, fit statistics) actually predict the error of the resulting estimate, or only describe the fitted model, has never been quantified. Relatedly, cross-validation is reported at a hierarchical level that often does not match the prediction the analysis is making, so a good statistic can accompany a failed transport.”
What was wrong with it. The source said predictive validity has never been quantified; the literature auditor found an ISPOR Europe 2024 simulation abstract identifying an ESS threshold below which bias appears, and Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511) tying small ESS to sandwich-variance underestimation. Neither treats a diagnostic as a classifier with discrimination and calibration against known truth, so the narrowed claim stands.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. The blanket ‘has never been quantified’ fails for at least one diagnostic. An ISPOR Europe 2024 / Value in Health simulation abstract (MSR65, ‘Can Low Effective Sample Size in Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons (MAICs) Lead to Bias?’) simulated unanchored MAICs of time-to-event and binary outcomes across sample size, event rate and overlap and reported bias when absolute ESS fell below roughly 30-35, irrespective of whether the low ESS came from small n or poor overlap. That is a diagnostic evaluated against realized error with a threshold. Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 similarly ties a diagnostic to a performance failure, reporting that the robust sandwich variance estimator underestimates variability where ESS is small. Neither treats a diagnostic as a classifier with discrimination and calibration against known truth, and I found nothing on hierarchical-level-matched cross-validation or per-level PSIS reporting for PAIC, so the substantive gap stands. I read only abstract-level material for the ISPOR item, hence the low confidence. Cites https://www.valueinhealthjournal.com/article/S1098-3015(24)05162-3/fulltext: Quantifies, in simulation with known truth, whether a standard PAIC diagnostic (ESS) predicts bias, identifying an approximate ESS threshold below which bias appears. Conference abstract; I retrieved title and venue plus a summary of findings, not the full text.. Cites 10.1002/jrsm.1511: Links a diagnostic quantity (small ESS) to a documented inferential failure (sandwich variance underestimation), i.e. a diagnostic with demonstrated predictive content for one error mode..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2, C4, and C5 are technically correct: descriptive fit is not automatically error-predictive, and patient-level versus study-level validation target different deployments. But computing a diagnostic from fitted data does not logically prevent it from predicting error. Sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves, and calibration are defined only relative to a specified distribution of scenarios and a prespecified material-error threshold; they are not intrinsic properties of a diagnostic. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, PSIS-LOO is explicitly observation-level and documented as incapable of validating cross-gap prediction, while grouped study-level LOO is not implemented. The field-wide claims that predictive validity has “never” been quantified are unsourced. A systematic evaluation remains an open research task, but the report overstates what follows from same-data computation.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)
