title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text: IDN-07 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Statement
Refitting an ITC or PAIC model with one connected trial withheld and comparing the predicted contrast with the observed one is a coherent falsification design, but only if removing the trial leaves the required contrast identifiable and the withheld population’s target covariate distribution can be specified without using its outcome contrast. We are not aware of a standardized protocol saying how to run it or when a discrepancy counts as falsifying, and neither auditor could certify that absence: the literature auditor found no source asserting it, and the source-code auditor treated a literature-wide absence claim as outside the technical lens. The nearest work found is adjacent rather than on point, namely leave-one-trial-out influence and outlier diagnostics for network meta-analysis (arXiv:1910.13080) and formal falsification tests for external validity with defined test statistics and error control from outside the ITC literature (Hussain et al., AISTATS 2023). The two secondary claims survive: study-level held-out prediction and patient-level cross-validation answer different questions, and withholding a trial changes the evidence base and can change the implied target population, though not when the target is externally prespecified.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Why it is open
There is no agreed pass or fail rule: the predictive interval has to absorb weight estimation, target-moment uncertainty and between-study heterogeneity, and neither the discrepancy metric nor a calibration threshold is defined. Networks contain few trials, so the check has low power and its verdict depends heavily on which trial is withheld. Because predicted and observed contrasts can refer to different populations once the evidence base changes, a discrepancy is ambiguous between an estimand mismatch and a genuine transport failure, and current practice further conflates study-level held-out prediction with patient-level cross-validation, which answers a different question.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




arXiv:1910.13080, leave-one-trial-out influence and outlier diagnostics for network meta-analysis
study-level leave-one-out diagnostics for network meta-analysis aimed at influence and outlier detection, not at falsifying a predicted treatment contrast against an observed one with prespecified thresholds


Hussain et al. 2023, Falsification of Internal and External Validity in Observational Studies via Conditional Moment Restrictions, AISTATS, PMLR volume 206
formal falsification tests for external validity with defined test statistics and error control, developed outside the ITC literature and not specialized to held-out-trial prediction in an evidence network

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write the protocol rather than the method: specify the identifiability precondition for removal, a target-standardized comparison of predicted and observed contrasts, a discrepancy metric, prespecified failure thresholds, and full propagation of weight and target-moment uncertainty. Calibrate it where held-out truth is available so the threshold has known operating characteristics instead of being asserted, and keep it explicitly distinct from patient-level cross-validation in reporting. The conditional-moment falsification machinery developed for external validity is the closest formal template and is worth adapting rather than reinventing.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “No protocol for held-out-trial falsification of predicted contrasts” The title asserts flatly that no protocol exists, an absence neither auditor could certify, so the entry now says only that it is not aware of one.
The source said. “An ITC/PAIC method can be refit with one connected trial withheld and used to predict that trial’s treatment contrast, which is then compared with the observed contrast. No standardized protocol defines how such a leave-one-trial-out emulation should be conducted or when a discrepancy should count as falsifying the analysis.”
What was wrong with it. The source asserted flatly that no standardized protocol exists. Neither auditor could verify a literature-wide absence, so the claim is now stated as one we are not aware of, and the nearest work is named: arXiv:1910.13080, an ISPOR 2024 abstract on predictive cross-validation for network meta-analysis that the literature auditor could not retrieve in full (Value in Health, PII S1098-3015(24)05231-8), and Hussain et al. 2023 on falsification of external validity via conditional moment restrictions.

Literature and prior-art check

open / unverifiable. The headline claim is an absence claim (‘no standardized protocol defines how leave-one-trial-out emulation should be conducted or when a discrepancy counts as falsifying’), and I found no source that asserts that absence, so by the audit’s own rule this is unverifiable rather than supported. I searched PubMed and the web and found only adjacent work, none of which is an ITC/PAIC held-out-trial falsification protocol with prespecified thresholds: leave-one-trial-out influence and outlier diagnostics for NMA (arXiv 1910.13080); an ISPOR 2024 conference abstract on predictive cross-validation for NMA that I could not retrieve in full (Value in Health S1098-3015(24)05231-8); and, outside the ITC literature, formal falsification tests for external validity with defined test statistics and error control (Hussain et al., ‘Falsification of Internal and External Validity in Observational Studies via Conditional Moment Restrictions’, PMLR v206, AISTATS 2023). The two secondary claims are sound: study-level held-out prediction and patient-level LOO-CV do answer different questions, and in ML-NMR the target population is study-indexed, so withholding a trial does change the implied estimand. Publish the sub-claims; soften the absence claim to ‘we are not aware of’.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

abstain / unverifiable. The technically assessable subclaims need conditions. A held-out-trial prediction is feasible only if removal leaves the required contrasts identifiable and the withheld population’s target distribution is specified without using its outcome contrast. Study-level prediction and patient-level cross-validation do answer different questions. Withholding changes the evidence base, but it need not change the target population when that target is externally prespecified; C4 correctly says only that it can. The headline assertion that no standardized protocol currently exists is a literature-wide absence claim. Verifying it would require the novelty and literature review that this audit was expressly instructed not to perform, so neither openness nor support for that central claim can be established under the assigned lens.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R10:no-accessible-source

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text: IDN-09 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Statement
Prespecified negative-control outcomes and negative-control covariates can provide qualitative falsification for indirect comparisons under explicit null-effect, shared-bias and estimand-scale conditions, and a calibrated signal is evidence against a joint set of assumptions rather than a measurement of bias in the primary contrast. The calibration machinery the source treats as nonexistent does exist outside this setting: control outcome calibration corrects estimates for unobserved confounding using control outcomes and comes with a sensitivity analysis for its own identifying assumption (doi:10.1093/aje/kwt303), and empirical calibration of confidence intervals from banks of negative and synthesized positive controls is routine in OHDSI network studies (doi:10.1073/pnas.1708282114, cran:EmpiricalCalibration). Both were built for unmeasured confounding within observational data and have not been adapted to cross-study transport, and for indirect comparisons specifically there are no disease-area catalogues of design-sensitive control outcomes, no power or specificity characterization under correlated baseline covariates and non-collapsible scales, and no validated mapping from a control signal to a bias parameter for the primary contrast.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Why it is open
A valid negative-control outcome must have no causal treatment effect on the specified scale while sharing the confounding, selection, measurement and follow-up pathways of the primary outcome, and a valid negative-control covariate must be known not to modify the effect, which is exactly the knowledge that is incomplete and that data-driven modifier selection cannot supply. The data are usually absent as well, since control outcomes are rarely reported in the aggregate publications indirect comparisons rely on, which is where the check is most needed. With few trials and correlated baseline covariates an apparent placebo interaction can reflect collinearity with a true modifier, a scale artifact or multiplicity, so specificity is unknown. The existing calibration methods assume a confounding structure within one data source rather than a transport gap between two, so importing them is real work rather than a citation.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Tchetgen Tchetgen, the control outcome calibration approach, American Journal of Epidemiology
goes beyond using control outcomes for detection and corrects causal effect estimates for bias due to unobserved confounding, with a sensitivity analysis for its identifying assumption; developed for observational confounding, not cross-study transport


Schuemie et al. 2018, empirical calibration of confidence intervals from negative and synthesized positive controls, PNAS
calibrates confidence intervals using banks of negative and synthesized positive controls, the calibration step the source says does not exist, again for observational confounding rather than for transport across studies


EmpiricalCalibration R package
ships the empirical calibration procedure used routinely in OHDSI network studies, along with the negative-control concept sets that are the kind of catalogue the source says is absent, in a neighboring field

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adapt rather than invent: take control outcome calibration and empirical calibration from the observational-confounding setting and re-derive what they require when the bias is cross-study transport instead of within-source confounding. Build disease-area catalogues of candidate control outcomes and prespecified control-covariate lists elicited from clinicians, and require their reporting in trial publications and submissions so comparator studies can be checked at all. Characterize the power and specificity of placebo-covariate tests under realistic covariate correlation and non-collapsible scales, and wire a positive test into modifier selection so it forces respecification rather than being reported as an incidental finding.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Negative-control outcomes and negative-control covariates have no disease-area catalogues, no power or specificity characterization, and no calibration mapping validated for the cross-study transport bias that indirect comparisons face; calibration machinery that converts negative-control signals into bias corrections does exist (control outcome calibration, empirical calibration of confidence intervals) but has been developed for unmeasured confounding in observational data and not adapted to ITC/PAIC.
The source said. “Two negative-control devices are proposed for indirect comparisons: outcomes unlikely to be modified by treatment but sensitive to design differences, whose nonzero apparent contrast signals residual cross-study bias, and covariates that should not modify the treatment effect, whose apparent interaction falsifies the effect-modification model. Neither has the catalogues, operating characteristics or calibration needed to be used as evidence.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no accepted transfer function converts a negative-control discrepancy into a bias magnitude and that neither device can be used as evidence at all. The literature auditor found that machinery in use since 2013 and 2018 for unmeasured confounding in observational data (doi:10.1093/aje/kwt303, doi:10.1073/pnas.1708282114 with cran:EmpiricalCalibration), so the correct claim is that it has not been adapted to indirect comparison, and the source-code auditor added that negative controls already carry qualitative evidence.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. The ITC-specific problem is real and I found nothing that solves it: no disease-area catalogue of design-sensitive negative-control outcomes for indirect comparisons, and no power or specificity study under correlated baseline covariates and non-collapsible scales. But why_open’s assertion that ‘no accepted transfer function converts an observed negative-control discrepancy into a bias magnitude’ is wrong as stated. Tchetgen Tchetgen’s control outcome calibration approach does exactly that and has done since 2013, with an accompanying sensitivity analysis for its identifying assumption; and Schuemie et al. (PNAS 2018, 10.1073/pnas.1708282114) calibrate confidence intervals from banks of negative and synthesized positive controls, shipped as the CRAN package EmpiricalCalibration and used routinely in OHDSI network studies. Both live in the confounding-in-observational-data setting, not the cross-study transport setting, so importing them is a genuine open task; but the entry should say ‘not yet adapted to ITC’ rather than ‘does not exist’. Note also that OHDSI-style negative-control concept sets are precisely the kind of catalogue the entry says is absent, in a neighbouring field.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1-C2 require a sharper negative-control null: no causal treatment effect on the control outcome on the specified estimand scale, plus sufficiently shared bias pathways. An outcome that is merely unlikely to be affected and sensitive to design is not enough, and a discrepancy rejects a joint set of assumptions rather than transportability alone. C4 is correct. For C5-C6, a prespecified covariate null can be a placebo check, but a nonzero point estimate is expected under sampling and can arise from proxy correlation with a true modifier, scale or non-collapsibility, omitted modifiers, or multiplicity; only calibrated incompatibility with the null falsifies the joint model. C7 is substantially correct because the structural null needs external or design knowledge, whereas C8’s instability claim is not universal. C3 is an empirical prevalence claim outside this audit. Negative controls can already contribute qualitative evidence, so saying that calibration is required before they can be used as evidence inflates the gap; quantitative mapping to primary-outcome bias remains open.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text: IDN-11 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Statement
Trial participation can itself affect outcomes through monitoring, adherence support, visit frequency, diagnostic intensity and access to rescue care, and because engagement is a property of the protocol rather than of the patient, reweighting or regressing on baseline covariates cannot remove it. The source’s dichotomy, that transport assumes either no engagement effect or an explicitly incorporated one, misses a third case established in the paper it cites: Ung, VanderWeele and Dahabreh (doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863, erratum doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001891) define engagement-aware estimands and show that under a no participation-by-treatment-assignment interaction condition the identifying functionals are the same as those obtained under the stronger conditions invoked previously. What stays open is the ITC and PAIC specific part: where engagement is study-constant it is absorbed into the study intercept and is observationally identical to prognostic imbalance, and in a single-arm versus randomized comparison engagement is confounded with treatment, which is exactly where the no-interaction condition fails.

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Why it is open
An anchored randomized contrast can cancel an engagement main effect, so the problem is not universal; it bites when engagement interacts with treatment and in unanchored comparisons. Where engagement is constant within a study it is collinear with study membership, so covariate-balance diagnostics say nothing about it and it cannot be told apart from baseline-risk differences. The protocol features that would let it be modeled, visit schedules, imaging frequency, adherence-support programs and rescue-therapy rules, are recorded as narrative design descriptions rather than analyzable variables and are rarely reported in aggregate publications. Study-design bias parameters can represent the remainder but they are sensitivity parameters, not identified corrections.

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ung, VanderWeele and Dahabreh 2025, Generalizing and Transporting Causal Inferences From Randomized Trials in the Presence of Trial Engagement Effects, Epidemiology
defines engagement-aware transport estimands and gives identification results under a no participation-by-treatment-assignment interaction condition, under which the identifying observed-data functionals are the same as those obtained under the stronger conditions invoked in prior work


Erratum to Ung, VanderWeele and Dahabreh 2025, Epidemiology 36(5):e25
correction to the trial-engagement transport paper, which the literature auditor flagged should be cited alongside it

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Carry the engagement-aware estimands and identification results into the ITC and PAIC setting instead of restating the problem: say whether the no participation-by-treatment interaction condition is being assumed, and say what breaks in the single-arm versus randomized case where it cannot hold. Code protocol-intensity features as design covariates so crossed variation across studies can be exploited where it exists, and calibrate against pragmatic trials and real-world data where care intensity differs. Carry the unexplained remainder into quantitative bias analysis through study-design bias parameters that are varied in sensitivity analysis rather than assumed to be zero.

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Trial participation itself can affect outcomes through monitoring, adherence support, visit frequency, diagnostic intensity and access to rescue care, so cross-study outcome differences are not fully explained by patient characteristics. Standard transportability assumes either that no relevant engagement effect exists or that it has been explicitly incorporated, and in PAIC engagement differences masquerade as prognostic imbalance or baseline-risk heterogeneity.”
What was wrong with it. The source cited Ung et al. as background while stating the assumption as a two-way choice. Both auditors found that the cited paper supplies the missing third case, identification under no participation-by-treatment interaction, so the usual functionals still apply with engagement effects present; the literature auditor also flagged the paper’s erratum, doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001891.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The citation is accurate and the abstract supports it verbatim: ‘Most work on extending (generalizing or transporting) causal inferences from a randomized trial to a target population has, explicitly or implicitly, assumed that trial engagement effects are absent.’ But the paper the entry cites as background is also the paper that partly resolves the problem, and the entry does not register this. Ung et al. define estimands and give identification results for transport in the presence of engagement effects under no interaction between trial participation and treatment assignment, and show ‘The identifying observed data functionals under these no-interaction assumptions are the same as those obtained under the stronger identifiability conditions that have been invoked in prior work.’ That is a third option the why_open dichotomy excludes: engagement effects present, standard estimators reinterpreted rather than assumed away or explicitly modelled. Genuinely open: the ITC/PAIC-specific case where engagement is absorbed into a study intercept and is observationally identical to prognostic imbalance, and the single-arm-versus-randomized case where engagement is confounded with treatment (which violates Ung et al.’s no-interaction condition). Housekeeping: an erratum exists (Epidemiology 2025;36(5):e25, 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001891) and should be cited alongside. Cites 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863: Supplies estimands and identification results for transport when trial-engagement effects are present, under no participation-by-treatment interaction; partially answers the entry’s call for explicit engagement causal models.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C1 and C4 are correct: a study-level engagement exposure is not changed by reweighting baseline patient covariates. C2 needs an estimand- and scale-specific third case: engagement may affect outcomes yet cancel from the randomized treatment contrast under a suitable no trial-participation-by-treatment interaction condition, without estimating an engagement coefficient. C3 holds when engagement or protocol intensity is study-constant and collinear with source, especially in a single-arm-versus-randomized comparison; it is not universal when crossed protocol variation, measured engagement, or multiple studies exist, and engagement-by-treatment heterogeneity is not merely baseline-risk heterogeneity. C5 describes sensitivity parameters, not identified corrections. C6 is accurate. Ung et al. partly resolves the causal estimand and identification problem, while the PAIC-specific confounded single-arm setting remains open. This is high priority for unanchored comparisons but less universal for anchored randomized contrasts whose engagement main effect cancels. Cites 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863: Defines engagement-aware transport estimands and identification under a no trial-participation-by-treatment-assignment interaction condition; it does not resolve the ITC or PAIC setting where engagement is confounded with treatment or study..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text: IDN-13 Confirmed open High priority Emerging

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Statement
When calendar period, geography and care setting are each constant within each of two non-crossed studies, all three are affine functions of the binary study indicator, so only one composite between-study difference is identified and a failed transport check cannot be attributed to a dimension. This is a property of non-crossed evidence rather than of indirect comparison as a whole: once a network carries crossed structure, network meta-regression and multilevel network meta-regression can carry region, period or setting as study-level covariates, which multinma supports. Separating the dimensions therefore requires crossed variation, external information or explicit identifying restrictions, and no estimator can do it by computation alone.

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Why it is open
Assembling evidence with crossed structure, such as multi-regional or multi-period trials and registries spanning more than one care setting, is rarely done for an indirect comparison, so the standard two-study case carries the collinearity by construction. Without separation a failed transport check yields no targeted remedy, and a bias parameter elicited for undifferentiated study differences mixes mechanisms whose plausible magnitudes and directions differ, which degrades both elicitation and sensitivity analysis. The remedy is evidence design, measurement and explicit restriction rather than a better estimator, and tooling reflects that: in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, study intercepts and generic covariates are available but no calendar-time, geography or setting specific transport diagnostics are exported.

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




multinma R package
supports network meta-regression on study-level terms, including baseline risk, so region, period or setting can be carried as covariates once the network has enough crossed structure


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Design evidence sets with separately indexed transport dimensions, using multi-regional and multi-period trials plus real-world data to estimate dimension-specific drift, and report dimension-specific transport diagnostics so that failures are attributable. Where crossed structure is unavailable, state the identifying restriction that assigns the composite difference to a dimension instead of leaving it implicit, and elicit separate bias parameters for period, region and setting rather than one undifferentiated study effect. Since study-level regression already exists in released software, the work is assembling the crossed evidence and the diagnostics on top of it, not building a new estimator.

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “Calendar time, geography and setting are not separately identified” The title states the non-identification as a general fact, but both auditors narrowed it to non-crossed evidence, since crossed networks can carry these as study-level covariates.
The source said. “Transportability should be tested separately across calendar time, geography and care setting rather than conflated into a single study or source indicator, but standard practice indexes everything by a study identifier so these dimensions cannot be separated.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated the non-identification as a fact about ITC and PAIC practice in general. Both auditors narrowed it to non-crossed evidence in which each dimension is constant within a study, and the literature auditor noted that regression on study-level terms such as region or period is already available in multinma, so the missing qualifier belongs in the statement.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I found no work resolving this and no work asserting the absence, so I am judging the claims on their merits. The load-bearing claim, that in a two-study indirect comparison calendar time, geography and care setting are not separately identified, is a straightforward collinearity fact: with two studies the study indicator is binary and every study-level covariate is a deterministic function of it, so no contrast can attribute a discrepancy to a dimension. That is defensible without citation. The caveat is scope. The title generalizes to ITC/PAIC as a whole, but the identification failure is specific to two-study (and more generally to non-crossed) evidence structures; network meta-regression and ML-NMR can and do carry study-level covariates such as region or period once the network has enough crossed structure, and multinma supports regression on study-level terms including baseline risk. The entry’s own why_open concedes this (‘separating them requires evidence with crossed structure’), so the fix is to move that qualifier into the title and statement rather than to change the vote. The remaining claims are descriptive of practice and I found nothing contradicting them.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C4 are sound when all three dimensions are relevant to the target decision. C3 is a rank statement only under the missing qualifier that each dimension is constant within each of two studies: then every dimension is an affine function of the binary study indicator, so the design identifies at most one composite between-study contrast, not three dimension-specific effects. A two-study label alone does not imply failure if multiregional, multiperiod, site-level, or registry data provide crossed variation. C2 is a broad practice claim, not a mathematical necessity. At cpaic@9d150e9, study intercepts and generic covariates are available but no separate calendar-time, geography, or setting transport diagnostics are exported. No estimator can solve perfect collinearity without external restrictions; the open task is evidence design, measurement, and sensitivity analysis rather than computation. The asserted high severity is context-dependent.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text: MIS-01 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Statement
PAIC missingness spans three layers that rest on different assumptions and admit different remedies: participant-level missing covariates or outcomes inside the IPD, trial-level non-reporting in the aggregate publication, and structurally unavailable IPD for whole studies. Fang et al. (2026, doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00914-2) closes the first layer for MAIC by multiplying an inverse-probability-of-being-observed weight into the matching weights, with simulation evidence; the other two layers are untouched, and multiple imputation congenial with the transport model, missing-not-at-random sensitivity analysis, and imputation of missing target summaries remain unbuilt. Complete-case handling is not a single default that collapses all three, because it acts on individual records while an absent aggregate summary and an unavailable IPD study are identification and data-access problems it cannot reach. What survives is narrower: complete-case deletion changes the identifying sample, and any imputation, weighting, or standardization has to preserve the target estimand and the conditional distributions the transport step relies on.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Why it is open
Deleting a record for a missing covariate does not only lose a variable; it removes a patient from the balancing constraint set, so the population actually being matched shifts with nothing in the output to signal it. The other two layers resist the same treatment: an unreported aggregate moment cannot be imputed from nothing without auxiliary information or an identified model, and a study with no IPD is an access problem rather than a missing-data problem. The one solution that exists is specific to MAIC and to missingness inside the IPD, so nothing yet propagates uncertainty jointly across imputation, weighting, and target-summary estimation, and packages still do not record which strategy was used; the literature auditor found that maicplus 0.1.2 and outstandR 2.0.0 declare no missing-data dependency at all. Missing-not-at-random departures stay unidentifiable from the data, so sensitivity analysis is needed wherever a missing-at-random assumption is not defensible rather than as a blanket requirement.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Fang, Li, Lai and He 2026, Missing Data Handling in the Application of Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison, Ther Innov Regul Sci 60(4):1103-1111
states that the literature lacks guidance on how to handle missing data in the application of MAIC, then proposes weighting-based methods for missing outcomes and covariates inside the IPD, formed as the product of an inverse probability of not missing the outcome and the usual MAIC balancing weights, with extensive simulation studies; it does not address unreported aggregate summaries or structurally unavailable IPD


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
handles the three layers differently rather than collapsing them: cstc() delegates NA handling to glm() and coxph(), cmaic() rejects nonfinite weights caused by missing matching covariates, cmlnmr() rejects missing covariates and outcomes outright, missing aggregate moments raise an error, and aggregate-only edges keep their published study-population contrast; it has no coherent missing-data framework

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Layer one now has a weighting solution for MAIC, so the work there is validation and extension: test it outside MAIC, against multiple imputation, and under conditions the original simulations did not cover. Multiple imputation congenial with a transport model still has to be built, with imputation variables chosen by their causal role rather than from a fixed checklist, since a selection indicator is usually unavailable when target microdata do not exist. Missing target summaries need auxiliary information or an explicit identified model rather than imputation from nothing, and missing-not-at-random departures need declared sensitivity analysis. At minimum, software should record which missing-data strategy was applied, because the choice is currently invisible in the output; a negligible-missingness threshold is the wrong test, since it is neither necessary nor sufficient for complete-case validity.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “Three missingness layers in PAIC collapse to a complete-case default” The title says all three missingness layers collapse to a complete-case default, which the audit found too strong since the layers are handled differently and layer one has been closed by weighting.
The source said. “PAIC missingness has three distinct layers with different mechanisms: participant-level missing covariates or outcomes inside the IPD, trial-level non-reporting in the aggregate publication, and structurally unavailable IPD for whole studies. Packages default to complete-case handling that collapses all three, and standard imputation is not automatically compatible with the transport model, so imputations valid in the source need not be valid in the target.”
What was wrong with it. The three-layer taxonomy was unattributed in the source, and its central claim, that packages default to a complete-case handling that collapses all three layers, was too strong. The literature auditor supplied the missing source, Fang et al. 2026 (doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00914-2), which states that the literature lacks guidance on handling missing data in MAIC and then closes layer one by weighting; the code auditor found that at commit 9d150e9 of the unreleased cpaic development package the layers are handled differently rather than collapsed, since cmlnmr() rejects missing covariates and outcomes outright, missing aggregate moments raise an error, and aggregate-only edges keep their published contrast.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Retrieved Fang, Li, Lai & He (2026), Ther Innov Regul Sci 60(4):1103-1111, which both confirms the absence claim and partly closes it. The paper states outright: ‘However, the literature lacks guidance on how to handle missing data in the application of MAIC.’ That is a source asserting the absence, which is what the entry’s unsourced claims need. It then proposes a solution for layer one only: ‘we propose some weighting-based methods to handle missing data in the outcome variable and/or covariates when applying MAIC. These weights can be expressed as products of the inverse probability of not missing the outcomes and weights that account for the difference in baseline characteristics… Extensive simulation studies are conducted.’ So participant-level missing covariates and outcomes inside the IPD are now handled, by inverse-probability weighting nested inside the MAIC weights, with simulation evidence. The other two layers are untouched: trial-level non-reporting in the aggregate publication, and structurally unavailable IPD. Multiple imputation congenial with the transport model remains unbuilt (Fang et al. use weighting, not MI), as does MNAR sensitivity analysis and imputation of missing target summaries. maicplus 0.1.2 and outstandR 2.0.0 declare no missing-data dependency, consistent with the complete-case-default claim. codex dissented (open): C2 is a useful taxonomy, but complete-case analysis cannot collapse all three layers: it acts on individual records, while absent aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD create different identification or data-access problems. C3, C4, and C6 are unsourced prevalence or maturity claims. C5 is correct when the missing variables are required for identification. C7 is possible, not inevitable; dependence between missingness, study selection, and transport must be represented by an explicit causal or selection model. C8 and C9 are broadly sound as conditional recommendations. C10 is too prescriptive: treatment, outcome, study, and selection indicators belong in an imputation model only when their variation and causal roles require them, and a selection indicator cannot ordinarily be used in standard MI when target microdata do not exist. C11 is not universally required, although MNAR sensitivity analysis is warranted when MAR is not defensible. C12 requires auxiliary information or an identified model; missing target summaries cannot simply be imputed from nothing. C13 uses the wrong criterion: negligible missingness is neither necessary nor sufficient for complete-case validity. title: Nothing propagates sampling error in reported target moments
text: MIS-03 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: Nothing propagates sampling error in reported target moments
text:
Statement
Published aggregate-data means and standard deviations are estimates when they are sample summaries of a superpopulation, yet population-adjustment estimators condition on them as fixed and no study has quantified the coverage that costs. The weight-estimation half of the problem is settled: sandwich, ESS-rescaled, and bootstrap variance estimators exist, are implemented in maicplus, and were benchmarked across 108 scenarios by Chandler and Proskorovsky (2024, doi:10.1002/jrsm.1759), who found the fixed-weight conventional estimator materially anticonservative only under poor or moderate overlap and all methods valid under strong overlap. G-MAIC (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10021) propagates population-adjustment uncertainty by Bayesian bootstrap, and cmaic() in the unreleased cpaic development package on GitHub re-estimates weights inside a stratified bootstrap. None of these resamples the target moments.

title: Nothing propagates sampling error in reported target moments
text:
Why it is open
Weights are functions of estimated parameters and of published target moments, and only the first part has been addressed. Sandwich, ESS-rescaled, bootstrap, and Bayesian-bootstrap estimators now cover weight estimation, and the correction matters mainly when overlap is poor or moderate. The published-moment part is untouched because a table of means and standard deviations arrives without the covariance among those moments or a sampling model for them, so there is nothing to resample and no nuisance equation to stack. The gap bites only when the estimand is a superpopulation quantity; where the supplied summaries define the target by construction, or are exact administrative counts, conditioning on them is the correct thing to do.

title: Nothing propagates sampling error in reported target moments
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chandler and Proskorovsky 2024, Uncertain about uncertainty in matching-adjusted indirect comparisons? A simulation study to compare methods for variance estimation, Res Synth Methods 15(6):1094-1110
compares conventional estimators on raw weights, conventional estimators on ESS-rescaled weights, robust sandwich estimators, and bootstrapping across 108 scenarios, anchored and unanchored, for binary and time-to-event outcomes; finds variability underestimated by conventional estimators with raw weights when population overlap is poor or moderate, and all methods producing valid coverage probabilities and standard errors under strong overlap


Gao, Heath and Baio 2025, Regression augmented weighting adjustment for indirect comparisons in health decision modelling
G-MAIC employs a Bayesian bootstrap to propagate the uncertainty of population-adjusted estimates rather than conditioning on estimated weights


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
cmaic() runs a stratified-by-arm bootstrap that resamples the IPD, re-estimates the MAIC weights, and refits the outcome model, so weight-estimation uncertainty enters the interval; target means and standard deviations are held fixed throughout that bootstrap, and cstc() and cmlnmr() likewise condition on the supplied target summaries

title: Nothing propagates sampling error in reported target moments
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not rebuild weight-estimation variance; it exists, is implemented, and is benchmarked. The open work is a sampling model for the published target moments, either deriving their covariance from reported sample sizes and design or a Bayesian formulation that places a distribution over the target covariate law and integrates the treatment effect over posterior draws. With such a model, resampling the moments alongside the individual data, or stacking a moment-estimation equation into the estimating system, becomes well defined; without one, a bootstrap over target summaries is not identified. Then run the simulation the source proposed, restricted to the part nobody has done: how much coverage is lost by conditioning on target moments at realistic aggregate-data sample sizes.

title: Nothing propagates sampling error in reported target moments
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Published aggregate-data means and standard deviations are estimates, yet every population-adjustment estimator I could find conditions on them as fixed, and no study has quantified the resulting coverage loss. Uncertainty from weight estimation itself is a different matter: sandwich, ESS-rescaled and bootstrap estimators exist, are implemented in maicplus, and were benchmarked across 108 scenarios by Chandler & Proskorovsky (2024), who found the fixed-weight conventional estimator is only materially anticonservative under poor or moderate overlap.
The source titled this. “Weights and reported target moments are treated as known constants” The title says estimated weights are treated as known constants, but weight-estimation variance is solved, benchmarked across 108 scenarios and implemented in maicplus.
The source said. “Many population-adjusted analyses condition on estimated weights and on published aggregate-data moments as if both were fixed inputs, so the reported uncertainty omits weight-estimation and target-summary variability.”
What was wrong with it. The source said reported uncertainty omits both weight-estimation and target-summary variability, and that the omission is directional so intervals come out systematically too narrow. Both auditors judged that overstated: the weight-estimation half was benchmarked across 108 scenarios by Chandler and Proskorovsky (2024, doi:10.1002/jrsm.1759) and is shipped in maicplus, in G-MAIC (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10021), and in the cmaic() bootstrap of cpaic at commit 9d150e9, and the direction is not guaranteed, since estimating calibration weights can raise or lower variance and fixed-weight sandwich calculations can be conservative; only the target-moment half survives.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The weight-estimation half of this entry has already been done, including the simulation the proposed direction asks for. Chandler & Proskorovsky (2024), Res Synth Methods 15(6):1094-1110: ‘One of the primary challenges in MAIC is the need to properly account for the additional uncertainty introduced by the matching process… we conducted a comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation study to evaluate the performance of different statistical methods across 108 scenarios. Four general approaches for variance estimation were compared in both anchored and unanchored MAICs of binary and time-to-event outcomes: (1) conventional estimators (CE) using raw weights; (2) CE using weights rescaled to the effective sample size (ESS); (3) robust sandwich estimators; and (4) bootstrapping.’ Their finding narrows the entry materially: undercoverage from treating weights as fixed appears only under poor or moderate overlap, and ‘All methods produced valid coverage probabilities and standard errors in cases of strong population overlap.’ The tooling is shipped: maicplus 0.1.2 imports both sandwich and boot, and G-MAIC (Gao, Heath & Baio 2025) ‘employs Bayesian bootstrap to propagate the uncertainty of population-adjusted estimates.’ The target-moment half is where I found nothing: no method propagating sampling error in published aggregate means and SDs. Cites doi:10.1002/jrsm.1759: Executes the entry’s proposed simulation for the weight-estimation component: 108 scenarios, four variance approaches, anchored and unanchored, binary and time-to-event, reporting empirical coverage.. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10021: G-MAIC uses Bayesian bootstrap to propagate population-adjustment uncertainty rather than conditioning on estimated weights..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 and C2 are unsourced prevalence claims, although the corresponding conditional analyses certainly occur. C3 is true when published means and SDs are sample estimates of superpopulation moments, but not when they are exact administrative quantities, user-defined targets, or the supplied summaries define a conditional finite-population estimand. C4 is correct only conditionally: stacked equations must include every relevant nuisance equation and cross-covariance, while a bootstrap must resample both data sources at their actual sampling units. Published moments alone usually do not permit such a bootstrap without their covariance or an additional sampling model. Most importantly, omission is not directionally guaranteed to make intervals narrower; estimating calibration weights can increase or decrease variance, and fixed-weight sandwich calculations may be conservative in some settings. cpaic partially resolves C1: cmaic() stratified-bootstraps the IPD, re-estimates the weights, and refits the outcome model. It nevertheless holds target means and SDs fixed throughout that bootstrap; cstc() and cmlnmr() likewise condition on supplied target summaries. The remaining target-summary component can matter with small target samples or unstable overlap but is not universally a very-high-severity defect. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: The cmaic() bootstrap resamples IPD within treatment arms, re-estimates MAIC weights, and refits the outcome model, resolving the weight-estimation component for that estimator. Target moments remain fixed..

title: Conventional STC reports a conditional effect at target means
text: MOD-01 Partially addressed Very high priority Established

title: Conventional STC reports a conditional effect at target means
text:
Statement
A conventional or anchored STC that fits a generalized linear or Cox model in the IPD trial and reports the treatment coefficient evaluated at the aggregate trial’s covariate means returns a conditional parameter at a mean covariate profile, which on non-collapsible scales is not the marginal effect the aggregate-data trial reports. The mismatch is real and was demonstrated by simulation in Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511), but it is no longer an open methods problem: parametric g-computation (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565, 2022) and multiple imputation marginalization (doi:10.1186/s12874-024-02157-x, 2024) standardize the fitted model over the target covariate distribution, and outstandR ships both on CRAN. What is still open is the input those methods need. The target joint covariate law is rarely published, and implementations condition on reported target means and standard deviations as if they were known constants.

title: Conventional STC reports a conditional effect at target means
text:
Why it is open
The mismatch persists in practice rather than in theory. Evaluating a fitted model at target means is numerically trivial and produces something that looks like a treatment effect, so the estimand error leaves no trace in output, diagnostics or balance tables, while the compatible route needs the target joint covariate distribution that aggregate reports rarely provide. Standardization also replaces one identification problem with two estimation problems, because the target covariate law must be modeled alongside the outcome and neither model can be validated against the aggregate data that motivated the analysis. GPT-5.6 Sol added that target-summary uncertainty is a genuine omission when the estimand indexes a superpopulation, but may properly be conditioned on when the estimand indexes the realized finite target sample.

title: Conventional STC reports a conditional effect at target means
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar, Heath & Baio 2022, Parametric G-computation for compatible indirect treatment comparisons with limited individual patient data, Research Synthesis Methods (PMID 35485582)
Standardizes a GLM or Cox outcome model over the target covariate distribution to recover a marginal effect compatible with the aggregate-data trial. This is the resolution of the estimand mismatch the entry describes, and it is the entry’s own citation.


Model-based standardization using multiple imputation, BMC Medical Research Methodology 2024 (PMID 38341552)

Methods for population adjustment with limited access to individual patient data: a review and simulation study, 2021 (PMID 34196111)
Establishes the entry’s central bias claim by simulation across 162 survival scenarios, showing that typical STC targets a conditional effect where the estimand should be marginal, and names the fix that was delivered in 2022.


outstandR: Population-Adjusted Indirect Treatment Comparison in R (described in arXiv:2601.07532)
Ships maximum-likelihood and Bayesian G-computation plus multiple imputation marginalization, so the compatible alternative is a released package rather than research-only.

title: Conventional STC reports a conditional effect at target means
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use the existing standardization implementations rather than rebuilding them, and state the conditional or marginal status and the indexing population of every reported STC quantity. The research work left is the target law: propagate uncertainty in it instead of fixing it, using a Bayesian distribution over the target law or bootstrap and influence-function expansions that include target-summary estimation, and reconstruct the joint distribution from published marginals with copulas, maximum entropy or synthetic target populations while reporting sensitivity to that reconstruction. State which estimand each uncertainty statement is for, since conditioning on the realized target sample is legitimate for a finite-population estimand.

title: Conventional STC reports a conditional effect at target means
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “A conventional or anchored simulated treatment comparison fits a generalized linear or Cox model in the IPD trial and reports the treatment coefficient evaluated at the aggregate trial’s covariate means. That quantity is a conditional parameter at a mean covariate profile; on non-collapsible scales it is not the marginal effect the aggregate-data trial reports, so the two arms of the indirect comparison are not the same estimand.”
What was wrong with it. The source framed the conditional versus marginal mismatch as an open problem. Both auditors voted it partially solved: the fix is the entry’s own citation (parametric g-computation, doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565, 2022), extended by multiple imputation marginalization (doi:10.1186/s12874-024-02157-x, 2024) and shipped on CRAN in outstandR, so what survives is the treatment of reported target summaries as fixed known constants.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Retrieved the cited work (Remiro-Azocar, Heath & Baio 2022, Res Synth Methods, PMID 35485582). Its abstract states verbatim: ‘Current outcome regression-based alternatives can extrapolate but target a conditional treatment effect that is incompatible in the indirect comparison. When adjusting for covariates, one must integrate or average the conditional estimate over the relevant population to recover a compatible marginal treatment effect.’ The prior_work description is accurate. The same abstract also supports the extrapolation claim (‘MAIC … cannot extrapolate beyond the observed covariate space’) and the efficiency claim (‘Parametric G-computation achieves more precise and more accurate estimates than MAIC, particularly when covariate overlap is poor’). However, the entry’s OWN citation is the fix: the estimand mismatch was diagnosed in Remiro-Azocar 2021 (jrsm.1511), solved by parametric G-computation (2022), extended by multiple imputation marginalization (2024, PMID 38341552), and is now shipped on CRAN in outstandR. What remains genuinely open is the sub-claim I could not verify: that implementations ignore uncertainty in the reported target summaries. Vote partially-solved, not open.

At choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, NAMESPACE exports cstc(), R/cstc.R centers effect modifiers at target means and explicitly labels the result conditional, and R/effects.R and R/cmlnmr.R state that no marginal standardized path is returned. title: Ecological versus within-study effect modification
text: MOD-03 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: Ecological versus within-study effect modification
text:
Statement
Aggregate study means inform between-study associations, not individual-level treatment-by-covariate interactions, so meta-regression on study means can misattribute an ecological association to individual effect modification and then transport it to a target population. This is established rather than new: it is Berlin et al. 2002 (doi:10.1002/sim.1023), and the remedy the entry proposes, separating within-trial from across-trial information by trial-mean centering, was formalized, simulated and demonstrated by Hua et al. 2017 (doi:10.1002/sim.7171). The auditors split on ML-NMR (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579): the literature auditor read it as avoiding the ecological bias of aggregate-data network meta-regression, while GPT-5.6 Sol held that it avoids mean plug-in aggregation but that an interaction informed only by aggregate arms stays ecological unless within-study information or an identifying restriction separates the coefficients, pointing to a development implementation that fits one interaction matrix for IPD covariates and aggregate means and thereby imposes equality of the two (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9). What remains open is aggregate-only interaction identification and a formal ecological-bias sensitivity analysis over the gap between the coefficients, since an IPD-informed prior transfers information under exchangeability but does not create likelihood identification.

title: Ecological versus within-study effect modification
text:
Why it is open
In an aggregate-data study the covariate takes a single value per arm, so no within-study contrast exists to identify the individual-level interaction and the fitted coefficient is a between-study slope confounded with everything else that varies across studies. The two coefficients coincide only under an assumption the aggregate data cannot check, and because the regression is well behaved either way the substitution leaves no signature in fit statistics. Where IPD supply within-study variation the remedy is known and validated, so the residual problem is specifically the aggregate-only case, in which the identifying restriction is imposed by the model rather than tested by the data.

title: Ecological versus within-study effect modification
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Berlin et al. 2002, Individual patient- versus group-level data meta-regressions for the investigation of treatment effect modifiers: ecological bias rears its ugly head, Statistics in Medicine (PMID 11813224)
Original source for the entry’s central claim that group-level meta-regression can substitute an ecological association for an individual-level interaction.


Hua, Burke, Crowther, Ensor, Tudur Smith & Riley 2017, One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis models: estimation of treatment-covariate interactions must avoid ecological bias by separating out within-trial and across-trial information, Statistics in Medicine (PMID 27910122)
Formalizes and validates the entry’s proposed remedy, showing by simulation and an applied epilepsy example that trial-mean centering separates within-trial from across-trial information and that failing to do so distorts interaction estimates.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A (PMID 32684669)
Integrates an individual-level model over the aggregate covariate distribution rather than plugging in means, removing the aggregation bias of standard aggregate-data meta-regression. Whether that also removes ecological bias in an aggregate-only interaction is what the two auditors disputed.


cpaic development source at commit 9d150e9 (choxos/cpaic)
Source-code evidence cited by GPT-5.6 Sol that fitting one interaction matrix across IPD covariates and aggregate means imposes equality of the within-study and between-study interaction. cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub; an auditor confirmed it is not on CRAN and cannot be installed from there.

title: Ecological versus within-study effect modification
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use the established remedy wherever IPD allow it: separate within-study and between-study coefficients by trial-mean centering, and integrate an individual-level model over the aggregate covariate distribution rather than plugging in means. The work genuinely left is the aggregate-only case: report which coefficient a transported effect relies on, and run an explicit ecological-bias sensitivity analysis over the gap between the within-study and between-study coefficients rather than assuming it is zero. IPD-informed priors on the individual-level interaction can regularize a posterior and should be reported as an assumption, not as identification.

title: Ecological versus within-study effect modification
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Aggregate-data study means identify between-study gradients rather than individual-level treatment-by-covariate interactions, so meta-regression on study means can misattribute an ecological association to individual effect modification and then transport it to a target population.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated a result established in 2002 with an empty prior_work list; the literature auditor sourced it to Berlin et al. 2002 (doi:10.1002/sim.1023) and its proposed remedy to Hua et al. 2017 (doi:10.1002/sim.7171), so the claim is now sourced. The two auditors disagreed about how much ML-NMR (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579) resolves, and both readings are kept above.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): prior_work is empty, but every substantive claim here is established literature I retrieved. The problem statement is Berlin et al. 2002, Stat Med 21:371-387 (PMID 11813224), whose title is literally ‘ecological bias rears its ugly head’. The entry’s own proposed remedy (separating within-study and between-study coefficients by mean-centering) was formalized, simulated and empirically demonstrated by Hua, Burke, Crowther, Ensor, Tudur Smith & Riley, Stat Med 2017 (PMID 27910122), which reports the epilepsy example where the age interaction moves from -0.011 (95% CI -0.019 to -0.003, p=0.004) when within- and across-trial information are amalgamated to -0.007 (95% CI -0.019 to 0.005, p=0.22) when they are separated. C2 is the standard remedy when IPD provide within-study variation. C3 is only conditionally true. ML-NMR avoids mean plug-in aggregation by integrating an individual-level model, but an interaction informed only by aggregate arms remains ecological unless within-study information or an identifying restriction separates the coefficients. cpaic ground truth is explicit: cmlnmr() uses one Gamma for IPD covariates and aggregate means and therefore imposes equality of within-study and between-study interactions. C4 is also too strong: an IPD-informed prior can transfer information under exchangeability assumptions and regularize a posterior, but a prior does not create likelihood identification. The broad ecological-bias problem and its main remedy are established; aggregate-only interaction identification remains structurally unresolved and decision-critical when a transported contrast relies on it.

title: No doubly robust PAIC estimator is indexed by bias parameters
text: MOD-05 Partially addressed Very high priority Established

title: No doubly robust PAIC estimator is indexed by bias parameters
text:
Statement
An augmented estimator combining an outcome model with a sampling or transport weight model is consistent if either nuisance model is correct, given conditional exchangeability, positivity and the usual consistency conditions. The seven failures the source enumerates (unmeasured effect modifier, lack of overlap, wrong treatment or outcome version, both nuisance models wrong, wrong target moments, network inconsistency, false component bridge) are true by construction, but they are the agenda’s own list and the paper it cites asserts none of them. Campbell and Remiro-Azocar (doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106) do supply the augmented entropy-balancing MAIC estimator, demonstrated in simulation for binary outcomes with a logistic outcome model, and drMAIC ships doubly robust MAIC for practitioners. What is open is the layer around the estimator: no doubly robust estimator indexed by bias parameters and nested inside quantitative bias analysis exists, and network versions are absent.

title: No doubly robust PAIC estimator is indexed by bias parameters
text:
Why it is open
Double robustness is a union-model property for two measured-data nuisance models with the identification assumptions held fixed, so every threat operating through those assumptions or through data support is untouched by construction and cannot be repaired by better nuisance estimation. Packages return a single augmented point estimate with an interval that conditions on identification holding, so the residual-bias layer is never displayed to a decision maker; drMAIC ships E-values and weight trimming as separate sensitivity analyses rather than an estimator indexed by bias parameters. The estimators have also been developed for a single source and a single target rather than for the network structures HTA submissions contain, and no AIPW or TMLE network estimator was found in the implementations the auditors read.

title: No doubly robust PAIC estimator is indexed by bias parameters
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Campbell & Remiro-Azocar 2026, Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for the analysis of externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons, Research Synthesis Methods (preprint arXiv:2505.00113)
Places externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored ITCs in one causal framework and proposes an augmented entropy-balancing MAIC estimator that is doubly robust to misspecification of the weighting or outcome model. Demonstrated in simulation for binary outcomes with a logistic outcome model.

Released implementation of augmented doubly robust MAIC. Ships E-values and weight trimming as separate sensitivity analyses, not the bias-parameter-indexed estimator this entry asks for.

title: No doubly robust PAIC estimator is indexed by bias parameters
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Nest the augmented estimators that already exist inside quantitative bias analysis, reporting the estimate as a function of bias parameters rather than as a single number, and state in every report which layer double robustness covers (measured-data outcome and transport models) and which it does not (unmeasured modifiers, positivity, treatment version, target moments, network consistency, component additivity). Extend the demonstration beyond binary outcomes with a logistic outcome model, since that is the extent of the current evidence for the augmented MAIC estimator. Combine augmented estimation with overlap diagnostics and partial identification so the residual-bias layer stays visible, and extend to network settings where nothing is implemented.

title: No doubly robust PAIC estimator is indexed by bias parameters
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Double robustness is routinely read as general robustness” The title asserts that double robustness is routinely misread, a prevalence claim neither auditor could establish, and the seven-failure list came from the entry rather than its citation.
The source said. “An augmented estimator combining an outcome model with a sampling or transport weight model is consistent under standard conditions if either nuisance model is correct, given conditional exchangeability. The report holds that the label doubly robust is routinely read as general robustness and enumerates seven distinct failures it does not protect against: an unmeasured effect modifier, lack of overlap, an incorrect treatment or outcome version, both nuisance models being wrong, wrong target moments, network inconsistency, and a false component bridge.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented a seven-item enumeration of what double robustness does not protect against as though it came from its cited paper; the literature auditor found that the paper makes no such negative claims and that its double robustness demonstration covers binary outcomes with a logistic outcome model only (doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106). Neither auditor could establish the prevalence claim carried by the word ‘routinely’.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Retrieved Campbell & Remiro-Azocar, ‘Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for the analysis of externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons’, Res Synth Methods 2026 (doi 10.1017/rsm.2026.10106; preprint arXiv:2505.00113). The abstract confirms the entry’s description exactly: an entropy-balancing MAIC augmented with a conditional outcome expectation model, doubly robust to misspecification of either. Two caveats make this supported-with-caveat rather than fully supported. First, the demonstration is binary outcomes with a logistic outcome model only, so ‘doubly robust’ is evidenced for that case; the entry does not say so. Second, the seven-item enumeration of what double robustness does NOT protect against is the agenda’s own construction, not anything the cited paper asserts; the paper makes no such negative claims. Those seven items are nonetheless true by construction, since double robustness is a property of two measured-data nuisance models with identification held fixed. The ‘no reference implementation of a DR estimator indexed by bias parameters inside QBA’ claim I could not falsify; drMAIC ships E-values and weight trimming as separate sensitivity analyses, not a bias-parameter-indexed DR estimator.

Literature and prior-art check

The abstract confirms the entry’s description exactly: an entropy-balancing MAIC augmented with a conditional outcome expectation model, doubly robust to misspecification of either. Two caveats make this supported-with-caveat rather than fully supported. First, the demonstration is binary outcomes with a logistic outcome model only, so ‘doubly robust’ is evidenced for that case; the entry does not say so. Second, the seven-item enumeration of what double robustness does NOT protect against is the agenda’s own construction, not anything the cited paper asserts; the paper makes no such negative claims. Those seven items are nonetheless true by construction, since double robustness is a property of two measured-data nuisance models with identification held fixed. The ‘no reference implementation of a DR estimator indexed by bias parameters inside QBA’ claim I could not falsify; drMAIC ships E-values and weight trimming as separate sensitivity analyses, not a bias-parameter-indexed DR estimator.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C1-C2 state the usual double-robustness result, provided consistency, conditional exchangeability, positivity, and any required treatment and censoring mechanisms also hold. C3-C11 are technically correct: double robustness is a union-model property for specified measured-data nuisances and does not repair identification, support, target-definition, network-consistency, or component-additivity failures; C4 and C5 are duplicates. C12 is supported for the measured-data weighting and outcome models in the estimator’s stated scope. C13 and the word ‘routinely’ are literature and prevalence claims outside this lens. Source-code ground truth adds that cpaic@9d150e9 exports no AIPW, TMLE, or other doubly robust network estimator. The underlying limitations are decision-critical, but they are established assumptions rather than a new technical discovery; nesting a DR estimator in QBA and extending it to networks are roadmap items. Existing augmented estimation partly addresses the agenda, while the residual-bias and network layers remain open. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106: Supplies an augmented entropy-balancing MAIC estimator with consistency under either the measured-data weighting model or outcome model in its stated setting; it does not resolve identification failures or the proposed QBA and network extensions..
