title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text: MOD-07 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising Tractability 2/5

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Statement
No efficient influence function or TMLE is established for a mixed-IPD and aggregate-data, multi-arm network that transports arm-level potential outcomes to one declared population while retaining shared-arm covariance. The claim needs that narrowing, because adjacent problems are solved: Schnitzer et al. 2016 (doi:10.1515/jci-2016-0014) adapt doubly robust locally efficient TMLE to network meta-analysis with individual data, Dahabreh et al. (arXiv:1908.09230) build efficient robust transport estimators across multiple randomized trials, Su et al. (arXiv:2405.10769) derive the semiparametric efficiency bound of the transported average treatment effect from multi-source data, and Le et al. (arXiv:2408.04854) mix aggregate and individual data, though by M-estimation, without double robustness, and for two-arm binary treatment only. Two of the entry’s requirements also overreach: an aggregate study need not enter through a full aggregate likelihood, since summary-estimate covariance, calibration constraints or estimating equations can carry it, and small-study uncertainty is difficult rather than universally unsolved.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Why it is open
Standard semiparametric transport theory assumes one source sample and one target sample, whereas a network has many source studies with heterogeneous data granularity, multi-arm covariance and randomization inside each study that must survive estimation. Fluctuating or pooling an outcome model across studies can destroy the within-study randomization that supplies the network’s identification, and the usual workaround of replacing contrasts pairwise loses exactly the joint covariance the network needs. A network estimand is a vector of correlated contrasts rather than a scalar, so both a multivariate fluctuation and an influence function combining outcome models, study-participation models and aggregate contributions would have to be derived, and valid uncertainty would then have to come from a handful of studies where asymptotics in the number of studies are unavailable.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Schnitzer, Steele, Bally & Shrier 2016, A Causal Inference Approach to Network Meta-Analysis, Journal of Causal Inference
Adapts single-study causal estimators, including doubly robust semiparametric locally efficient TMLE, to network meta-analysis. Requires individual data throughout.


Dahabreh, Robertson, Petito, Hernan & Steingrimsson, Efficient and robust transport estimators across multiple randomized trials
Builds efficient and robust estimators for transporting effects from multiple randomized trials to a target population. Requires IPD from every source.


Su, Rytgaard, Ravn & Eriksson, semiparametric efficiency for the transported average treatment effect from multi-source data
Derives the semiparametric efficiency bound of the transported average treatment effect and characterizes a class of doubly robust asymptotically linear estimators. Requires IPD from every source.


Le, Beclin, Afach & Vo, combining aggregate and individual data
Mixes aggregate and individual data, the granularity the entry cares about, but uses M-estimation, is not doubly robust, and covers binary treatment in two-arm trials only.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Derive the efficient influence function for a connected network with IPD in a subset of studies and a declared target population, starting from the multi-trial transport and NMA-TMLE results that already exist rather than from first principles, with an estimator that respects within-study randomization, accounts for multi-arm covariance, targets arm-level potential outcomes in one population and permits cross-fitting by study. Let the aggregate studies enter through whichever coherent device fits the model, whether a likelihood contribution, a summary-estimate covariance or a calibration constraint, rather than assuming a full aggregate likelihood is required, and validate on multi-arm networks where the correct joint covariance is known by construction. A component extension replaces treatment indicators with component and interaction design vectors, which is valid only once component additivity and the interaction structure are assumed.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “No network efficient influence function or network TMLE exists” The title says no network efficient influence function or TMLE exists, but TMLE for network meta-analysis with individual data and multi-trial transport estimators are published.
The source said. “The report asks whether a network-level efficient influence function can be derived for evidence in which some studies contribute IPD and others contribute only aggregate data, and makes such an estimator the core of a proposed doubly robust network transport project. Its targeted counterpart, a network TMLE that preserves randomized within-study contrasts and multi-arm covariance while transporting to a declared population, is likewise stated not to exist.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no network-level efficient influence function has been derived, with an empty prior_work list; the literature auditor supplied four adjacent results (doi:10.1515/jci-2016-0014, arXiv:1908.09230, arXiv:2405.10769, arXiv:2408.04854) that narrow the novelty to the mixed-granularity multi-arm case. GPT-5.6 Sol rejected the requirement that aggregate studies must enter through a likelihood and the blanket claim that small-study uncertainty is unsolved.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Searched for a network-level efficient influence function and a network TMLE over mixed IPD and aggregate-data evidence and found nothing matching. The nearest prior art, all of which the entry omits (prior_work is empty), narrows the novelty claim considerably. Schnitzer, Steele, Bally & Shrier, ‘A Causal Inference Approach to Network Meta-Analysis’, J Causal Inference 2016 (doi 10.1515/jci-2016-0014) already adapts single-study causal estimators including a doubly robust semiparametric locally efficient TMLE to network meta-analysis, but with individual data. Dahabreh, Robertson, Petito, Hernan & Steingrimsson (arXiv:1908.09230) build efficient and robust transport estimators across MULTIPLE randomized trials to a target population, and Su, Rytgaard, Ravn & Eriksson (arXiv:2405.10769) ‘derive the semiparametric efficiency bound of the TATE’ from multi-source data; both need IPD from every source. Le, Beclin, Afach & Vo (arXiv:2408.04854) mix aggregate and individual data but use M-estimation, are not doubly robust, and cover binary treatment in two-arm trials only. So the genuinely open part is the mixed-granularity, multi-arm-covariance-preserving network version, which is a narrower and more defensible claim than ‘no network-level EIF has been derived’. The scoring claim (impact 5, novelty 5, tractability 2) is self-referential to the source report and unverifiable externally.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. At cpaic@9d150e9, cmlnmr() is a Bayesian mixed-IPD/aggregate network model, but NAMESPACE contains no EIF, AIPW, or TMLE estimator, so cpaic does not resolve C1-C2. Those absence claims are defensible only for the exact class specified: a target-transporting, mixed-granularity, multi-arm network estimator retaining shared-arm covariance. Absence is not a mathematical consequence and cannot be generalized to all network EIF or TMLE work. C3-C4 are valid design requirements in substance, although a valid joint arm-level model may respect randomization without literally preserving precomputed contrasts. C5 is false as a necessity: aggregate studies may enter through likelihoods, summary-estimate covariance, calibration constraints, or estimating equations. C6 is correct when pairwise replacement discards shared-arm covariance. C7 is too broad because small-study inference depends on the asymptotic regime and can use small-sample or Bayesian methods, although it remains difficult for the proposed semiparametric estimator. C8 works only after assuming component additivity and specified component interactions. C9 is a self-reported score, not technical evidence. The narrow mixed-granularity network target remains open, but the title and several ‘must’ or ‘unsolved’ formulations overreach.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text: MOD-09 Confirmed open Very high priority Established

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Statement
ML-NMR combines IPD and aggregate data in one model and avoids the aggregation bias of aggregate-data meta-regression (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), now extends to general likelihoods including time-to-event outcomes (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169), and allows key assumptions to be assessed but not eliminated, as the 2023 psoriasis application showed (PMID 35997006), while practice remains dominated by MAIC and STC (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004). The auditors split on the recommendation that follows. The literature auditor verified every checkable claim and read the adoption gap as open; GPT-5.6 Sol held that partial IPD plus suspected effect-modifier imbalance is not sufficient to declare ML-NMR the default, because method choice also depends on the estimand, network structure, target-distribution information, overlap and model credibility, and that the absence of a designated default is not itself an unresolved methodological problem. The premise that ML-NMR is harder to specify, fit, diagnose and explain is plausible and widely repeated but unmeasured; neither auditor found a study of it.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Why it is open
ML-NMR is harder to specify, fit, diagnose and explain than MAIC or STC, so the barrier to adoption is practical rather than theoretical and default behavior has not shifted. Conditional constancy, shared effect-modifier assumptions, overlap and target-population relevance remain only partially testable inside ML-NMR, so switching buys coherence rather than assumption relief and the case for the extra effort is not self-evident to analysts or reviewers. On the weaker reading the missing thing is not a default but the material that would let an analyst make the comparison at all: diagnostics, training and reporting templates that state what has and has not been relieved.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




dmphillippo/multinma
R package implementing Bayesian NMA, NMR and ML-NMR with IPD plus aggregate data, time-to-event support, integration checks and target-population prediction.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A (PMID 32684669)
Defines ML-NMR: an individual-level regression model whose aggregate data are fitted by integrating over the covariate distribution, avoiding the aggregation bias of standard meta-regression.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades & Welton 2025, JRSS-A (preprint arXiv:2401.12640)
Removes the requirement that the aggregate-level likelihood have a known closed form, which had prevented application to time-to-event outcomes. This is the general-likelihood and survival support the entry claims.


Phillippo et al. 2023, psoriasis application, Medical Decision Making 43(1):53-67 (PMID 35997006)
Demonstrates for the first time how ML-NMR allows key assumptions to be assessed, finding little evidence that conditional constancy or shared effect-modifier assumptions were invalid. Assumptions were assessed, not eliminated.


Serret-Larmande et al. 2023, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (PMID 37717707)
Methodological review of published PAIC analyses, overwhelmingly MAIC and STC, which is the evidence that practice has not moved to ML-NMR.


NICE quizartinib appraisal (PMID 39627603)
Cited by the literature auditor as one of the isolated applied appraisals using ML-NMR, consistent with adoption being sparse rather than absent.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the operational layer rather than legislating a default: standardized integration and fit diagnostics, worked training material, and reporting templates that state which assumptions ML-NMR has and has not relieved. Set out explicit criteria for when ML-NMR is preferable and when it is infeasible, expressed in terms of estimand, network structure, available target-distribution information, overlap and model credibility, so the method choice is argued rather than asserted. Measuring the specification, fitting and communication burden against MAIC and STC would also convert the entry’s central unsourced premise into evidence.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “ML-NMR is not the default despite being the most coherent framework” The title declares ML-NMR the most coherent framework and presumptive default, which the audit rejected since method choice also depends on estimand, network structure and overlap.
The source said. “The report recommends making ML-NMR the default upgrade path when IPD exist for a subset of trials in a connected network and clinically meaningful effect-modifier imbalance is suspected, because it is the most coherent framework currently available and now has survival and general-likelihood support. Practice has not moved, and the report is explicit that ML-NMR does not solve the underlying scientific problem.”
What was wrong with it. The source made a default-method recommendation with nothing cited. The literature auditor sourced each factual component (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579, doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169, PMID 35997006, doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004), so the claim is now sourced, and voted the entry open; GPT-5.6 Sol voted it not a problem, because no universal default follows from partial IPD plus suspected imbalance. Both readings are kept above.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Every checkable claim verified against retrieved sources. ‘Extends to general likelihoods including survival’: Phillippo, Dias, Ades & Welton, JRSS-A 2025 (doi 10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169, arXiv:2401.12640) states that ML-NMR ‘currently requires the aggregate-level likelihood to have a known closed form. Notably, this prevents application to time-to-event outcomes’ and then removes that restriction. ‘Integrates IPD and AgD and avoids aggregation bias’: Phillippo et al. 2020 JRSS-A and the 2023 Med Decis Making psoriasis paper, which says ML-NMR ‘coherently synthesizes evidence from IPD and AgD studies in networks of any size while avoiding aggregation bias and noncollapsibility bias’. The ‘2023 psoriasis application’ claim is exactly right: Phillippo et al., Med Decis Making 2023;43(1):53-67 (PMID 35997006) demonstrates ‘for the first time how ML-NMR allows key assumptions to be assessed’ and found ‘little evidence that the conditional constancy or shared effect modifier assumptions were invalid’ - assessed, not eliminated. ‘Practice has not moved’ is consistent with Serret-Larmande et al. 2023 (288 PAICs, overwhelmingly MAIC/STC) and with only isolated NICE applications such as the quizartinib appraisal (PMID 39627603). The one unsourced claim is that ML-NMR is harder to specify, fit, diagnose and explain; plausible and widely echoed, but I found no study measuring it.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

not-a-problem / overstated. C3 through C5 are broadly correct with important conditions. ML-NMR combines IPD and AgD coherently and can avoid conventional aggregation and non-collapsibility errors by integrating an individual-level model, but only when the outcome model, modifier structure, covariate distributions and numerical integration are adequate. It does not remove overlap, transportability or shared-modifier assumptions. C2 and C6 are comparative judgments rather than statistical results, and C1 is not a substantive claim. The presence of some IPD plus plausible modifier imbalance is insufficient to declare ML-NMR the default: method choice also depends on the estimand, network structure, target-distribution information, overlap and model credibility. C7 is a paper-specific claim outside this technical and cpaic-source audit. Training and implementation guidance may be useful, but failure to designate a universally preferred default is not an unresolved methodological problem, and the asserted very-high priority is inflated.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

text:
Statement
Dirichlet-process and finite-mixture representations are not undeveloped for this literature: Disher et al. (arXiv:2506.22154) put a Dirichlet-process prior with a regularized horseshoe base measure inside network meta-analysis, extend it to baseline-risk meta-regression so that clustering works under heterogeneity, and apply it to rheumatology and pain case studies. What has not been built is the narrower object this entry needs, a mixture over study populations combined with transport to a declared target population and aggregate-data integration. The generalized or safe Bayes half survives intact, since no calibrated learning-rate procedure exists for hierarchical evidence synthesis with transport. GPT-5.6 Sol also corrected two premises: with few studies these models can be strongly prior-sensitive but are not necessarily almost entirely prior-driven, and tempering does not widen intervals roughly uniformly, because it can change posterior location, shrinkage and the relative information of parts of a nonlinear hierarchical model.

title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text:
Why it is open
With the small number of studies typical of an ITC, a nonparametric mixture over study populations can be substantially prior-driven, so the apparent gain from non-normal heterogeneity or latent subpopulations is hard to separate from prior structure, although rich IPD or well-separated mixture components can supply real information. Tempering has the mirror problem: a learning rate must be chosen, no calibration procedure exists for a multi-study transport setting where the misspecification may sit in the outcome model, the study-effect structure or the integration over the target distribution, and a tempered posterior can look appropriately cautious while the structural error it was meant to guard against is untouched. Neither device identifies a cross-gap contrast that the likelihood does not touch. No worked implementation combines either with transport to a declared target and aggregate-data integration, so the trade-off between robustness and lost precision has never been quantified for ITC.

Take the Dirichlet-process machinery that already works inside network meta-analysis and extend it to study-population heterogeneity with transport and aggregate-data integration, reporting prior sensitivity and prior-to-posterior movement for every contrast so the contribution of the nonparametric structure is visible, and use it for heterogeneity and non-normality rather than as a device to identify cross-gap contrasts. The claim that Dirichlet-process and mixture representations of heterogeneity have not been ‘developed, calibrated, or validated for this setting’ is too strong if ‘this setting’ includes network meta-analysis. title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Statement
Posterior means, credible intervals, convergence diagnostics and ordinary fit diagnostics do not establish likelihood identification, and a proper prior yields a proper posterior for a contrast the likelihood does not touch. The tooling to expose this is not missing. Power-scaling sensitivity analysis (doi:10.1007/s11222-023-10366-5), shipped in the CRAN package priorsense and working with rstan, cmdstanr and brms, gives a diagnostic that indicates prior-data conflict or likelihood non-informativity and attaches to Stan-based models such as multinma with no new theory, and the development source cpaic already returns NA for contrasts its component design cannot uniquely identify, labels the information basis, refits under tighter and looser priors and plots prior against posterior (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9; an unreleased development package on GitHub that an auditor confirmed is not on CRAN). What is open is an ITC and PAIC reporting convention that makes this routine, plus exact identification diagnostics for nonlinear and aggregate-data likelihoods; GPT-5.6 Sol also notes the phenomenon is better named prior-dominated inference for a nonidentified contrast than prior-driven identification.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Why it is open
A proper prior always produces a finite posterior for a nonidentified contrast, so a posterior mean plus credible interval cannot by itself separate an answer supplied by the data from one supplied by the prior, and routine convergence and fit diagnostics do not test whether the likelihood is flat in the specific contrast a decision depends on. The diagnostics that would catch the substitution exist but are requested by no reporting template, so nothing in the workflow forces their use. Every flexible direction proposed for this setting, including nonparametric mixtures, Gaussian processes, BART, commensurate and robust priors and generalized Bayes, adds prior structure, so the exposure problem grows as the models improve, and exact identification diagnostics for nonlinear or aggregate-data likelihoods are still missing.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Make the existing diagnostics routine rather than proposing new ones: require Bayesian ITC and PAIC analyses to run power-scaling or an equivalent prior and likelihood sensitivity check on each cross-gap or transported contrast, and to label parameters identified, partially identified or nonidentified. Use prior classes instead of one arbitrary prior, consider modular or cut-feedback models so outcome data do not spuriously update elicited sensitivity distributions, and report deterministic parameter grids alongside posterior mixtures. The research work left is exact identification diagnostics for nonlinear and aggregate-data likelihoods, plus bridge-deletion demonstrations.

text: OUT-02 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Statement
Rare events and concentrated weights leave the binary likelihood weakly informative, so estimates can separate and become strongly sensitive to the prior or penalty that is then doing the identification work. The failure is narrower than the source said: a contrast-level log-odds estimate is infinite or undefined with a zero cell, but zero counts can enter an arm-based binomial, Bayesian or penalized likelihood without a continuity correction, and a double-zero study carries no conditional odds-ratio information that any likelihood choice can recover. Rare-event machinery does exist in the unweighted network meta-analysis literature, specifically penalized likelihood regression (Evrenoglou et al., arxiv:2109.10221, PMC9805041), which the source asserted without citing. Weight diagnostics still report a patient effective sample size that says nothing about how many events support the contrast, and no effective event sample size convention has been implemented.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Why it is open
Reweighting concentrates the effective sample on few individuals without reducing the number of covariates, so the weighted binary likelihood can flatten exactly where population adjustment is most needed. Where the prior or penalty supplies the identification, the resulting interval is still finite and reads as evidence, and there is no accepted way to report how much of the answer came from the data rather than the penalty. Effective sample size is computed from the weights alone and ignores the outcome, so it cannot detect that the weights landed on patients who contribute no events, and neither an effective event sample size nor a rare-event-plus-overlap workflow has been implemented anywhere the auditors looked. The literature auditor searched for any composition of rare-event likelihoods with MAIC weighting, STC or ML-NMR integration and found none, an absence they could not confirm from a source, so that part is recorded as unverified rather than established.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Compose the existing penalized and Bayesian rare-event likelihoods with the weighting and integration steps that population adjustment adds, and report the prior or penalty contribution explicitly instead of only a finite interval. Define and report an effective event sample size alongside the weighted patient effective sample size, paired with local ESS, leverage, influence and density-ratio diagnostics, since the diagnostics that already exist stop at the weights and do not reach the outcome. Drop the expectation that a beta-binomial or noncentral hypergeometric likelihood rescues individual-level separation or double-zero studies, and benchmark the remaining candidates in a simulation that varies event risk independently of nominal sample size, includes single-zero and double-zero studies, and reports type I error, coverage and prior dominance.

Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text: OUT-04 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Statement
Trials in a network may measure the same construct with different instruments, and a linear rescaling makes them equivalent only where the instruments are defensibly affine-equivalent and measurement-invariant. Latent-variable linking is not a new proposal: common-metric and item-response linking of different patient-reported instruments is deployed methodology (PMC5069858) and has been built for individual participant data across studies (PMC6582193), so what is missing is its integration into network or population-adjusted synthesis together with the anchor items, co-administration or calibration data it requires. On the standardized mean difference side, the standardizer is a property of the population in which it was measured, which is documented (PMC12358740; doi:10.1002/sim.10114), so the same mean difference yields different SMDs in populations with different outcome variability. The transport behavior of an SMD is not mathematically undefined; it is a mean difference divided by a specified reference standard deviation, so the real problem is choosing and identifying a scientifically meaningful common scale, and no transport theory for the standardized scale is established.

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Why it is open
Instruments differ in item content, scoring range and precision, and publications rarely include the co-administration, anchor items or calibration data a linking model needs, so the mapping is unidentified from what is published. Because the standardizer is a population property, transporting an SMD mixes a change in the effect with a change in the standardizing variance, and the target-population standard deviation is one of several defensible denominators rather than the compelled one. The native-scale fallback does not rescue this, since it cannot create a common metric across different instruments without a mapping. In cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, Gaussian individual-patient analyses accept mean differences only and explicitly reject SMD, so no cross-instrument path exists there at all.

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Bring the existing latent-variable and item-response linking machinery into network and population-adjusted synthesis rather than building it afresh, and state the identifying data it needs, whether anchor items, co-administration or external calibration, with explicit sensitivity to the linking assumptions. Where a standardized scale is unavoidable, make the denominator part of the estimand and report which population’s standard deviation was used, since the choice defines a different quantity rather than a different estimate of the same one. Develop transport theory for that declared standardized estimand, or report target-standardized mean differences on the native scale alongside study-specific residual variances.

Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Trials in a network may measure the same continuous construct with different instruments, so the reported means are not on a common metric before any population adjustment. The usual fix, the standardized mean difference, has unclear interpretation and unclear behavior under transport to a different target population.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented latent-variable measurement models as a proposed remedy; the literature auditor found instrument linking to be established methodology in integrative data analysis (PMC5069858, PMC6582193), so what is being proposed is its composition with population adjustment, not the models themselves. The code auditor rejected the framing that SMD transport is unclear in principle and noted that no unique denominator is compelled, since pooled, control-arm, baseline, external-reference and target-population standard deviations define different quantities; the auditors also split on status, with literature judging the entry partially solved and the code auditor judging it open, and that split is left standing.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Two halves with different maturity. The instrument-linking half is not new: I retrieved the common-metrics literature (www.common-metrics.org, PMC5069858, which estimates scores from different patient-reported outcome measures on a common latent scale) and a multi-group multivariate higher-order IRT model for linking individual participant data from multiple studies (PMC6582193). Latent-variable linking of different instruments is therefore an established methodology in integrative data analysis, not merely a ‘proposed remedy’; what is missing is its integration into a network/population-adjusted synthesis, and the co-administration data needed to fit it. The SMD half is better supported: I retrieved ‘Standardized Mean Differences: Not So Standard After All’ (PMC12358740) and Hopkins, ‘Standardization and other approaches to meta-analyze differences in means’ (Stat Med 2024, doi 10.1002/sim.10114), which document that the standardiser is a population property so SMDs vary with within-study SD variability. I found no formal transport theory for the SMD scale, so that specific gap stands. Cites https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5069858/: Shows latent-variable/IRT linking of different PRO instruments onto a common metric is an existing, deployed methodology, so the cross-instrument problem is not unaddressed outside PAIC.. Cites https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6582193/: Retrospectively establishes a common metric across independently conducted studies with different items, i.e. the measurement-model half of the proposed direction, in the IPD-synthesis setting..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C2, C3, and C5 are sound. A simple rescaling is sufficient only when instruments are defensibly affine-equivalent and measurement-invariant. A latent-variable link requires anchor items, co-administration, calibration data, or other identifying restrictions. The SMD’s transport behavior is not mathematically undefined: it is a mean difference divided by a specified reference standard deviation, so changing the population or denominator changes the estimand. The genuine problem is selecting and identifying a scientifically meaningful common scale. C6’s claim about an accepted convention is a literature-consensus claim outside this lens; technically, no unique denominator is compelled, and pooled, control-arm, baseline, external-reference, and target-population SDs define different quantities. The proposed native-scale fallback cannot create a common metric across different instruments without a mapping. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, Gaussian IPD analyses accept MD only and explicitly reject SMD, so no cross-instrument PAIC path exists. High priority is proportionate only for networks that actually mix non-equivalent instruments.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text: OUT-06 Overstated Medium-high priority Promising

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Statement
Mixing endpoint and change-score results in a population-adjusted comparison is an estimand and variance-handling choice rather than an unprincipled conversion: the change-score treatment contrast equals the endpoint contrast minus the baseline contrast, and the baseline-endpoint correlation is required for the variance of a change score, not for its mean contrast. Under randomization the baseline contrast is zero in expectation, so endpoint and change analyses can target the same follow-up effect, and meta-epidemiological work across 21 meta-analyses, 189 trials and 41,256 patients found combining them in conventional meta-analysis generally valid, with a mean difference in standardized mean differences of -0.04 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06) (pmid:23747228). What remains unresolved is the adjustment step: baseline severity is often itself an effect modifier and regression to the mean acts differently in populations with different baseline distributions, and neither target-standardized mean trajectories nor latent-model responder probabilities has an established population-adjusted formulation.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Why it is open
The unresolved part is the population-adjustment step rather than the combination itself: where baseline severity modifies the effect, change and endpoint analyses can imply different effect-modification structures, so the representation interacts with the adjustment instead of being a fixed offset. Trials measure the outcome repeatedly and on several scales, and joint repeated-measures models need compatible time definitions and within-trial covariances that aggregate publications do not report. Target-standardized trajectories and model-derived responder probabilities are optional estimands with no established formulation under population adjustment, and dichotomizing a reported mean remains invalid without the outcome distribution. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, models one Gaussian outcome and a raw mean difference with no trajectory or responder path.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Prespecify whether the analysis uses change or endpoint data, following the meta-epidemiological guidance, and handle the variance correctly rather than converting between representations by ad hoc rescaling. Where baseline severity is a plausible effect modifier or more than one timepoint matters, model baseline and follow-up jointly so the adjustment and the estimand stay consistent. Treat target-standardized trajectories and responder probabilities as declared optional estimands, deriving responder probabilities from directly standardized individual-level indicators where individual patient data allow it and from a latent model only where they do not, and keep a prespecified decision-relevant timepoint alongside any trajectory.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. In population-adjusted comparisons the change-versus-endpoint representation is an estimand choice that interacts with baseline severity as an effect modifier, and neither target-standardised mean trajectories nor latent-model responder probabilities have an established formulation; empirical meta-epidemiological work finds that simply combining change and follow-up estimates in conventional meta-analysis is generally valid, so the unresolved part is the adjustment step, not the combination itself.
The source said. “Continuous outcomes in population-adjusted comparisons are reduced to a single-timepoint summary that is sometimes a change from baseline and sometimes an endpoint value, combined without a principled conversion. The report instead calls for target-standardized mean trajectories, multivariate models for repeated measures and multiple scales, and responder probabilities derived from a latent outcome model.”
What was wrong with it. The source treated change-versus-endpoint combination as unresolved and said conversion between them requires the baseline-endpoint correlation; the literature auditor produced da Costa et al. (pmid:23747228, doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.03.009), which finds combining them generally valid and recommends prespecifying which is used, and the code auditor showed the correlation claim is mathematically wrong as written, since the correlation governs the variance rather than the mean contrast. The code auditor also rejected the claim that responder probabilities must come from a latent continuous model, because with individual patient data responder indicators can be formed and standardized directly.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. Retrieved da Costa et al., ‘Combining follow-up and change data is valid in meta-analyses of continuous outcomes: a meta-epidemiological study’ (J Clin Epidemiol 2013; PMID 23747228; doi 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.03.009), 21 meta-analyses, 189 trials, 41,256 patients. It directly addresses the change-versus-endpoint question the entry frames as unresolved and concludes combining them is generally valid, with a mean difference in SMDs of only -0.04 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06). The entry’s framing that the two are ‘combined without a principled conversion’ therefore overstates the problem for conventional synthesis; the empirically supported guidance is to prespecify which is used. What remains genuinely open is the population-adjustment-specific part: baseline severity as an effect modifier, regression to the mean differing across covariate distributions, and target-standardised mean trajectories or latent-model responder probabilities, none of which da Costa addresses and for which I found no PAIC literature.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2 is mathematically wrong as written. The treatment contrast in change is the endpoint contrast minus the baseline contrast; baseline-endpoint correlation is required to recover the variance or standard error of a change score, not its mean contrast. Under randomization the baseline contrast is zero in expectation, so endpoint and change analyses can target the same follow-up treatment effect, although finite-sample imbalance, baseline adjustment, and effect modification can matter in PAIC. C3 is therefore possible rather than inevitable. C4 and C6 are reasonable research outputs, but trajectories need not replace a prespecified decision-relevant timepoint and multivariate models require compatible time definitions and covariance information. C5 is right that a reported mean cannot be dichotomized into a responder probability, but a latent continuous model is not the only valid route: with IPD, responder indicators can be formed and standardized directly, while a latent-tail calculation adds distributional assumptions. cpaic currently models one Gaussian outcome and raw MD, with no trajectory or responder path. The unresolved PAIC-specific extensions are real, but the change-versus-endpoint issue and the Medium-high severity are overstated as universal problems.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text: OUT-08 Unverifiable High priority Emerging Tractability 2/5

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Statement
The population-adjusted implementations the auditors checked fit Poisson models for counts and offer no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle, zero-inflated, recurrent-event or frailty family, so those options are unavailable rather than merely uncommon. The consequence is narrower than the source said: where the conditional mean is correctly specified the Poisson estimating score remains unbiased under negative-binomial variance, so residual overdispersion invalidates likelihood-based uncertainty while leaving rate-ratio point estimates consistent, and transport bias instead requires misspecification of the conditional mean, the zero mechanism, the frailty or the exposure weighting. Time to first event and total event burden remain different estimands that can move in different directions, and general count meta-analysis evidence shows pooled effects and precision differ by whether a rate ratio, Poisson, negative-binomial, dichotomized risk ratio or time-to-first-event analysis is used (doi:10.1186/s13643-015-0144-x). The two auditors disagreed about how much of the source’s mechanism survives, and that disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Why it is open
No population-adjusted implementation the auditors checked offers an overdispersed, zero-inflated or recurrent-event likelihood, so an analyst facing exacerbation or relapse counts either accepts Poisson uncertainty or leaves the population-adjusted framework. On the survival side, transporting a recurrent-event effect requires transporting a frailty distribution that is itself population-dependent, and aggregate-data trials report first-event Kaplan-Meier curves or annualized rates rather than the full event history, so the joint and dispersion structure cannot be recovered from what is published. A structural-zero subgroup makes the population a mixture whose mixing proportion can vary across trial populations, which is a transport problem and not only a fitting problem. Whether the closed-form-likelihood barrier that blocks non-standard count likelihoods in ML-NMR has already been removed is an open question the literature auditor flagged but did not check.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend component ML-NMR to negative-binomial and Poisson-lognormal likelihoods so overdispersion is modeled rather than left to invalidate the reported interval, and add hurdle and zero-inflated formulations whose zero and count components are permitted, not required, to carry different effect-modification structure. Develop recurrent-event and joint frailty models for population-adjusted network synthesis so total burden and time to first event can both be estimated and standardized to the target population, and connect them to the count models for the same underlying process. Check the lead the literature auditor named but did not read, Bayesian synthetic likelihood for multilevel network meta-regression (arxiv:2603.11019), before rebuilding integration machinery, since if it does what its title says it removes the closed-form-likelihood constraint.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Repeated clinical events such as exacerbations or relapses are analyzed either as Poisson counts, which forces variance to equal the mean and ignores excess zeros, or as time to first event, which discards the recurrent process entirely. Neither negative-binomial and zero-inflated component ML-NMR nor recurrent-event and joint frailty models exist for population-adjusted network synthesis.”
What was wrong with it. The source said a mis-specified count likelihood distorts the transported effect and not only its standard error; the code auditor showed this is false as a general rule, since a correctly specified conditional mean leaves Poisson point estimates consistent under overdispersion. The same auditor narrowed the claim that Poisson is too restrictive to cases with observed residual conditional overdispersion, and rejected the claim that hurdle and zero-inflated formulations require separate effect-modification structure, since those coefficients may be constrained, shared or omitted in one component; the literature auditor judged the entry supported, so the adjudicated verdict is unverifiable with both positions on the record.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): At the requested cpaic revision, cmlnmr() accepts only binomial, Gaussian, Poisson, and survival families. NAMESPACE and the Stan models contain no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle, zero-inflated, recurrent-event, or frailty path. The core cpaic gap is therefore open, and C6-C7 correctly distinguish first recurrence from total burden. However, C1 needs observed residual conditional overdispersion; Poisson is not universally too restrictive. C3 is false as a general rule: when the conditional mean is correctly specified, the Poisson estimating score can remain unbiased under negative-binomial variance, leaving point effects consistent while model-based uncertainty is wrong. Transport bias requires misspecification of the conditional mean, zero mechanism, frailty, or exposure weighting. C5 also overstates necessity: hurdle and zero-inflated models have two predictors, but their effect-modifier coefficients may be constrained, shared, or omitted in one component. C8-C9 are universal prevalence or absence claims not established by cpaic source inspection.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Verified from the multinma nma() reference that the supported count/rate likelihoods are binomial, bernoulli, poisson and normal plus the survival families, with no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle or zero-inflated option, so ‘proposed but not yet available’ is accurate for the leading ML-NMR implementation. The general count-meta-analysis literature supports the Poisson-restriction claim: ‘Do alternative methods for analysing count data produce similar estimates? Implications for meta-analyses’ (doi 10.1186/s13643-015-0144-x) shows precision and pooled effects differ by whether rate ratio, Poisson, negative binomial, dichotomised risk ratio or time-to-first-event is used, which also supports the claim that time to first event and total burden are different estimands. I found no recurrent-event or joint-frailty model for population-adjusted network synthesis. One lead worth watching that I did not read: arXiv 2603.11019, ‘Don’t Disregard the Data for Lack of a Likelihood: Bayesian Synthetic Likelihood for Enhanced Multilevel Network Meta-Regression’, which if it does what its title says would remove the closed-form-likelihood barrier for non-standard count likelihoods in ML-NMR.

NAMESPACE and the Stan models contain no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle, zero-inflated, recurrent-event, or frailty path. The core cpaic gap is therefore open, and C6-C7 correctly distinguish first recurrence from total burden. C3 is false as a general rule: when the conditional mean is correctly specified, the Poisson estimating score can remain unbiased under negative-binomial variance, leaving point effects consistent while model-based uncertainty is wrong. C5 also overstates necessity: hurdle and zero-inflated models have two predictors, but their effect-modifier coefficients may be constrained, shared, or omitted in one component. title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text: OUT-10 Overstated High priority Emerging

title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Statement
Population-adjusted ordinal synthesis already exists and target-standardized category probabilities are already produced: multinma ships ordered multinomial models through the multi() helper, and its predict() method averages over the target population by integrating over the joint covariate distribution or by averaging predictions for a sample of individuals. This is not hypothetical; Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) fit ordered PASI 75, 90 and 100 outcomes by ML-NMR and report the estimated percentage achieving each endpoint on each treatment in external target populations, under proportional odds. What remains undeveloped is the relaxation half, namely partial proportional odds, adjacent-category and continuation-ratio models in a population-adjusted network, and decision analyses that combine joint category-probability draws with explicitly specified and possibly uncertain utilities.

title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Why it is open
Proportional odds imposes one treatment coefficient across all cut-points, and a treatment may shift patients out of the worst category without changing the top of the scale; threshold-specific conditional effects can differ, and even a conditional proportional-odds model yields population-dependent marginal odds ratios through non-collapsibility. Aggregate-data publications often report a dichotomized version or a single ordinal odds ratio, so the cut-point-specific pattern needed to test the assumption is unavailable. Utility weights usually come from a preference source outside the trials, though they can also be elicited within a trial, and their uncertainty and cross-population variation add a second transport problem on top of estimation uncertainty. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, has no ordinal family at all, so non-proportional ordinal component PAIC is unavailable there.

text:

title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build partial proportional odds, adjacent-category and continuation-ratio models for population-adjusted ordinal synthesis on top of the ordered multinomial machinery that already works, rather than rebuilding target-standardized category probabilities. Because joint posterior category probabilities already exist, utility-weighted estimands are largely posterior post-processing, so the work is in specifying and propagating preference uncertainty and in handling preference transport between source and target populations. Add an ordinal family to component PAIC implementations that lack one.

title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Population-adjusted ordinal synthesis exists and target-standardised category probabilities are already produced by multinma and reported in the published plaque-psoriasis ML-NMR application, but that work assumes proportional odds; relaxations that let cut-point-specific and treatment-specific departures be represented, and utility-weighted ordinal estimands with utility uncertainty propagated, remain undeveloped.
The source said. “Ordinal endpoints are common in trials but underdeveloped in population-adjusted comparison: proportional odds can fail differently by treatment and by population, results are reported as a single transported ordinal odds ratio rather than as target-standardized category probabilities, and no framework attaches explicit category utilities to produce a decision-relevant scalar.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed no established PAIC implementation returns target-standardized ordinal category probabilities; both auditors found this false, citing multinma’s ordered multinomial models with the multi() helper and the published plaque-psoriasis ML-NMR application (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162, PMID 35997006). The auditors dated the multinma feature differently, the literature auditor to the 0.6.0 release notes and the code auditor to 0.2.0, and that discrepancy is left standing; the code auditor also corrected two side claims, that an ordinal odds ratio plus the target covariate distribution still does not identify absolute category probabilities without comparator cut-points or baseline category probabilities, and that not every scalar summary implies fixed implicit category utilities, since medians, cumulative odds ratios and probabilities of superiority are nonlinear functionals.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim ‘No established PAIC implementation currently returns target-standardized ordinal category probabilities’ is false. multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24) added ordered multinomial models via the multi() helper, and predict.stan_nma produces absolute predictions ‘averaged over the target population (i.e. standardised/marginalised), either by (numerical) integration over the joint covariate distribution or by averaging predictions for a sample of individuals’. This capability is not hypothetical: Phillippo et al., ‘Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis’ (Med Decis Making 2023, doi 10.1177/0272989X221117162, PMID 35997006) fits ordered PASI 75/90/100 outcomes by ML-NMR and reports the estimated percentage achieving each PASI endpoint on each treatment in external target populations. What remains genuinely open is the model-relaxation half (partial proportional odds, adjacent-category, continuation-ratio in a population-adjusted network) and utility-weighted ordinal estimands with propagated utility uncertainty; I found nothing on either. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162: Published ML-NMR with an ordered multinomial outcome producing category probabilities standardised to external target populations, contradicting the claim that no established PAIC implementation returns them.. Cites repo:dmphillippo/multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24): Ships ordered multinomial ML-NMR with the multi() helper; predict() marginalises over the target covariate distribution..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C2-C3 are defensible after distinguishing conditional from marginal proportional odds: threshold-specific conditional effects may differ, while even a conditional proportional-odds model can yield population-dependent marginal odds ratios through non-collapsibility. C6 is incomplete because an ordinal odds ratio plus the target covariate distribution still does not identify absolute category probabilities without comparator cut-points or baseline category probabilities. C7 is false: ordered multinomial ML-NMR and target-standardized category predictions already exist in multinma and have been used in the cited psoriasis application. C9 is mathematically sloppy. An expected-utility estimand uses explicit category weights, but medians, cumulative odds ratios, and probabilities of superiority are nonlinear scalar functionals rather than fixed implicit utility weights. C10 is also too categorical because utilities can be elicited within a trial. Once joint posterior category probabilities exist, utility-weighted outcomes are straightforward posterior post-processing, although preference uncertainty and transport may still matter. cpaic itself has no ordinal family, so non-proportional ordinal component PAIC remains open there. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162: Demonstrates ordered-outcome ML-NMR with estimated category-specific response percentages in external target populations.. Cites CRAN:multinma@0.2.0: Implements ordered multinomial outcomes through multi(), contradicting the claimed absence of an established ordinal PAIC implementation..

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text: OUT-12 Not supported High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Statement
Flexible study-specific baseline hazards for survival ML-NMR are not open. The paper this entry cited as prior work develops them, proposing M-splines for the baseline hazard, stratifying the baseline by study to respect randomization, and controlling the resulting nuisance parameters with a weighted random-walk prior on the inverse-softmax transformed spline coefficients so the analyst can choose a large enough number of knots and let the model shrink to appropriate complexity; multinma and cpaic both implement study-stratified flexible baselines with shared smoothing. What is open is that survival beyond the observed support is not identified, so the chosen tail model rather than the data drives extrapolation, and observed-window fit statistics cannot separate models that are observationally equivalent or nearly equivalent on that support. Mixture-cure network meta-analysis exists for the unadjusted case (Chan et al., doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10038, PMID 41626893) and has not been connected to population adjustment or to component treatment models.

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Why it is open
Beyond the last observed event time the survival function is not identified, so parametric families that fit the observed period equally well diverge afterwards and no fit statistic computed on that window can choose between them; this is assumption management rather than something more data of the same kind can settle. Population adjustment adds a layer because the extrapolation is performed in a target population whose long-term covariate-outcome relationship was never observed, and baseline flexibility, non-proportional hazards and cure structure change the tail interactively. Mixture-cure models split the population into cured and uncured fractions that depend on covariates differently, so the cure fraction and the uncured survival distribution would have to be transported separately, and neither multinma nor cpaic has a cure family or a component-cure path.

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton 2025, Multilevel network meta-regression for general likelihoods: synthesis of individual and aggregate data with applications to survival analysis, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
proposes M-splines to model the baseline hazard flexibly over time, stratifies the baseline hazard by study to respect randomization, and uses a weighted random-walk prior on the transformed spline coefficients to control smoothing and shrinkage in small networks; this is the capability the entry listed as open


Chan et al. 2026, mixture-cure network meta-analysis in resected stage III/IV melanoma, Research Synthesis Methods (PMID 41626893)
incorporates the possibility of cure into network meta-analysis of recurrence-free survival in a resected melanoma case study; it does not involve population adjustment or component treatment models


multinma (CRAN) 0.6.0, flexible study-stratified survival models
implements flexible M-spline and piecewise-exponential hazards with auxiliary parameters such as shapes and spline coefficients always stratified by study to respect randomization


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
cmlnmr() offers piecewise-exponential and continuous cubic M-spline baselines, gives every study its own spline or step coefficients smoothed toward a common shape by a shared random-walk scale, and has no cure family or component-cure path

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not rebuild flexible study-specific baselines; instead assess how the baseline choice that is already available drives extrapolation, and report the data-supported horizon separately from the extrapolated portion with the tail treated as a declared assumption carrying its own sensitivity analysis. Connect mixture-cure network meta-analysis to population adjustment and component models so that both the cure fraction and the uncured survival distribution can be transported and can depend on treatment components. Where follow-up is short, state that the cure fraction rests on parametric assumptions rather than on empirical separation from a long uncured tail.

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Verification

Verdict. Not supported. No accessible source substantiates the claim as stated.
The source titled this. “Baseline hazard flexibility, cure fractions, and extrapolation” The title lists flexible baseline hazards as open, which the entry’s own cited paper develops and which multinma implements.
The source said. “Health technology assessment needs lifetime survival, so population-adjusted survival results are extrapolated far beyond observed follow-up, where the answer comes from the parametric assumption rather than the data. Flexible study-specific baseline hazards remain an open problem for survival ML-NMR even after the 2025 general-likelihood extension, and mixture-cure network meta-analysis has only begun to develop and has not been connected to population adjustment or component models.”
What was wrong with it. The lead claim, that flexible study-specific baseline hazards remain open for survival ML-NMR after the 2025 general-likelihood extension, is contradicted by the paper the entry itself cites: Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169) stratify the baseline hazard by study and propose M-splines with a shrinkage random-walk prior, which is this entry’s own proposed direction. The code auditor found the same capability implemented in multinma 0.6.0 and at commit 9d150e9 in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, and narrowed two supporting claims: observed-window fit statistics do discriminate models that fit the observed data differently, and a cure fraction can be estimated under shorter follow-up through strong parametric assumptions, so it is empirical separation of cure from a long uncured tail that needs mature follow-up.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is directly false at the requested cpaic revision. cmlnmr() offers piecewise-exponential and continuous cubic M-spline baselines, gives every study separate baseline coefficients, and applies shared random-walk smoothing. multinma likewise supplies study-stratified flexible baselines. C2-C5 are otherwise sound: data do not identify survival beyond observed support, so the chosen tail model drives extrapolation. C6 needs its omitted condition. Observed-window fit statistics can distinguish models that fit the observed data differently; they cannot validate different tails when models are observationally equivalent or nearly equivalent on the observed support. cpaic has no cure family or component-cure path, so connecting cure and uncured components to PAIC remains open. C9 is a plausible model, not a necessity. C10 is too categorical: a cure fraction can be estimated under shorter follow-up only through strong parametric assumptions, while empirical separation of cure from a long uncured tail requires sufficiently mature follow-up, not necessarily follow-up longer than most trials. Extrapolation is an assumption-management problem rather than a capability that data alone can solve.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text: OUT-14 Overstated High priority Emerging

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Statement
Population-adjusted survival likelihoods do represent this structure: multinma has supported left, right and interval censoring and left truncation for survival outcomes since 0.6.0, and cpaic’s exact survival likelihood supports observed events, right, left and interval censoring and delayed entry for both individual and aggregate pseudo-patient rows when those fields are supplied. What survives is an information problem rather than a likelihood problem: pseudo individual data reconstructed from a published right-censored Kaplan-Meier curve cannot express delayed entry or interval censoring, because the publication does not report entry times or assessment intervals. Assessment schedules are design features that patient-level covariate balancing cannot correct, though they can be represented in the observation model or, with enough studies, modeled at study level. Once an outcome is dichotomized into an event-by-time proportion the follow-up length and assessment grid disappear from the reported number, and there is no method for placing binary endpoints from trials with different windows on a common time scale.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Why it is open
The capability exists but the inputs often do not, so an analysis built on reconstructed pseudo individual data silently reverts to complete follow-up with exactly observed event times, because reconstruction cannot recover information absent from the publication. Interval censoring induced by different assessment grids coarsens event times differently across trials, and substituting exact times for interval-censored ones can shift progression-type curves in a way that resembles a treatment effect. Different maximum follow-up means trials identify the survival function over different ranges, so any common summary requires either truncation to the shortest window or extrapolation, and each choice changes the estimand. Cross-trial binary event-by-time proportions remain non-comparable when the windows differ, and covariate balancing cannot repair a difference that arises purely from follow-up length.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows

Work
What it contributes




multinma (CRAN) 0.6.0, survival models with censoring and truncation support
its release notes list left, right and interval censoring and left truncation as supported, and its set_ipd() reference states that right, left and interval censoring and left truncation, that is delayed entry, are supported for survival outcomes specified with Surv()

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use the censoring and truncation support that already exists by carrying entry times and assessment intervals into the analysis data rather than accepting reconstruction defaults, and say when an analysis has silently reverted to exactly observed event times. Choose a primary horizon supported by all contributing trials and declare anything beyond it as extrapolation. Develop the missing piece, which is treating a binary event-by-time endpoint as a coarsening of a time-to-event process so endpoints from trials with different windows can be placed on a common time scale, and model assessment timing jointly only where that timing is plausibly informative.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Delayed entry and interval censoring are supported in population-adjusted survival likelihoods (multinma implements right, left and interval censoring and left truncation), but reconstructed pseudo-IPD from published curves cannot express them, differing assessment grids and follow-up windows are design features that covariate adjustment cannot balance, and there is no method for putting binary endpoints from trials with different windows on a common time scale.
The source titled this. “Delayed entry, interval censoring, and differing follow-up windows” The title lists delayed entry and interval censoring as unrepresented, but population-adjusted survival likelihoods have supported left truncation and interval censoring since multinma 0.6.0.
The source said. “Trials in a network observe patients over different windows and on different assessment grids, with delayed entry and interval-censored endpoints such as radiologically assessed progression; the same heterogeneity is hidden entirely when the endpoint is reported as a binary event-by-time-t proportion. Population-adjusted likelihoods do not represent any of this structure.”
What was wrong with it. The statement that population-adjusted likelihoods do not represent any of this structure is false; the literature auditor cited multinma’s release notes and set_ipd() documentation for left, right and interval censoring and left truncation, and the code auditor found the same support at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN. The code auditor also narrowed two claims: differing follow-up under independent censoring is handled by an appropriate survival likelihood, so what remains is unsupported horizons and estimand alignment, and joint modeling of assessment timing is warranted where the timing is informative, whereas a known noninformative grid needs only an interval-censored likelihood.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim ‘Population-adjusted likelihoods do not represent any of this structure’ is false. multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24) lists ‘Left/right/interval censoring and left truncation supported’ among the new survival features, and the set_ipd() reference states that right, left and interval censoring and left truncation (delayed entry) are supported for survival outcomes specified with Surv(). So delayed entry and interval censoring are already representable in the leading ML-NMR implementation, for both the individual-level likelihood and, via the general-likelihood integration, the aggregate side. Two claims survive intact and are the defensible core: reconstructed pseudo-IPD from published Kaplan-Meier curves cannot represent left truncation or interval censoring (the Guyot-style algorithm assumes right censoring only), and assessment schedules are design features that no covariate adjustment can balance. I found no work on placing binary endpoints from trials with different follow-up windows on a common time scale by joint modelling of assessment timing and event status, so that part is genuinely open. Cites repo:dmphillippo/multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24): Population-adjusted survival likelihoods that do represent interval censoring and delayed entry..

partially-solved / overstated. The blanket statement and C1 are false. At the requested cpaic revision, the exact survival likelihood explicitly represents observed events, right, left, and interval censoring, plus delayed entry, for both IPD and aggregate pseudo-patient rows when those fields are supplied. multinma also supports these structures. C3 remains correct only for conventional pseudo-IPD reconstructed from a published right-censored Kaplan-Meier curve that does not report entry or assessment intervals; the likelihood can represent the structures, but reconstruction cannot recover information absent from the publication. C2 is also too broad: differing follow-up under independent censoring is handled by an appropriate survival likelihood, although unsupported horizons and binary endpoints measured at different times remain estimand problems. C4-C5 are sound when exact event times are naively substituted for interval-censored times. C6 is true only of patient-level covariate balancing; assessment schedule can be represented as a design feature in the observation model or, with adequate studies, modeled at study level. C7-C8 are correct. C9 is warranted when assessment timing is informative, but a known noninformative grid needs only an interval-censored likelihood, not necessarily a joint timing model. title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text: OUT-16 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 2/5

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text:
Statement
A treatment may reduce progression while increasing competing mortality, and where the analysis collapses to a single endpoint that trade-off is not visible; a composite endpoint may still reflect the net first-event effect while obscuring which cause moved. The mathematical core holds: the cumulative incidence for a cause integrates that cause-specific hazard against event-free survival, which depends on the cumulative hazards of every cause, so transporting one cause-specific effect cannot determine target absolute risk without target-standardized baseline hazards for all causes. The converse is the qualification the source omitted, since transporting the complete set of cause-specific hazards does determine the cumulative incidence. Neither auditor found any population-adjusted method for competing risks or cumulative incidence, and the general causal literature makes the same transportability point (doi:10.1002/bimj.70153).

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text:
Why it is open
Cause-specific hazards and cumulative incidence functions answer different questions, and population adjustment changes the competing-risk mix because the target population has different background mortality, so the direction of net benefit can flip between populations. Aggregate-data publications typically report a single composite or a single cause without the competing-event information needed to reconstruct cumulative incidence, so the full set of cause-specific hazards is unavailable on the comparator side. A composite, an all-cause first event, a cause-specific hazard and a cumulative incidence are distinct estimands, so collapsing to one endpoint changes the question rather than simplifying the answer. The mechanism is well understood outside evidence synthesis and simply has not been composed with population adjustment.
